pools.title: The Question, the Lamprey, and the Cambrian
pools.covers: reading §6.0 (the unnumbered Opening), §6.1.1, §6.1.2 · lecture 6.1 slides title, meet_the_lamprey, two_seafloors, food_stopped_lying_still

items.stem: Earlier modules asked what a neuron is and what a circuit does. What new kind of question does this module ask about a brain?

options.text: Why a brain is divided into separate parts at all, and when having separate structures is favored.
options.why: Correct. The module is about the parts a vertebrate brain is made of, and its first question is when separate structures are favored at all, and why.

options.text: How a single neuron decides whether to fire, now that a vertebrate brain holds billions of neurons.
options.why: Whether a neuron fires was a question about one cell. This module takes cells and circuits as given and asks about an arrangement of parts.

options.text: Which of the brain’s parts first learned from experience, since vertebrates were the first animals that could learn.
options.why: Learning is older than the vertebrates; it runs in the worm of Modules 4 and 5. The new question is about dividing the work among parts.

options.text: How the human brain differs from every other brain, since the human brain is the one the module is ultimately about.
options.why: The module is read against a lamprey, and it asks about parts that most vertebrate brains share, not about what makes the human brain unique.

items.stem: All four kinds of learning in Module 5 ran on one principle, in the same kind of tissue, wherever there were synapses. Why does the chapter treat that generality as a problem rather than only as an achievement?

options.text: A principle general enough to be reused anywhere is, for that very reason, specialized for nothing.
options.why: Correct. One set of machinery was doing every job, and the price of being usable everywhere is not being tuned for anything in particular.

options.text: A principle that runs wherever there are synapses would make every synapse change at once, so nothing could stay stable.
options.why: The chapter does worry about stability, but not on these grounds. Its complaint about the general principle is that it is tuned for nothing in particular.

options.text: A principle shared by four kinds of learning would make the four kinds impossible to tell apart in any experiment.
options.why: Module 5 told the four kinds apart by what information reaches the synapse, so they are distinguishable. The problem raised here is specialization.

options.text: A principle that works in the same kind of tissue everywhere is too expensive to run for an animal with many neurons.
options.why: Cost matters later in the chapter, but it is charged per neuron, not to the generality of a learning rule. The problem here is that a general rule is specialized for nothing.

items.stem: Suppose a nervous system does everything in one place, with one set of machinery. Which two costs does the chapter say that arrangement risks?

options.text: It may not be very good at any one thing, and it may struggle to do two incompatible things at once.
options.why: Correct. Those are the two costs of doing everything in one place, and they are what make separate structures worth considering at all.

options.text: It will use more energy than a divided brain, and it will need more wiring to connect its parts together.
options.why: Energy and wiring are the costs the chapter charges to separate structures, not to doing everything in one place.

options.text: It cannot learn anything new, and it cannot keep anything it has already learned for more than a short time.
options.why: A single general mechanism can learn; Module 5 showed four kinds of learning running on one. The costs named here are about specialization.

options.text: It will fire too slowly to steer the body, and it will lose track of the senses whenever the animal moves.
options.why: Neither speed nor tracking is the chapter’s point here. The costs are being good at nothing in particular and struggling with incompatible jobs.

items.stem: Why is the nematode of Modules 4 and 5 a poor candidate for dividing its nervous system into separate specialist parts?

options.text: With only 302 neurons in its whole body, it has little to divide; setting neurons aside for separate jobs needs many of them.
options.why: Correct. Dividing the work requires something to divide, and an animal with vastly more neurons can set some aside for one job and others for another.

options.text: Its neurons cannot change their weights, so no part of its nervous system could ever become specialized for a single job.
options.why: The worm does learn, as Module 5 established. The obstacle here is how few neurons there are, not whether they can change.

options.text: It lives in a world with no predators, so there are no conflicting demands for separate parts to resolve in it.
options.why: The worm meets several demands, one at a time. The chapter’s point about it is that 302 neurons offer little to divide.

options.text: Its body has no head, so there is no single place at the front where specialist parts could be gathered together.
options.why: The worm is a bilaterian, with neurons gathered toward the front as Module 4 described. What it lacks is enough neurons to set aside for separate jobs.

items.stem: If one mechanism doing everything is specialized for nothing, why is it still “not obvious” that separate parts are the better arrangement?

options.text: Separate parts need wiring between them, and some way of settling what happens when they disagree.
options.why: Correct. Splitting the work is never free. The connections between parts and a way of resolving their disagreements are the costs the chapter names.

options.text: Separate parts cannot learn, so dividing the work would give up everything the general mechanism made possible.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter says separate parts lose the ability to learn. The costs it names are connection and conflict.

options.text: Separate parts evolve more slowly, so a lineage that divided its brain would fall behind one that kept a single mechanism.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim about evolutionary speed. The trouble with separate parts is that they must be wired together and their disagreements settled.

options.text: Separate parts must each sit next to the sense they serve, so they would be scattered through the body instead of gathered.
options.why: The chapter later argues for exactly the opposite placement, specialists gathered in one organ. Placement is not the cost named here.

items.stem: The chapter promises that in this module the three levels behave differently from each other for the first time. What is the pattern it promises?

options.text: One level stands almost still while another is rebuilt again and again on top of it.
options.why: Correct. That is the new thing about this module: the levels come apart, one nearly fixed while another is remade repeatedly.

options.text: All three levels change together, each new structure bringing a new problem, a new procedure and new tissue at once.
options.why: That is the lockstep picture the module is promised to break. One level barely moves while another is rebuilt.

options.text: The levels swap places, so that what was a problem in earlier modules becomes a physical mechanism in this one.
options.why: The levels keep their meanings throughout the course. What changes is that they stop moving in step with one another.

options.text: Only one level applies to brains, because a brain divided into parts can be described at the implementational level alone.
options.why: All three levels apply, and the module uses all three. The new pattern is that one of them stands almost still while another changes.

items.stem: An eel-shaped fish is pulled from a river. It has no paired fins, and at the front, in place of a jaw, it has a round disc lined with small hard teeth. What is it most likely to be?

options.text: A lamprey, which swims by a wave down its whole body and has a toothed sucking disc where a jaw would be.
options.why: Correct. A lamprey looks at first like an eel, and the difference is at the front: no jaws, and a round sucking disc lined with small, hard teeth.

options.text: An eel, since eels are long and slender, lack paired fins, and grip their prey with a disc of small teeth.
options.why: An eel has jaws. The toothed disc in place of a jaw is exactly what tells a lamprey from an eel.

options.text: A nematode, since nematodes also swim by sending a wave down the whole body and feed on the blood of fishes.
options.why: The body wave is similar, but a nematode is not a fish and has no disc of teeth. The animal described is a vertebrate.

options.text: A shark, since sharks are jawless cartilaginous fishes whose mouths hold rows of small, hard, replaceable teeth.
options.why: Sharks have jaws; they are among the jawed fishes. Only lampreys and hagfishes survive as jawless fishes.

items.stem: How does an adult sea lamprey feed?

options.text: It fastens its sucking disc to the side of a larger fish and draws off the fish’s blood.
options.why: Correct. With no jaws to bite, the adult attaches by its toothed disc and feeds on blood.

options.text: It filters small animals out of the water by pumping it through the gill openings behind its head.
options.why: Filtering is how some early armored jawless fishes probably fed. The adult sea lamprey feeds on the blood of larger fishes.

options.text: It seizes small fish with its jaws and swallows them whole, then digests them slowly in the gut.
options.why: A lamprey has no jaws. In place of a jaw it has a sucking disc, and it uses the disc to feed on blood.

options.text: It scrapes microbial mats off the riverbed with the teeth of its disc, much as an early crawler did.
options.why: Scraping a microbial mat is how Kimberella is thought to have fed. The adult sea lamprey attaches to a larger fish.

items.stem: Which of these animals are vertebrates: a sea lamprey, a hagfish, a frog, a sparrow, and an octopus?

options.text: The lamprey, the hagfish, the frog and the sparrow, but not the octopus.
options.why: Correct. A vertebrate has a skull and a backbone, or at least the beginnings of one. Fish, including the jawless ones, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals all qualify; an octopus does not.

options.text: The frog and the sparrow, but not the lamprey or the hagfish, which lack jaws, nor the octopus.
options.why: Lacking jaws does not exclude an animal. Lampreys and hagfishes are vertebrates; they are the jawless ones.

options.text: All five of them, since each has a brain at the front of the body and a nervous system running back from it.
options.why: Having a brain at the front does not make an animal a vertebrate. The octopus has a large brain and no backbone.

options.text: The sparrow alone, since only birds and mammals have a true backbone rather than the beginnings of one.
options.why: Every fish, amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal is a vertebrate, and the beginnings of a backbone are enough.

items.stem: What makes lampreys and hagfishes unusual among living vertebrates?

options.text: They are the only jawless fishes still alive, and their branch was the first to separate from the rest of the living vertebrates.
options.why: Correct. Their branch split off more than 500 million years ago, before any other living vertebrate lineage separated.

options.text: They are the only vertebrates without a skull, which is why they are sometimes placed outside the vertebrates altogether by anatomists.
options.why: Lampreys and hagfishes are vertebrates. What sets them apart is that they have no jaws, not that they have no skull.

options.text: They are the only fishes that live in both fresh and salt water, and their branch was the last to leave the sea.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim about water. What sets their branch apart is how early it split from the other living vertebrates.

options.text: They are the direct ancestors of the jawed fishes, and the rest of the living vertebrates descend from lampreys.
options.why: No living animal is an ancestor of another. Lampreys are modern animals whose lineage split from ours long ago.

items.stem: A classmate says, “Studying a lamprey is studying our ancestor, frozen in time”. What is wrong with that statement?

options.text: A living lamprey is a modern animal whose lineage has been evolving for exactly as long as the lineage that led to human beings.
options.why: Correct. Living lampreys are not ancestors of anything. What makes them useful is an inference about what their brains and ours share, not a claim that they stopped changing.

options.text: A lamprey is not a vertebrate, so nothing about its brain could tell us anything at all about the human brain’s history.
options.why: Lampreys are vertebrates, which is why they are useful. The problem with the statement is calling a living animal an ancestor.

options.text: A lamprey is our ancestor, but it has changed so much in half a billion years that it is no longer useful evidence about anything.
options.why: A lamprey is not our ancestor at all. Its lineage and ours share a common ancestor from which both descend.

options.text: A lamprey split from the rest of the vertebrates too recently to tell us about any brain older than a mammal’s.
options.why: The lamprey’s branch was the first to split, more than 500 million years ago. That is what makes it evidence about an old brain.

items.stem: A structure is found in both a shark’s brain and a human brain. Using the chapter’s comparative reasoning, what is the most reasonable conclusion about it?

options.text: It was most likely present in the last common ancestor of sharks and human beings.
options.why: Correct. A part two lineages both have was most likely inherited from their common ancestor, though the inference is a probability rather than a proof.

options.text: It evolved twice, once in sharks and once in human beings, because the two lineages are so far apart.
options.why: Separate origins are possible, but the chapter’s inference runs the other way: a shared part is most likely a shared inheritance.

options.text: It arose first in sharks and was later passed from the shark lineage to the lineage that led to human beings.
options.why: Sharks are not ancestors of human beings. Both lineages descend from a common ancestor, which is where the shared part most likely came from.

options.text: It must be exactly the same structure in both, with the same form and the same job it had in their ancestor.
options.why: The inference says where a part most likely came from. It says nothing about the part being unchanged in either lineage since.

items.stem: A human brain has a part that no lamprey brain has. Which conclusion does the chapter’s comparative inference support?

options.text: The part most likely arose after the two lineages split, on the side that led to us.
options.why: Correct. A part the human brain has and the lamprey’s lacks most likely arose after the split, on the human side. The hedge matters: it is the likeliest reading, not a certainty.

options.text: The part was certainly present in the common ancestor, and the lamprey’s lineage must have lost it along the way.
options.why: Loss is possible, but it is not the likeliest reading, and the inference is never a certainty. The simpler explanation is a later origin on the human side.

options.text: The part must be unimportant, since an animal that has lived for half a billion years without it has plainly done fine.
options.why: The inference is about where and when a part arose, not about how much it matters to the animals that have it.

options.text: Little can be concluded, since a comparison between two living animals says little about the history of either lineage.
options.why: The chapter treats exactly this comparison as evidence. It licenses a hedged conclusion about where the part most likely arose.

items.stem: How does a lamprey’s brain compare with a human brain, part for part?

options.text: Most of the parts a human brain is organized around are already in the lamprey’s, and one is conspicuously missing.
options.why: Correct. The lamprey’s brain is divided into pieces, most of which a human also has, and it has had them for more than five hundred million years.

options.text: The lamprey’s brain has none of the human brain’s parts, being an undivided cord that thickens slightly at the front.
options.why: The lamprey’s brain is already divided into pieces. That is exactly why it is the animal the module is read against.

options.text: The lamprey’s brain has every one of the human brain’s parts, differing from it only in overall size and weight.
options.why: The chapter says one part is conspicuously missing from the lamprey, so the match is close but not complete.

options.text: The lamprey’s brain has about half of the human brain’s parts, the other half having arisen with the first mammals.
options.why: Most of the parts, not half, are already present in a lamprey, and only one is singled out as conspicuously missing.

items.stem: A living lamprey is not an ancestor of anything. In a short paragraph, explain how a modern lamprey can still be evidence about a brain that existed more than five hundred million years ago.
items.answer: A lamprey is a modern animal, and its lineage has been evolving for exactly as long as ours. But a lamprey and a human being share a common ancestor. A part that both of their brains have was most likely present in that ancestor, and a part the human brain has and the lamprey’s lacks most likely arose later, on the human side. So comparing the two tells us, with some uncertainty, what the ancestor’s brain probably contained. Since most of the parts a human brain is organized around are already in a lamprey’s, the comparison suggests those parts are very old.
rubric: States that the lamprey is a modern animal, not an ancestor.
Invokes the common ancestor that both lineages descend from.
Gives the inference: a shared part was most likely in that ancestor.
Keeps the inference hedged (most likely, probably) rather than certain.

items.stem: A rock layer is dated to about 700 million years ago. Based on the chapter, what kind of life would its fossils most likely record?

options.text: Mostly single cells, preserved mainly as the traces of microbial mats.
options.why: Correct. The Ediacaran, with the first large fossils that include animals, began about 635 million years ago. Before then nearly all life was single cells.

options.text: Crawling animals up to a meter long, leaving trails across shallow seafloors.
options.why: Crawlers are part of the Ediacaran’s second assemblage, about 560 million years ago, well after this rock was laid down.

options.text: Armored jawless fishes, scooping and filtering food from the seafloor mud.
options.why: Armored jawless fishes come from the Ordovician onward, beginning about 485 million years ago, far later than this rock.

options.text: Arthropods with claws and image-forming eyes, hunting one another.
options.why: Those are Cambrian animals, from about 540 million years ago onward, more than 150 million years after this rock formed.

items.stem: What was new about the Ediacaran seafloor, compared with everything before it?

options.text: It held bodies big enough to see, some of them up to a meter long.
options.why: Correct. Before the Ediacaran nearly all life was single cells; the Ediacaran held visible bodies, some a meter long.

options.text: It held the first animals with shells, claws and spines to protect them.
options.why: The Ediacaran is notable for lacking claws, spines and shells. Hard parts arrive with the Cambrian.

options.text: It held the first animals with eyes, arranged in pairs on stalks.
options.why: Eyes that form images are a Cambrian arrival. Nothing in the chapter credits the Ediacaran with eyes.

options.text: It held the first vertebrates, small and slender with no jaws or teeth.
options.why: The first vertebrates appear in the early Cambrian, after the Ediacaran had ended.

items.stem: How did the oldest Ediacaran assemblage differ from the second one?

options.text: The oldest was anchored and frond-shaped in deep dark water; the second lived on shallow mats and included animals that moved.
options.why: Correct. About 575 million years ago the organisms stood in place in water too dark for photosynthesis. About 560 million years ago, on shallow mat-covered floors, some of the animals moved.

options.text: The oldest lived on shallow sunlit mats and could crawl; the second was anchored in deep, dark water and could not move at all.
options.why: That reverses them. The frond-shaped organisms came first, in deep water; the movers came second, in the shallows.

options.text: The oldest was made up entirely of animals; the second included organisms that may not have been animals.
options.why: The doubt runs the other way. It is the oldest, frond-shaped organisms that may not all have been animals.

options.text: The oldest included hunters with claws; the second had lost them and was a quieter, gentler seafloor altogether.
options.why: No Ediacaran assemblage shows claws or hunting. The quieting the chapter describes comes in the third assemblage.

items.stem: The 2018 discovery of cholesterol traces in Dickinsonia fossils is sometimes summarized as “proving the Ediacaran organisms were animals”. Why does the chapter state its conclusion more narrowly?

options.text: The finding shows at least some Ediacaran organisms were animals; some of the frond-shaped ones may still not have been.
options.why: Correct. Cholesterol is a hallmark of animals, so Dickinsonia was one. The anchored deep-water fronds remain open, and the chapter says some may not have been animals at all.

options.text: The finding was about Kimberella, not Dickinsonia, so it says nothing about the flat, bath-mat-shaped organisms.
options.why: The cholesterol traces were found in Dickinsonia, the flat, oval, bath-mat-shaped organism.

options.text: Cholesterol is found in every living thing, so its presence can only show that the fossils were once alive at all.
options.why: Cholesterol is a hallmark of animals specifically, which is why finding it in Dickinsonia was informative.

options.text: The finding was later withdrawn, so whether any Ediacaran organisms were animals remains wide open.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter says the finding was withdrawn. It is what establishes that at least some were animals.

items.stem: A fossil bed shows a row of faint, oval, body-shaped impressions, one after another, on an old microbial mat. Which Ediacaran animal’s behavior does this pattern match?

options.text: Dickinsonia, which grazed on the mat, then moved on and grazed again.
options.why: Correct. Dickinsonia, flat and oval like a bath mat, left a row of faint body-shaped impressions as it grazed and moved on.

options.text: Kimberella, which left a single continuous furrow as it scraped the mat.
options.why: Kimberella scraped the mat as it crawled. A row of separate oval impressions is the grazing-and-moving-on pattern of Dickinsonia.

options.text: Opabinia, which swept its long clawed snout across the mat for prey.
options.why: Opabinia is a Cambrian animal, and its snout was for grasping, not for leaving body-shaped prints on a mat.

options.text: Anomalocaris, which rested on the mat between bursts of swimming.
options.why: Anomalocaris was a Cambrian swimming predator. The row of impressions is an Ediacaran grazer’s trail.

items.stem: What happened to the crawling animals of the second Ediacaran assemblage by the third, at the end of the period?

options.text: They disappeared from the fossil record, and no one knows what caused it.
options.why: Correct. The third assemblage is quieter again. The crawlers are gone, and the cause is unknown.

options.text: They were eaten by the first predators, whose claws appear in the same beds.
options.why: The Ediacaran shows almost no signs of predation, and claws are a Cambrian arrival. The chapter offers no cause.

options.text: They grew jaws and bony armor, and became the first fishes of the next period.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter links the Ediacaran crawlers to the first vertebrates. The crawlers simply disappear.

options.text: They moved into deep, dark water, where the oldest assemblage had once lived.
options.why: The chapter says only that the crawlers disappear and that no one knows why. It records no move into deep water.

items.stem: Small burrowing tracks on an Ediacaran seafloor run to the bodies of other animals and stop there. What do these tracks show, and what do they not show?

options.text: They show scavenging and movement aimed at something sensed; they do not show hunting of living prey.
options.why: Correct. The tracks are the earliest fossil evidence of scavenging, and the first physical trace of aimed movement. The Ediacaran shows almost no signs of predation.

options.text: They show predation and the first arms race; they do not show aimed movement, which came later.
options.why: That reverses the evidence. The tracks show aimed movement toward bodies, and the period shows almost no predation.

options.text: They show the first vertebrates moving; they do not show any other kind of animal on the seafloor.
options.why: The tracks were left by small burrowing animals. The first vertebrates appear in the Cambrian, after the Ediacaran.

options.text: They show the animals avoiding each other; they do not show any animal moving toward a particular thing.
options.why: The tracks run to other animals’ bodies and stop there. They are exactly movement toward something the animal sensed.

items.stem: What evidence does the Ediacaran seafloor give that nothing there was hunting?

options.text: There are no half-eaten bodies, and no claws, spines or shells.
options.why: Correct. The absences are the evidence. Even animals packed together on one surface seem to have had little to do with each other.

options.text: There are no trails at all, since nothing on the seafloor could move.
options.why: There are trails, and some Ediacaran animals moved. What is missing are the signs of predation.

options.text: There are no animals at all, only the traces of microbial mats.
options.why: The Ediacaran held bodies big enough to see, and at least some of them were animals.

options.text: There are no eyes preserved, and without eyes no animal could hunt.
options.why: Eyes are not the evidence the chapter uses. The missing half-eaten bodies and defenses are.

items.stem: Why does the chapter describe the control problem of the Ediacaran seafloor as “small”?

options.text: Food lay still and nothing was hunting, so an animal had to find food that did not move and had nothing to escape.
options.why: Correct. The small control problem is the baseline the Cambrian breaks: still food, and no predators.

options.text: Ediacaran animals had so few neurons that only a small problem could have been solved by any of them, however it was posed.
options.why: The chapter defines the problem by the world, not by the animals’ neurons. A problem is small when little is asked of the animal.

options.text: Ediacaran animals did not move, so they never had to control their bodies at all.
options.why: Some Ediacaran animals did move, grazing and crawling. What was small was what their movement had to accomplish.

options.text: Ediacaran animals lived in deep water where there was nothing to sense, so there was nothing to respond to.
options.why: Only the oldest assemblage lived in deep water, and the movers lived in the shallows. The problem was small because food lay still and nothing hunted.

items.stem: What is the Cambrian explosion?

options.text: The appearance of a great diversity of animals over a geologically short stretch of time, beginning about 540 million years ago.
options.why: Correct. Many of the new animals had hard parts, jointed legs, claws and image-forming eyes. Whether it was a true explosion is still argued.

options.text: The sudden spread of microbial mats across the seafloor, beginning about 635 million years ago, that made visible animals possible.
options.why: About 635 million years ago is the start of the Ediacaran, and microbial mats predate it. The Cambrian explosion is a burst of animal diversity.

options.text: The extinction of most jawless fishes, about 360 million years ago, which left only the hagfishes and the lampreys alive.
options.why: That loss of the jawless fishes is a later event, well after the Cambrian. The Cambrian explosion is an appearance, not a disappearance.

options.text: The rapid enlargement of the vertebrate brain, beginning about 540 million years ago, when the first vertebrates appeared.
options.why: The first vertebrates do appear in the early Cambrian, but they were small and slender. The explosion names a burst of animal diversity in general.

items.stem: What is the name for the appearance of a great diversity of animals, many with hard parts, jointed legs, claws and image-forming eyes, over a geologically short stretch of time about 540 million years ago?

options.text: The Cambrian explosion.
options.why: Correct. It is only “sometimes” called that, since whether it was a true explosion is still argued.

options.text: The predator–prey arms race.
options.why: The arms race is part of what followed, hunters and hunted each getting better senses and faster movement. The burst of new animals is the Cambrian explosion.

options.text: The Ediacaran assemblage.
options.why: The Ediacaran assemblages came before the Cambrian and lacked hard parts, claws and image-forming eyes.

options.text: The rise of the neural crest.
options.why: The neural crest is a vertebrate cell population. It names nothing about animal diversity in general.

items.stem: Which of these arrived with the Cambrian animals rather than being present on the Ediacaran seafloor?

options.text: Shells, jointed legs, claws, and eyes that form images, with arthropods leading the change.
options.why: Correct. Hard parts are the Cambrian’s signature, and arthropods, the group that includes insects, crabs and spiders, led it.

options.text: Bodies big enough to see, with vertebrates leading the change.
options.why: Visible bodies were already on the Ediacaran seafloor, and the first vertebrates were small, slender prey animals.

options.text: Movement across the seafloor, with worm-like crawlers and grazers leading the change.
options.why: Movement was already present in the Ediacaran’s second assemblage, among grazers and crawlers.

options.text: Microbial mats as a new source of food, with grazers like Dickinsonia leading the change.
options.why: Microbial mats and their grazers belong to the Ediacaran. The Cambrian brought hard parts.

items.stem: An arthropod’s skeleton is on the outside of its body. What does the chapter say it provides besides protection?

options.text: A rigid frame for the muscles to pull against, so that the movements of many jointed parts can be organized and repeated.
options.why: Correct. The external skeleton does more than protect. It gives the muscles something to pull against, which makes many-jointed movement possible.

options.text: A place to store neurons outside the body, so that the arthropod’s nervous system can run along the surface of the shell.
options.why: The chapter says nothing about neurons in the skeleton. Its point is mechanical: a frame for muscles.

options.text: A surface for image-forming eyes to grow on, so that the arthropod can see in every direction at once.
options.why: The eyes arrived with the same animals, but the skeleton’s added role is to give muscles a frame, not to carry eyes.

options.text: A way to float in open water without swimming, so that the arthropod can drift toward food with little effort.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter credits the skeleton with buoyancy. It gives muscles a rigid frame for organized, repeatable movement.

items.stem: What did Anomalocaris and Opabinia have that fits the chapter’s picture of the Cambrian?

options.text: Parts for grasping and eyes to aim them: Anomalocaris had two grasping front limbs, Opabinia five eyes and a clawed snout.
options.why: Correct. Claws, and image-forming eyes to aim them, are what these two poster animals of the period show.

options.text: Flat, oval bodies that grazed on microbial mats and left rows of faint body-shaped impressions behind them as they moved on.
options.why: That describes Dickinsonia, an Ediacaran grazer, not the Cambrian animals.

options.text: Skulls and the beginnings of a backbone, making them among the first vertebrates found in early Cambrian rocks.
options.why: The first vertebrates were Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia. Anomalocaris and Opabinia were not vertebrates.

options.text: A toothed sucking disc in place of a jaw, which they used to feed on the blood of larger swimming animals.
options.why: That describes the modern lamprey, not these Cambrian animals.

items.stem: The chapter treats the Cambrian change that matters for nervous systems as a sequence. Which step comes immediately after “several animals are after the same food, so moving faster helps”?

options.text: Sometimes the easiest food to find is another living animal, so scavenging shades into predation.
options.why: Correct. The boundary between scavenging and predation is blurry, and that step is what turns competition for still food into hunting.

options.text: Hunters and hunted both get better senses and faster movement, in an arms race between them.
options.why: The arms race comes last. It needs animals already hunting one another, which is the step that comes first.

options.text: Animals begin building hard parts that fossilize well, so the record suddenly fills with them.
options.why: That is the skeptics’ explanation of why the Cambrian looks sudden. It is not a step in the chapter’s sequence.

options.text: Animals move slowly toward food that lies still on the seafloor, with nothing to escape from.
options.why: That is the starting point of the sequence, the Ediacaran situation, not the step after competition.

items.stem: Module 3 already described a predator–prey arms race. What does the chapter say is new about the Cambrian one?

options.text: Where it started: with food that stopped lying still.
options.why: Correct. The race itself is Module 3’s. What is new is its starting point, a world in which food began to move and to be hunted.

options.text: That only the predators improved, while the prey stayed as they were.
options.why: In any arms race better senses and faster movement help the hunted as much as the hunters. That is what makes it a race.

options.text: That it was the first time any animal moved toward food.
options.why: Aimed movement toward food was already on the Ediacaran seafloor, in the scavengers’ tracks.

options.text: That it was driven by rising oxygen rather than by the animals themselves.
options.why: Oxygen is one proposed cause of the Cambrian explosion, and the chapter leaves the cause open. It does not describe the arms race that way.

items.stem: After the Cambrian change, what did other animals become for some animals?

options.text: Their main source of food, and also one of their biggest threats.
options.why: Correct. Once animals hunted one another, other animals were both what an animal ate and what might eat it.

options.text: Their main source of shelter, and also one of their main sources of food.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter makes other animals shelter. The double role it names is food and threat.

options.text: Their only competitors for food, but never a direct danger to them.
options.why: Once hunting began, other animals were a danger as well as competition. That is the point of the double role.

options.text: Their partners in finding food, and a reason to live packed together.
options.why: Packed-together animals that had little to do with each other describe the Ediacaran, not the Cambrian.

items.stem: A textbook states flatly that “rising oxygen caused the Cambrian explosion”. How does the chapter’s account differ?

options.text: Oxygen is one proposed cause among several, and some researchers doubt the Cambrian was an explosion at all.
options.why: Correct. Rising oxygen, ocean chemistry and the new ecology of predators and prey have all been proposed. Why it happened when it did is still argued.

options.text: Oxygen is ruled out, and the chapter settles the question in favor of changes in ocean chemistry instead.
options.why: The chapter does not rule out oxygen or settle on any other cause. It leaves the explanation open.

options.text: Oxygen is correct, and the chapter adds only that predators then drove the rest of the diversification.
options.why: The chapter does not endorse oxygen as the cause. It lists it as one proposal among several.

options.text: Oxygen is irrelevant, because the chapter says the Cambrian explosion never happened and is an error of dating.
options.why: The skeptics doubt it was a sudden explosion, not that anything happened. They think animals had diversified for longer.

items.stem: Some researchers doubt that the Cambrian was an explosion at all. On their view, what explains why so many animals seem to appear so suddenly?

options.text: Animals had been diversifying for a long time, and the Cambrian is when they began building hard parts that fossilize well.
options.why: Correct. On that view the burst is partly in the record rather than in the animals: soft bodies leave few fossils, and shells and jointed legs leave many.

options.text: The Cambrian rocks are much thicker than the rocks before them, so they simply had more room in which to hold fossils.
options.why: The chapter says nothing about the thickness of the rock. The skeptics’ point is about which bodies fossilize well.

options.text: The earlier animals were all destroyed by the end of the Ediacaran, so the Cambrian started life over again from single cells.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter says life restarted. The skeptics hold that diversification had been going on for a long time.

options.text: The new animals migrated into the shallow seas from deep water, where there had been no rocks to record them.
options.why: The chapter proposes no migration. The skeptics’ point is that hard parts, once built, fossilize well.

items.stem: The cause of the Cambrian change is still argued. What does the chapter say holds either way, and why does that matter for the argument?

options.text: The early Cambrian animals lived in a world the Ediacaran animals never faced, and that new world is what poses the demands on a nervous system.
options.why: Correct. Whatever the cause, the world changed from still food to hunting, and the chapter’s argument rests on the change rather than on its cause.

options.text: The early Cambrian animals were all vertebrates, and that is why the argument can proceed from them to the vertebrate brain directly.
options.why: Arthropods led the Cambrian change, and the first vertebrates were small prey. The argument does not rest on who the animals were.

options.text: The early Cambrian animals had larger brains than the Ediacaran ones, and brain size is what the chapter’s argument depends on.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim about Cambrian brain size here. What holds either way is that the world was new.

options.text: The early Cambrian animals were soft-bodied like the Ediacaran ones, and only the fossil record changed between the two.
options.why: That goes beyond even the skeptics’ view, and it is not what the chapter says holds either way.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, trace the sequence by which a world of still food on the Ediacaran seafloor became a Cambrian arms race, and say what is new about that arms race.
items.answer: On the Ediacaran seafloor animals moved slowly toward food that lay still. Once several animals were after the same food, moving faster helped. The boundary between scavenging and predation is blurry, since sometimes the easiest food to find is another living animal, so competition shaded into hunting. Once animals were hunting each other, better senses and faster movement helped the hunted as much as the hunters, which is the predator–prey arms race. What is new is not the race but where it started, with food that stopped lying still.
rubric: Starts from still food on the Ediacaran seafloor.
Says competition for the same food made moving faster pay.
Says the easiest food is sometimes another animal, so scavenging shades into predation.
Describes the arms race as benefiting hunted and hunters alike.
Names the new element as the starting point, food that stopped lying still.

items.stem: Compare the control problem of an Ediacaran grazer with that of an early Cambrian animal. What is the key difference?

options.text: The grazer only had to find food that did not move; the Cambrian animal also had to catch moving food and escape being caught.
options.why: Correct. Food that lay still and nothing hunting made the Ediacaran problem small. In the Cambrian other animals became both food and threat.

options.text: The grazer had to find food by sight; the Cambrian animal found food by smell, since image-forming eyes had not yet appeared.
options.why: That reverses the timing. Image-forming eyes arrive with the Cambrian animals, not before them.

options.text: The grazer had to escape predators constantly; the Cambrian animal lived in a quieter world where most predators had disappeared.
options.why: That reverses the two worlds. The Ediacaran shows almost no predation; the Cambrian is where hunting took hold.

options.text: The two faced the same control problem, and only the size of their bodies changed from one period to the next.
options.why: The chapter’s whole point is that the control problem changed, from finding still food to hunting and escaping.

items.stem: Two animals face the same conflicting demands. One has a few hundred neurons; the other has many millions. What does the chapter imply about which could divide its nervous system into separate parts, and whether it should?

options.text: Only the larger has enough neurons to set some aside for separate jobs, and even for it division pays only if it outweighs the wiring and coordination it needs.
options.why: Correct. Dividing the work needs something to divide, and separate parts are still not free, since they need wiring and a way of settling disagreements.

options.text: Both could divide their nervous systems equally well, since the number of jobs to be done, not the number of neurons, is what decides how many parts form.
options.why: The chapter makes the number of neurons a precondition. With only a few hundred there is little to divide.

options.text: Only the smaller should divide its nervous system, since fewer neurons are cheaper to wire together into separate parts than many.
options.why: The chapter’s point runs the other way: a small nervous system offers little to divide, and many neurons can be set aside for separate jobs.

options.text: The larger must divide its nervous system, since having many millions of neurons guarantees that separate parts are always the better arrangement.
options.why: Many neurons make division possible, not obligatory. Whether separate parts are better is not obvious, because they carry costs.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, lay out both sides of the module’s first question. Say what is wrong with one general mechanism that does every job, and what is wrong with the obvious fix of splitting the jobs among separate parts.
items.answer: A general mechanism can be reused anywhere, but for that very reason it is specialized for nothing. A nervous system that does everything in one place may not be very good at any one thing, and it may struggle to do two incompatible things at once. Splitting the jobs among separate parts is the obvious fix, but it is not free. Separate parts need wiring between them, and they need some way of settling what happens when they disagree. So the question is not whether splitting helps, but when separate structures are favored at all, and why.
rubric: Says a general mechanism is specialized for nothing.
Names at least one cost of doing everything in one place: being good at nothing in particular, or struggling with incompatible jobs.
Names the wiring that separate parts need.
Names the need to settle disagreements between parts.
States the question as when separate structures are favored, not whether splitting ever helps.

pools.title: What the Cambrian Asked, and Demands That Pull Apart
pools.covers: reading §6.1.3, §6.1.4 · lecture 6.1 slides three_demands, demands_that_pull_apart, one_answer_among_others

items.stem: According to the chapter, which three new demands did the Cambrian world place on a nervous system?

options.text: Senses became arrays, a moving animal had to tell its own doings from the world’s, and the demands arrived together.
options.why: Correct. Two of the demands are about signals, and the third is about the other two: they all had to be met at once.

options.text: Senses became sharper, bodies grew larger, and brains had to find room inside a skull for more neurons than before.
options.why: Better senses belong to the Cambrian picture, but the demands the chapter names are about what a nervous system must do with its signals, all at once.

options.text: Animals had to learn from reward, predict their own errors, and store what they learned for longer than a day at a time.
options.why: Those are kinds of learning, which the module sorts out later. The Cambrian demands are arrays, self-caused signals, and meeting everything at once.

options.text: Animals had to move faster than their prey, hide from predators, and grow hard parts that could protect their soft bodies.
options.why: Those describe the arms race and the hard parts of Cambrian animals. The demands on a nervous system are about arrays, self-caused signals, and simultaneity.

items.stem: Light from a small object lands on one particular region of an eye’s sheet of sensors. If something downstream can use it, what does the position of that spot tell the animal?

options.text: Where the object is in the world, since each place on the sheet corresponds to a place in the scene.
options.why: Correct. Where on the sheet a spot of light lands says where in the world its source is. A patch of skin covered in touch receptors works the same way.

options.text: How bright the object is, since a spot landing nearer the middle of the sheet is a brighter one.
options.why: Brightness is not carried by position. The arrangement of the sheet is what says where the source is.

options.text: What kind of object it is, since each region of the sheet is tuned to a different kind of object.
options.why: The chapter does not divide the sheet by kinds of object. Position on the sheet stands for position in the world.

options.text: How far away the object is, since a spot landing nearer the edge of the sheet comes from farther off.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter ties the edge of the sheet to distance. Where the spot lands says where in the world its source is.

items.stem: Imagine an eye with a thousand receptors, all wired to a single cell that fires whenever any of them is stimulated. What could that animal learn from its eye?

options.text: Little more than a single receptor could tell it, since the arrangement of the thousand is lost at the one cell.
options.why: Correct. The arrangement carries information only if something downstream can use it. Funneled into one cell, a thousand receptors report little more than whether light arrived.

options.text: A great deal about where things are, since a thousand receptors take in far more of the scene than one receptor does.
options.why: More receptors take in more light, but where it landed is lost when all of them converge on one cell. Numbers without processing add little.

options.text: Everything a normal eye could tell it, only more slowly, since the single cell has to wait for all thousand receptors.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter says the single cell is slow. What is lost is the arrangement, not speed.

options.text: The shapes of objects but not their positions, since shape is carried by how many receptors are active at once.
options.why: Finding a shape needs comparisons between neighboring receptors, which a single cell summing all of them cannot make.

items.stem: Two animals have the same image-forming eye. In one, the eye feeds circuitry that compares neighboring receptors; in the other, it does not. Which animal can make use of the arrangement of its eye, and why?

options.text: The first, since an array carries information only if something downstream can use it, by comparing neighbors, finding edges, and following shapes.
options.why: Correct. An array is useless without processing given over to understanding it.

options.text: The second as readily as the first, since where things are is already present in the eye itself and needs nothing further downstream.
options.why: The information is in the arrangement, but it becomes information for the animal only when something downstream can use it.

options.text: The second, since circuitry that compares neighbors would blur the sharp image the eye already forms by itself.
options.why: Comparing neighbors is how edges are found, not a source of blur. It is what makes the image usable.

options.text: The second, since an eye that passes its signals on unchanged keeps more of their detail than one whose signals are compared.
options.why: Passing signals on unchanged loses nothing, but it uses nothing either. The arrangement becomes useful only when something compares neighbors downstream.

items.stem: On a patch of skin covered in touch receptors, a small insect walks slowly from one side to the other. What kind of processing would let the animal track the insect?

options.text: Following a shape as it moves across the sheet, by comparing which neighboring receptors are active from moment to moment.
options.why: Correct. Skin works like the eye’s sheet of sensors, and following a shape as it moves across the sheet is one of the jobs an array needs done.

options.text: Summing the receptors into one total, so the animal knows how strongly its skin is being touched overall at any moment.
options.why: A total says how much touch there is, not where it is or where it is going. Tracking needs comparisons between neighbors.

options.text: Turning the receptors down whenever the animal moves, so that the insect’s touch stands out against a quiet background.
options.why: Separating self-caused signals is a different demand, and turning everything down would lose the insect along with the rest.

options.text: Storing the pattern of touch for good, so that the animal remembers each insect that has walked across that patch.
options.why: Keeping something for good is a question about learning, and it would not track a moving insect now.

items.stem: The worm of Modules 4 and 5 already changes what its own senses report whenever it moves. What, then, was new about the problem of self-caused signals for a Cambrian animal?

options.text: The scale: a fast animal with jointed limbs, a turning head, and sweeping eyes makes a flood of self-caused signals, not a trickle.
options.why: Correct. The problem is old. What changed was how many self-caused signals there were, from how many parts of the body at once.

options.text: The problem itself: before the Cambrian, no animal’s movement had ever changed what its senses reported, however it moved.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite. Any animal that moves changes what its senses report, the worm included.

options.text: The source: Cambrian animals received signals caused mostly by other animals, while the worm’s signals were caused mostly by itself.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter makes the worm’s signals mostly self-caused. The difference is in how many self-caused signals there are.

options.text: The solution: Cambrian animals had solved the problem completely, so they no longer needed to separate the two kinds of signal at all.
options.why: Nothing was solved outright. The flood of self-caused signals is what made separating them a new and larger demand.

items.stem: A swimming fish receives four signals at once. Which one did the fish cause itself?

options.text: The rush of water past its body that its own swimming produces.
options.why: Correct. Swimming makes water rush past the body, and that signal is self-caused. It has to be separated from the signals the world causes.

options.text: The pressure of a current sweeping across the reef it is swimming past.
options.why: A current is the world’s doing, not the fish’s. The self-caused signal is the water its own swimming pushes past it.

options.text: The touch of a predator brushing against its side from behind.
options.why: A predator’s touch is world-caused, and it is exactly the kind of signal the fish must not confuse with its own.

options.text: The smell of food drifting toward it from somewhere up ahead.
options.why: A smell arriving from food is caused by the world. The fish’s own swimming causes the rush of water past its body.

items.stem: A crab-like Cambrian animal brushes a rock with one of its legs, and its touch receptors fire exactly as they would if a predator had touched it. Why is this a problem its nervous system has to solve?

options.text: The receptors report the same thing either way, so the animal must be able to tell that its own movement caused this signal, not the world.
options.why: Correct. Brushing a rock stimulates the same receptors a predator’s touch would. The signal alone does not say who caused it, so self-caused signals have to be separated from the rest.

options.text: The receptors are badly built, since a well-built receptor would fire differently for a rock than for a predator, and a better one would tell the two apart.
options.why: Nothing about the receptors is faulty. The same touch is the same touch; what differs is who caused it.

options.text: The rock and the predator must be learned apart over many trials, since the animal is born unable to tell hard things from soft ones.
options.why: The difficulty is not hard against soft. It is that the animal’s own movement produced a signal like the world’s.

options.text: The animal must stop moving whenever it needs to feel anything, since touch works properly only in an animal that holds still.
options.why: Touch works in moving animals. Movement adds self-caused signals that must be separated, and it is also an opportunity.

items.stem: Self-caused sensation is a problem for a moving animal. In what way does the chapter say it is also an opportunity?

options.text: An animal that acts on the world can poke at it and see what comes back, a way of finding things out that a motionless animal lacks.
options.why: Correct. The same fact that floods the senses with self-caused signals lets an animal test the world by acting on it.

options.text: An animal that moves can ignore self-caused signals entirely, which frees its nervous system for the signals the world causes.
options.why: Ignoring them is not an option the chapter offers; they must be separated. The opportunity is in acting on the world to learn about it.

options.text: An animal that moves produces signals that confuse its predators, which gives it a way of escaping that a still animal lacks.
options.why: Confusing predators is not the chapter’s point. The opportunity is finding things out by poking at the world.

options.text: An animal that moves exercises all of its receptors, which keeps them sensitive in a way the receptors of a motionless animal are not.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter concerns keeping receptors sensitive. The opportunity is learning about the world by acting on it.

items.stem: The chapter’s third Cambrian demand is that the demands arrived together. How is that demand different in kind from the first two?

options.text: It is a demand about the other demands, that they be met at once, rather than one more kind of signal to be handled.
options.why: Correct. Arrays and self-caused signals are each something to handle. The third demand is that all of them, and the jobs they serve, press at the same time.

options.text: It is a demand about learning, that the animal remember its past encounters, rather than one more kind of signal to be handled.
options.why: Learning enters later, in the plasticity–stability pair. The third demand is that everything arrives at once.

options.text: It is a demand about the body, that the animal grow a heart and gills, rather than a demand made on its nervous system at all.
options.why: Keeping the heart and gills working is one of the jobs listed, but the demand is that such jobs all run at once, and it falls on the nervous system.

options.text: It is a smaller version of the first two demands, one that the worm of Modules 4 and 5 had already met in full.
options.why: The worm meets a few demands one at a time. Meeting all of them at once is exactly what is new.

items.stem: At one moment a Cambrian fish is closing on food, a shadow passes overhead, a current tilts its body, and its gills keep pumping. What does this moment illustrate?

options.text: Several jobs, each sending its own stream of signals and calling for its own kind of response, all at the same moment.
options.why: Correct. The demands arrived together, and much of the time several of them call for a response at once.

options.text: One job, finding food, with the shadow, the current and the gills as background noise the fish can safely leave unprocessed.
options.why: The shadow could be a predator, and staying upright and breathing cannot stop. Each is its own job with its own signals.

options.text: A tug of war between half-made movements, since the fish’s muscles are being driven by every signal at once.
options.why: A tug of war is what would happen if every proposal drove the muscles directly. The moment itself shows many demands at once.

options.text: Self-caused sensation, since every one of those signals was produced by the fish’s own swimming at that moment.
options.why: A shadow overhead and a tilting current are world-caused. The moment shows several jobs pressing at once.

items.stem: The worm of Modules 4 and 5 meets a few of the demands a Cambrian animal faced. What, then, is the real question about a Cambrian nervous system?

options.text: Not whether it can meet one of these demands, but what kind of nervous system can meet all of them at once.
options.why: Correct. The worm meets a few demands one at a time. The Cambrian question is about meeting all of them together.

options.text: Not whether it can meet all of these demands, but whether it can meet any one of them better than the worm did.
options.why: That inverts the question. Doing one job well is not the issue; doing all of them at once is.

options.text: Not whether it can meet these demands, but whether it can learn to meet them within a single lifetime.
options.why: Learning is not the question posed here. The question is what kind of nervous system meets every demand at once.

options.text: Not whether it can meet these demands, but how many more neurons its nervous system needs than the worm’s to meet each one.
options.why: Neuron count matters elsewhere in the module, but the question posed here is about meeting all the demands at once.

items.stem: Modules 3 to 5 asked why a signaling cell, a circuit, and an adaptable circuit would each be favored. What does the chapter ask the same question of in this module?

options.text: An arrangement of parts: why build separate structures rather than one general mechanism that runs everywhere.
options.why: Correct. The computational question moves from one cell, and from one circuit, to how a nervous system is divided.

options.text: A single synapse: why one connection would strengthen with use rather than stay at the strength it began with.
options.why: Why a synapse changes was the business of the adaptable circuit. The new object of the question is an arrangement of parts.

options.text: A whole species: why one lineage would survive a mass extinction rather than die out like the lineages around it.
options.why: The question is not about lineages surviving. It is asked of how a nervous system is divided into parts.

options.text: A single behavior: why an animal would approach food rather than avoid it when both are within easy reach.
options.why: Approach and avoidance are older questions. The new one asks why there would be separate structures at all.

items.stem: What observation does the chapter’s argument for separate structures start from?

options.text: Some demands pull a single mechanism in opposite directions, so improving it for one makes it worse for another.
options.why: Correct. That is the simple observation the argument rests on, and three such pairs matter for a Cambrian animal.

options.text: Some demands are harder than others, so a single mechanism must grow larger before it can meet the hardest of them.
options.why: Being harder is not the point. A merely harder problem does not earn its own name; incompatible demands are what matter.

options.text: Some demands are older than others, so a single mechanism keeps the old ones and adds new structures for the new ones.
options.why: Age is not what the argument turns on. It turns on demands that pull one mechanism in opposite directions.

options.text: Some demands arise in different parts of the body, so a single mechanism cannot reach all the places they come from.
options.why: Where signals come from matters for where specialists sit. The starting observation is about demands that conflict.

items.stem: An engineer builds one controller for a robotic fish that runs both its breathing pump and its turns toward food, and tunes it to switch instantly whenever food appears. What problem does the chapter’s argument predict?

options.text: The breathing pump will be easy to interrupt, since a mechanism tuned to switch easily is also easy to interrupt.
options.why: Correct. Keeping going and changing course pull one mechanism in opposite directions. Tuned for switching, it loses its steadiness.

options.text: The robot will be slow to reach food, since a mechanism tuned to switch easily is also slow to switch direction.
options.why: That reverses the trade-off. It is a mechanism that is hard to interrupt that is slow to switch.

options.text: Nothing will go wrong, since one controller can switch between food and breathing as often as the robot needs.
options.why: The chapter’s point is that one mechanism doing both jobs has to compromise. Easy switching costs steadiness.

options.text: The robot will forget where food was, since a mechanism tuned to switch easily also overwrites what it has learned.
options.why: Overwriting belongs to the plasticity–stability pair, a different trade-off. This pair trades switching against steadiness.

items.stem: A student summarizes the chapter’s three competing pairs this way: “In each pair, one demand is expensive and the other is cheap”. What is wrong with that summary?

options.text: Each pair is symmetric: tuning one mechanism toward either side makes it worse at the other, so neither side is the cheap one.
options.why: Correct. Easy to switch means easy to interrupt, and hard to interrupt means slow to switch. The other two pairs are built the same way.

options.text: Each pair is costly on both sides in a small animal, but in a large animal one side of each pair becomes the cheaper one.
options.why: Size does not change the structure of the pairs. Improving a mechanism for one side makes it worse for the other, whatever the animal.

options.text: Only the learning pair is balanced; in the other two pairs the switching side and the proposing side are the cheap ones.
options.why: No pair has a cheap side. Proposing strongly conflicts with comparing fairly, and switching conflicts with steadiness, in both directions.

options.text: The pairs cost nothing, since a well-built mechanism can meet both demands of a pair at full strength at once.
options.why: If that were so there would be no competing demands. The pairs matter because improving one side worsens the other.

items.stem: For keeping going and changing course, what does having two mechanisms, one that runs steadily and one that switches, avoid?

options.text: The compromise one mechanism doing both jobs would have to make between being steady and being quick to switch.
options.why: Correct. Two mechanisms avoid that particular compromise. Whether a real nervous system took that route is a separate, empirical question.

options.text: The need for any wiring between the two parts, since a steady mechanism and a switching one never need to exchange signals.
options.why: Separate mechanisms still need wiring and coordination. Those are costs of separation, not things it avoids.

options.text: The need to keep breathing while changing course, since the switching mechanism can take over breathing when it must.
options.why: Breathing cannot stop, not even briefly. The steady mechanism keeps it going while the other switches.

options.text: The trade-off between keeping what is learned and learning quickly, since each mechanism can learn at its own rate.
options.why: That is the plasticity–stability pair. Here the compromise avoided is between steadiness and switching.

items.stem: Choosing one action was already a demand of steering, and in the worm two groups of motor neurons that inhibit each other were enough to meet it. What changed in the Cambrian?

options.text: The number of proposals competing at once, and the number of parts of the body they came from.
options.why: Correct. The need to sharpen and commit is old. A Cambrian animal had many more proposals, from eyes, nose and skin at once.

options.text: The need to choose at all, since the worm never had to settle between two movements at the same moment.
options.why: The worm did have to choose, and its mutually inhibiting motor neurons did it. The need is old; its scale is new.

options.text: The kind of choice, since Cambrian animals chose among goals while the worm chose only among muscles.
options.why: The chapter draws no such line. What changed was how many proposals competed, and from how many parts of the body.

options.text: The speed of the choice, since Cambrian animals had to choose in a fraction of the time the worm took to choose.
options.why: Speed is not the chapter’s point here. The change is in the number of proposals and where they come from.

items.stem: A fish’s eyes propose a turn toward something bright, its nose a turn toward a smell, and its skin a turn away from a touch. What would happen if every one of those proposals drove the muscles directly?

options.text: A tug of war between half-made movements, since a fish cannot turn left and right at the same moment.
options.why: Correct. That is why something has to compare the proposals and let only compatible movements proceed at the same time.

options.text: A smooth average of all three turns, since the muscles would add the proposals together into one sensible path.
options.why: Averaging opposite turns is not what the chapter predicts. A fish cannot turn two ways at once, so the result is a tug of war.

options.text: The strongest proposal alone, since the muscles would respond to the largest signal and ignore the weaker ones.
options.why: Nothing in the muscles makes that choice. Something has to compare the proposals; without it, they fight.

options.text: No movement at all, since the three proposals would cancel each other out and leave the fish holding still.
options.why: The chapter describes half-made movements pulling against each other, not stillness.

items.stem: Suppose the part of a fish’s nervous system that proposes turns toward food were also the part that compared all of the fish’s proposals. Why does the chapter see a conflict in that arrangement?

options.text: A part proposing a turn toward food works well when it proposes strongly, while the comparison must not be biased toward any one proposal.
options.why: Correct. Making proposals and comparing them pull in opposite directions. A good proposer pushes hard; a fair comparer favors no one.

options.text: A part proposing a turn toward food works too slowly to compare proposals as well, since proposing uses up all of its neurons at every moment.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim about speed or neuron use here. The conflict is between proposing strongly and comparing without bias.

options.text: A part that proposes turns toward food cannot receive signals from the eyes, nose or skin, so it would have nothing to compare.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter cuts a proposer off from the senses. The trouble is that it would favor its own proposal.

options.text: A part proposing a turn toward food would compare fairly but too weakly, so every proposal would be released at once.
options.why: A proposer is working well when it is strong, not weak, and that strength is exactly what would bias the comparison.

items.stem: A fish updates its memory of where food was every few minutes, overwriting the old location each time. If that same learning mechanism also stored the look of a predator, what would the chapter’s argument predict?

options.text: The look of the predator would be overwritten as readily, since a mechanism that learns quickly also overwrites quickly.
options.why: Correct. That is the plasticity–stability trade-off. Some things should be kept for good, and others updated constantly.

options.text: The look of the predator would be kept for good, since memories of danger are stored more firmly than memories of food.
options.why: The chapter says nothing about danger being stored more firmly. A single fast-learning mechanism overwrites whatever it holds.

options.text: The fish would stop learning where food was, since storing a predator quickly fills the mechanism and blocks new learning.
options.why: That describes the stable end of the trade-off. A fast learner does not block new learning; it overwrites old learning.

options.text: Nothing would change, since how quickly a mechanism learns has no bearing on how long it keeps what it learned.
options.why: The chapter’s point is exactly that the two are linked: learning quickly means overwriting quickly.

items.stem: Module 5 gave a rule: a computational problem earns its own name when it changes what a solution must have, not when it is merely a harder example of the same problem. Applied to the parts of a nervous system, which case is a candidate for separate structures?

options.text: Keeping the heart beating while behavior switches, since the two jobs demand incompatible things of one mechanism.
options.why: Correct. When two problems demand incompatible things, one natural answer is to give each its own structure. The rule makes this a candidate, not a certainty.

options.text: Seeing prey at twice the distance, since a harder version of the same seeing problem needs many more neurons to solve.
options.why: That is a harder example of the same problem. By the rule, harder does not earn its own name, or its own structure.

options.text: Finding food in murkier water, since murkier water changes how hard the search is for the animal’s senses.
options.why: Murkier water makes the search harder but asks nothing incompatible of the mechanism. It is the same problem made harder.

options.text: Swimming farther each day, since a longer swim makes greater demands on the same muscles and the same circuits.
options.why: A longer swim is more of the same. Demands that pull a mechanism in opposite directions are what make a case a candidate.

items.stem: Consider two claims: that a Cambrian animal must keep breathing while it changes course, and that it has separate neural structures for the two jobs. How does the chapter classify them?

options.text: The first is a computational fact about the animal’s world; the second is one possible algorithmic and implementational answer to it.
options.why: Correct. The demand holds for any animal in that world, however its nervous system is built. Separate structures are one answer, not the only one.

options.text: The first is an implementational fact about the animal’s tissue; the second is the computational problem that the tissue has to solve.
options.why: That reverses the levels. The demand is computational, about the world; separate structures are how a nervous system might meet it.

options.text: Both are computational facts about the animal’s world, since any animal facing the first demand must also have the second structure.
options.why: Only the demand is a fact about the world. Whether separate structures meet it is left open, to be checked.

options.text: Both are implementational facts about vertebrate brains, since the demand exists only in animals whose brains already have those parts.
options.why: The demand exists for any animal in that world, whatever its brain. It is not a fact about any particular tissue.

items.stem: A classmate argues: “A Cambrian fish has to keep breathing while it changes course. Those demands conflict. So its brain must have one structure for breathing and another for changing course”. What is wrong with the argument?

options.text: The conflict is a fact about the fish’s world; whether its brain meets it with two structures is an empirical question, and one network could also meet it.
options.why: Correct. The argument from conflicting demands shows that separation would be one good answer. It does not show that separation happened; anatomy, physiology and behavior decide that.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it; two incompatible demands always require two separate structures, and the chapter’s whole argument is built to prove exactly that point.
options.why: This is the reading the chapter warns against. Separate structures are one answer among others, and whether a brain took it is checked, not deduced.

options.text: The demands do not really conflict; breathing and changing course can both be done by one mechanism without any compromise at all.
options.why: They do conflict: easy to switch means easy to interrupt. The flaw is in the step from conflict to structure, not in the conflict.

options.text: The argument is right about fish but wrong about mammals, since a mammal’s brain has a separate structure for breathing while a fish’s does not.
options.why: The chapter draws no such line between fish and mammals. The flaw is treating a good argument for separation as proof of it.

items.stem: What does the chapter describe as the main alternative to separate structures for meeting competing demands?

options.text: A single richly interconnected network in which each demand acts as a soft constraint, and the network settles into the state that best satisfies all of them.
options.why: Correct. This is constraint satisfaction. Each demand pushes the network’s activity toward some states and away from others.

options.text: A set of separate structures, each one meeting a single demand, joined by a chooser that picks whichever structure’s output happens to be the strongest at that moment.
options.why: That is the separate-structures answer, with something to choose. The alternative is one network settling among soft constraints.

options.text: A single general mechanism that meets each demand in turn, one at a time, switching between them as quickly as the animal needs.
options.why: Meeting demands one at a time is what the worm does. The alternative settles among all the demands together.

options.text: A network with no connections between its neurons, so that each demand is met by its own neurons without disturbing the others.
options.why: A network without connections could not settle among constraints. The alternative is richly interconnected.

items.stem: What is the name for the view that a single network, pushed by many soft constraints at once, settles into the state that best satisfies all of them, so that a well-weighted compromise is the solution rather than a failure?

options.text: Constraint satisfaction.
options.why: Correct. Researchers call it constraint satisfaction, and the chapter presents it as a genuine rival to separate structures.

options.text: Modularity.
options.why: Modularity describes a system built from units that each do their own job and connect through a limited set of connections, which is closer to the separate-structures answer.

options.text: Action selection.
options.why: Action selection is choosing which available action is performed now. It is a job, not a view about how one network meets many demands.

options.text: Central pattern generator.
options.why: A central pattern generator is a circuit that produces a rhythmic output without a rhythmic input driving it. It is a piece of circuitry, not a view about how one network meets many demands.

items.stem: One mechanism doing both keeping going and changing course has to compromise between them. How would a constraint-satisfaction researcher view that compromise?

options.text: As the solution, when the constraints are weighted well, rather than as a failure the network has to escape.
options.why: Correct. On the constraint-satisfaction view, settling on the best overall state is exactly what the network is for.

options.text: As a failure that shows the network is too small, and that more neurons would remove the need for any compromise.
options.why: Size does not enter the view. A well-weighted compromise counts as success, not as a symptom of too few neurons.

options.text: As a failure that shows the two demands need separate structures, so that neither has to give way to the other.
options.why: That is how the separate-structures answer reads a compromise. Constraint satisfaction treats a good compromise as the solution.

options.text: As a sign that the demands were never really in conflict, since a single network meets both of them in full.
options.why: The demands do conflict; that is why there is a compromise. The view is that the compromise, well weighted, is the answer.

items.stem: Recording from a region of a fish’s brain, a researcher finds that the same neurons are active during two different jobs. She concludes that the two jobs must interfere with each other. Why might a constraint-satisfaction researcher disagree?

options.text: One network can keep two demands from interfering by giving them patterns of activity that overlap very little, even in the same neurons.
options.why: Correct. Sharing neurons does not by itself mean sharing patterns. Two demands can be carried on nearly separate patterns in one population.

options.text: Two jobs that share neurons do not interfere, since neurons that serve two jobs split their time evenly between them.
options.why: Interference is a real cost of a single structure, so sharing does not rule it out. The point is that low-overlap patterns can prevent it.

options.text: Two jobs that share neurons must really be one job, since a region that serves two jobs is serving a single larger one.
options.why: The two jobs remain two. What keeps them apart is how little their patterns of activity overlap.

options.text: Interference is not possible within any single brain region, since interference happens only between separate structures that are wired together.
