options.why: Interference is a cost the chapter charges to a single structure. Low-overlap patterns are how one network can avoid it.

items.stem: Which pairing of gains and costs belongs to separate structures rather than to a single network?

options.text: No interference, and each part tuned to its job; but wiring and coordination are needed, and what one part learns is not easily shared.
options.why: Correct. That is the separate-structures side of the ledger.

options.text: Everything learned is shared, and many considerations are weighed at once; but the demands can interfere, and settling takes time.
options.why: That is the single-network side of the ledger, the mirror image of separate structures.

options.text: No interference, and everything learned is shared; but the parts must be kept small, since large parts cannot be tuned closely to their jobs.
options.why: Separate structures do avoid interference, but they give up easy sharing of learning, and the chapter sets no size limit.

options.text: Each part tuned to its job, and no wiring is needed; but coordinating the parts takes time, since they must take turns to act.
options.why: Separate structures do need wiring, and the chapter says nothing about parts taking turns. Wiring and coordination are both costs.

items.stem: A designer wants what a system learns in one job to be available at once in every other job, and wants many considerations weighed together. Which arrangement suits that goal, and what does it risk?

options.text: A single structure, at the risk that its demands interfere with one another and that settling on an answer takes time.
options.why: Correct. A single structure shares everything it learns and weighs everything at once. Interference and settling time are its costs.

options.text: Separate structures, at the risk that the wiring between them grows so long that signals cannot arrive in time.
options.why: Separate structures do not share learning easily, which is the goal here. Wiring is their cost, but they do not suit the goal.

options.text: A single structure, at the risk that it needs long wiring between its parts and a separate chooser to coordinate them all.
options.why: Wiring and a chooser are costs of separate structures. A single structure pays in interference and settling time.

options.text: Separate structures, at the risk that each part becomes tuned to its own job and cannot be retuned later on.
options.why: Tuning to a job is a strength of separate structures, not a risk, and they would not share learning as the designer wants.

items.stem: A region of a fish’s brain responds most to moving objects, but it shares inputs and connections with its neighbors, and its preference sharpens as the young fish grows and gains experience. Where does this region sit in the chapter’s account?

options.text: Between the two extremes: it leans toward one job while sharing with its neighbors, and part of its specialization emerges through development.
options.why: Correct. Real nervous systems sit between separate structures and one undivided network, and some specialization is not laid down in advance.

options.text: At the separate-structures extreme, since any region that responds most strongly to one kind of thing counts as a dedicated structure for that one job.
options.why: Leaning toward one job while sharing inputs and connections is exactly the middle ground, not a sealed-off structure.

options.text: At the single-network extreme, since any region that shares inputs with its neighbors cannot be specialized for anything.
options.why: Sharing inputs does not rule out leaning toward a job. The region is between the extremes.

options.text: Outside the account altogether, since specialization that keeps changing with experience cannot be part of how a brain is organized.
options.why: Some specialization emerges through learning and development. This region is an example of it.

items.stem: How does the chapter say it is decided whether a nervous system separates two jobs into two distinct structures?

options.text: By looking at anatomy, physiology and behavior, since it is an empirical question.
options.why: Correct. The argument that separation would be good does not settle whether it happened. Evidence does.

options.text: By the argument from conflicting demands, since incompatible jobs show that two structures are needed.
options.why: That is the step the chapter refuses. The argument makes separation worth considering, not established.

options.text: By counting the animal’s neurons, since separation happens once a nervous system passes a set size.
options.why: The chapter names no size at which separation happens. Whether it happened is checked in anatomy, physiology and behavior.

options.text: By asking which design would work best, since the best arrangement for a job is the one that animals end up with.
options.why: Brains are built from what came before, not to a best design. And what would be best does not settle what exists.

items.stem: For the structures this module discusses, where does the chapter say the evidence of real separation is clearest?

options.text: For choosing among actions, where vertebrates have a distinct circuit conserved since before the lamprey’s lineage split from ours.
options.why: Correct. The evidence of separation is strong for the module’s structures, and clearest for choosing among actions.

options.text: For plasticity against stability, where every vertebrate has one fast and one slow learning structure, found in the lamprey and in mammals alike.
options.why: The fast-and-slow proposal comes from the constraint-satisfaction tradition, and the chapter does not name it as its clearest case.

options.text: For keeping going against changing course, where the separate structure for breathing arose first in mammals and is missing in fishes.
options.why: The clearest case is choosing among actions, and nothing in the chapter makes breathing control a mammalian invention.

options.text: For separating self-caused signals, where each sense of a fish has its own separate structure in the brain for damping its own disturbances.
options.why: The chapter does not make self-caused signals its clearest case of separation. That case is choosing among actions.

items.stem: The evidence that vertebrate brains have separate structures is strong. Why does the chapter still say that behavior, at the scale of the whole brain, comes from many constraints combined at once?

options.text: The separate structures are densely connected to one another and work in loops, so their contributions combine.
options.why: Correct. Separation is real, and so is dense interconnection. At the whole-brain scale, many constraints still combine.

options.text: The separate structures are too small to act alone, so the brain falls back on one network whenever a job gets hard.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter makes the structures fall back on anything. They are connected and work in loops all the time.

options.text: The separate structures are found only in the lamprey, so the brains of later vertebrates run as a single network.
options.why: The structures have been conserved from before the lamprey’s split, into later vertebrates, mammals included.

options.text: The separate structures only look separate in anatomy, and physiology shows they are really one single structure.
options.why: The chapter treats the separation as real. What it adds is that the structures are densely connected and work in loops.

items.stem: A student describes constraint satisfaction as “the view that the brain has no separate systems, just one big network”. What does the chapter report that undercuts that description?

options.text: Researchers from the constraint-satisfaction tradition themselves argued that plasticity and stability need two interacting learning systems, one fast and one slow.
options.why: Correct. The debate cuts both ways. Constraint satisfaction is a rival answer to some problems, not a blanket rejection of separate systems.

options.text: Researchers from the constraint-satisfaction tradition later abandoned the view, after the evidence showed that vertebrates have separate systems.
options.why: The chapter reports no abandonment. It presents constraint satisfaction as a live rival, whose own researchers argued for two systems in one case.

options.text: Researchers from the separate-structures tradition showed that a single network cannot learn at all, so the student’s view is held by no one.
options.why: The chapter credits a single structure with sharing everything it learns. Nothing in it says one network cannot learn.

options.text: Researchers from the constraint-satisfaction tradition argued that every single demand an animal faces needs its own separate structure, the opposite of the student’s view.
options.why: That overstates it. They argued for two learning systems for one problem, stability against plasticity, not a structure for every demand.

items.stem: In ray-finned fishes the front of the brain develops folded outward rather than inward. Why does the chapter bring up this case?

options.text: As a division that seems to be a side effect, apparently of large larval eyes crowding the skull, rather than something favored for itself.
options.why: Correct. The argument from conflicting demands does not claim every division was favored for a reason, and this folding is the chapter’s example.

options.text: As a division that was favored, rather than a side effect, because outward folding gives the eyes more room, so that ray-finned fishes see better than any other fishes.
options.why: The large eyes leave too little room, which apparently causes the folding. Nothing about the folding itself seems to have been favored.

options.text: As the clearest evidence of real separation in vertebrates, since the outward fold divides the forebrain into two distinct structures.
options.why: The clearest evidence of separation is for choosing among actions. The fold is an example of a side effect.

options.text: As evidence that ray-finned fishes meet competing demands by constraint satisfaction, since their outward-folded forebrain has no parts.
options.why: The chapter does not tie the fold to constraint satisfaction. It uses the fold to show that some features are side effects.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, name the three new demands the Cambrian world placed on a nervous system, and explain why the third is a different kind of demand from the first two.
items.answer: First, senses became arrays: an image-forming eye is a sheet of many sensors, and where light lands on it says where its source is, but only if something downstream compares neighbors, finds edges and follows shapes. Second, a moving animal has to tell its own doings from the world’s. The worm already faced a version of this, but a fast animal with jointed limbs, a turning head and sweeping eyes makes a flood of self-caused signals rather than a trickle. Third, the demands arrived together: finding food, watching for predators, staying upright and keeping the gills working all had to happen at once. The third is a demand about the other demands, not one more kind of signal. So the question is not whether a nervous system can meet one demand, but what kind can meet all of them at once.
rubric: Names arrays, and says an array is useless without processing downstream.
Names separating self-caused signals from world-caused ones, with the change being one of scale.
Names the demands arriving together, all at the same time.
Explains that the third is about the other demands rather than another kind of signal.
States the reframed question: meeting all the demands at once, not one of them.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the chapter’s argument from conflicting demands does not settle whether a nervous system has separate structures. Describe the rival answer, and say what does settle the question.
items.answer: The conflicting demands are computational facts about a Cambrian animal’s world: it must keep breathing while it changes course, end up doing one thing when several are proposed, and keep some of what it learns while updating the rest. Those hold however its nervous system is built. Separate structures are one algorithmic and implementational answer to them, not the only one. The rival is constraint satisfaction: a single richly connected network in which each demand is a soft constraint, and the network settles into the state that best satisfies them all, so that a well-weighted compromise is the solution. Which answer a nervous system took is an empirical question, settled by anatomy, physiology and behavior. For this module’s structures the evidence of separation is strong, and clearest for choosing among actions.
rubric: States that the demands are computational facts that hold however the nervous system is built.
Says separate structures are one answer among others, at the algorithmic and implementational levels.
Describes constraint satisfaction as one network settling among soft constraints, where a well-weighted compromise is the solution rather than a failure.
Says the question is empirical, answered by anatomy, physiology and behavior.

items.stem: In a few sentences, give one strength and one weakness each for separate structures and for a single network, and say where real nervous systems sit between them.
items.answer: Separate structures keep two jobs from interfering and let each part be tuned to its own job, but they need wiring and something to coordinate them, and they cannot easily share what each has learned. A single network shares everything it learns and weighs many considerations at once, but its demands can interfere, and settling on an answer takes time. Real nervous systems sit between the extremes. A region can lean toward one job while sharing inputs and connections with its neighbors, and some specialization emerges through learning and development.
rubric: Gives a strength of separate structures: no interference, or tuning to a job.
Gives a weakness of separate structures: wiring, coordination, or unshared learning.
Gives a strength of a single network: shared learning, or weighing everything at once.
Gives a weakness of a single network: interference, or settling time.
Places real nervous systems between the extremes, with some specialization emerging through learning or development.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe two of the chapter’s three pairs of competing demands. For each, explain why a single mechanism tuned toward one side gets worse at the other.
items.answer: One pair is keeping going against changing course. Breathing, the heartbeat and upright posture cannot stop, while behavior switches constantly. A mechanism that switches easily is easy to interrupt, and one that is hard to interrupt is slow to switch. Another pair is plasticity against stability. The look of a predator should be kept for good, while where food was a moment ago should be updated constantly. A mechanism that learns quickly also overwrites quickly, and one that keeps what it learned is slow to learn anything new. In both pairs the trade-off runs in both directions, so neither side is the cheap one.
rubric: Names two of the three pairs: keeping going against changing course, proposing strongly against comparing fairly, or plasticity against stability.
Gives a concrete example of each side for at least one pair.
States the trade-off for the first pair named, in both directions.
States the trade-off for the second pair named, in both directions.

pools.title: What Specialists Cost, and a Body That Moves as One

items.stem: Why does the chapter say that separate structures are not free, even before their wiring is counted?

options.text: Neural tissue is expensive to run: an adult human brain is about two percent of body weight but uses about twenty percent of the body’s oxygen at rest.
options.why: Correct. Any structure made of neurons adds to an expensive bill, which is the first reason specialists are not free.

options.text: Neural tissue is slow to grow: an adult human brain takes about twenty years to reach its final size, and each new structure adds years to that.
options.why: Growth time is not the cost the chapter names. The cost is the energy neural tissue takes to run.

options.text: Neural tissue is heavy: an adult human brain is about twenty percent of body weight, and every added structure makes the head harder to hold up.
options.why: The brain is about two percent of body weight. The chapter’s point is that it takes far more than its share of oxygen.

options.text: Neural tissue is scarce: an adult human brain holds only about two percent of the body’s cells, so every added structure has to borrow neurons from another.
options.why: The chapter says nothing about borrowing neurons. Its point is that neurons are expensive to run.

items.stem: Two mammal brains weigh the same, but one has twice as many neurons as the other. On the finding the chapter reports, which costs more energy to run?

options.text: The brain with more neurons, since a brain’s energy use rises in step with its number of neurons.
options.why: Correct. Cost is set mainly by neuron count, not by weight, so the brain with twice the neurons costs roughly twice as much.

options.text: Neither, since two brains of the same weight use the same energy whatever their neurons happen to be like.
options.why: That prices a brain by the gram, which is the view the finding replaces. Neuron count sets the cost.

options.text: The brain with fewer neurons, since its neurons must be larger to fill the same weight, and larger neurons cost more.
options.why: Each neuron costs roughly the same, large or small. Larger neurons do not raise the bill.

options.text: Neither can be said, since energy use has been measured in whole bodies but not yet in brains of any kind.
options.why: Brain energy use has been measured, in mammals from mice to monkeys to human beings.

items.stem: A neuron in a mouse’s brain is compared with a much larger neuron in a human brain. On the finding the chapter reports, how does the cost of running one mouse neuron compare with the cost of running one human neuron?

options.text: Roughly the same, since each neuron costs about the same to run whether it is large or small and whichever brain it is in.
options.why: Correct. That is what makes neuron count, not weight, the measure of a brain’s cost.

options.text: Much less, since a smaller neuron has less membrane to pump ions across and so uses less energy after each signal it sends.
options.why: The reasoning sounds right, but the finding is that neurons cost roughly the same whatever their size.

options.text: Much more, since a smaller brain must work each of its neurons harder to keep up with the jobs of a larger one.
options.why: Nothing in the finding says small brains work their neurons harder. Each neuron costs about the same.

options.text: Impossible to compare, since cost per neuron has been measured only within human brains and in no other animal.
options.why: It has been measured across mammals, from mice to monkeys to human beings.

items.stem: A new specialist structure appears in the brains of some lineage of animals. What does the chapter say this usually means for the brain’s energy bill?

options.text: It rises, since a specialist structure usually means more neurons, and each added neuron adds to the bill.
options.why: Correct. Because cost is billed per neuron, a new structure built from new neurons raises the cost of running the brain.

options.text: It falls, since a specialist does its job more efficiently than a general mechanism and so saves energy overall.
options.why: Being tuned to a job is a gain of separate structures, but the chapter does not say it lowers the energy bill. More neurons cost more.

options.text: It stays the same, since the new structure usually means neurons the brain already had, simply reassigned to it.
options.why: A specialist usually means adding neurons, not reassigning them, so the bill rises.

options.text: It depends only on the structure’s weight, since a light structure costs little however many neurons it contains.
options.why: Cost is set by neuron count, not weight. That is the point of the per-neuron finding.

items.stem: A classmate says, “The cost per neuron has been measured in every kind of vertebrate, from lampreys to human beings”. How does the chapter’s account differ?

options.text: The measurements all come from mammals, and applying them to a lamprey or a Cambrian fish is an inference, not a finding.
options.why: Correct. The chapter volunteers this limit on its own reasoning. Nobody has measured the cost per neuron in a lamprey or a Cambrian fish.

options.text: The measurements all come from fishes, and applying them to mammals is an inference, since fish neurons were easier to study.
options.why: That reverses it. The measurements are mammalian, and the extension runs to fish.

options.text: The measurements come from lampreys and from human beings, and the mammals between them are covered by inference alone.
options.why: Lampreys have not been measured. The measured range is mice to monkeys to human beings.

options.text: The measurements have not been made in any animal yet, and the whole cost-per-neuron idea is so far a guess from theory.
options.why: The finding is real in mammals. What is inferred is its extension to animals where it has not been measured.

items.stem: Nobody has measured the cost per neuron in a lamprey. Why does the chapter still think it reasonable to suppose that a lamprey’s neurons are costly in much the same way as a mammal’s?

options.text: Much of what makes a neuron costly is shared by all animals with neurons: after every signal, ions have to be pumped back across the membrane.
options.why: Correct. The shared mechanism is what makes the extension reasonable, though it remains an inference rather than a finding.

options.text: Lampreys are the direct ancestors of mammals, so whatever makes mammalian neurons costly was already true of the neurons of the lamprey.
options.why: Lampreys are modern animals, not ancestors. The reason given is a mechanism shared by every animal with neurons.

options.text: Lamprey neurons have been shown to be the same size as mammalian neurons, and size is what sets the running cost of each neuron.
options.why: Size does not set cost per neuron, and nothing in the chapter reports such a measurement.

options.text: Lampreys have about as many neurons as small mammals, so their brains must use about the same total amount of energy each day as a mouse’s.
options.why: The chapter reports no such count. The argument rests on ion pumping, shared by every animal with neurons.

items.stem: Besides energy, what two further problems does the chapter say separate structures raise?

options.text: Wiring, since structures that exchange signals need connections, and coordination, since something must settle which output wins.
options.why: Correct. These are the two costs that are about more than energy.

options.text: Interference, since separate structures disturb each other’s signals, and settling time, since they must agree before either one acts.
options.why: Interference and settling time are the costs the chapter charges to a single network, not to separate structures.

options.text: Growth, since each structure takes time to develop, and repair, since separate structures are harder to fix when damaged.
options.why: Neither growth time nor repair is named. The two further costs are wiring and coordination.

options.text: Heat, since separate structures warm the head, and weight, since each structure adds to what the neck must hold up.
options.why: The chapter names no costs of heat or weight. Its two non-energy problems are wiring and coordination.

items.stem: Two specialist structures exchange signals constantly. In one brain they sit side by side; in another they sit far apart. What does the chapter say the distant arrangement costs?

options.text: Longer connections, which take up more space and add more delay to every signal passed between the two structures.
options.why: Correct. Connections take space and add delay, the more so the longer they are.

options.text: Nothing extra, since a signal travels between two structures just as fast however far apart the two happen to be placed.
options.why: Longer connections add delay. Distance is not free.

options.text: Less energy but more errors, since distant structures fire less often but misread each other’s signals more often.
options.why: The chapter says nothing about error rates. The costs of distance are space and delay.

options.text: A second chooser, since two distant structures cannot be coordinated by the same circuitry that coordinates two close ones.
options.why: Coordination is a separate cost from wiring, and the chapter does not say distance calls for a second chooser.

items.stem: A fish’s visual specialist proposes a turn toward prey at the same moment its touch specialist proposes a dart away from a touch. Which cost of separate structures does this situation illustrate?

options.text: Coordination, since specialists can each produce an output at the same moment and something has to settle which output wins.
options.why: Correct. Specialists doing their own jobs can conflict, and settling the conflict is a cost of having them.

options.text: Wiring, since the visual and touch specialists need connections to the muscles, and those connections take up space in the body.
options.why: Wiring is a real cost, but the situation here is two outputs at once, which is the coordination problem.

options.text: Interference, since the two specialists share the same neurons at that moment, and their two patterns of activity overlap far too much.
options.why: Shared neurons and overlapping patterns describe a single network. These are separate specialists producing rival outputs.

options.text: Energy, since two specialists firing at once use twice the oxygen that either specialist uses while firing alone.
options.why: Energy is billed per neuron, but the problem shown is that two outputs arrive together and one must win.

items.stem: Imagine an animal with unlimited food, so that energy is never in short supply. Which costs of separate structures would it still pay?

options.text: The space and the time that wiring and coordination cost, since those are costs no amount of energy can buy back.
options.why: Correct. Wiring and coordination have an energy side, but they also cost space and time, and energy cannot pay for those.

options.text: No further cost, since all of the costs of separate structures come down in the end to the energy needed to run their neurons.
options.why: Wiring and coordination do have an energy side, but they also cost space and delay, which food cannot buy back.

options.text: Only the cost of the neurons themselves, since space and time are free once there is enough energy to run the wiring.
options.why: That reverses it. Energy covers the neurons; space and time are exactly what it cannot cover.

options.text: The interference and the settling time that separate structures suffer from, since those have no energy side at all.
options.why: Interference and settling time are costs of a single network. Separate structures pay in space and time for wiring and coordination.

items.stem: The chapter charges wiring and coordination to specialists as costs. What else do those same two facts explain?

options.text: Why the specialists sit together in one organ: short connections save space and time, and proposals must meet in one place to be compared.
options.why: Correct. The two costs, turned around, become the two reasons for a single organ. They are not new arguments.

options.text: Why the specialists are spread through the body: long connections are cheap, and each specialist can simply decide on its own output alone.
options.why: That reverses both costs. Long connections take space and time, and competing outputs have to meet to be compared.

options.text: Why the brain is priced per neuron: wiring and coordination are the only parts of a brain that use any energy at all.
options.why: Every neuron is billed, not just the wiring. The two costs explain where specialists end up.

options.text: Why fishes have a lateral line: the line’s organs are wired together along the body and coordinate the fish’s swimming.
options.why: The lateral line is a sense, not an explanation of placement. Wiring and coordination explain why specialists are gathered in one organ.

items.stem: Much of a human body’s touch sensation and muscle is far from the head. Why, on the chapter’s account, are the systems that control them not placed out near the limbs they serve?

options.text: Brains were not designed from scratch; evolution builds from what came before, and the human brain began from something like a fish’s.
options.why: Correct. A from-scratch design might spread the systems out. Evolution does not work that way.

options.text: Signals from the limbs of a human body are too weak to be processed anywhere but in the head, where the neurons are the most sensitive.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim about signal strength. Its answer is historical, about what the human brain started from.

options.text: Systems placed near the limbs would be too far from one another to share a blood supply, so they would be starved of oxygen whenever they worked hard.
options.why: Blood supply is not the chapter’s reason. The reason is that evolution builds from what came before.

options.text: The head is the safest place in the body, and a control system placed anywhere else would be much more exposed to injury.
options.why: Safety is a design argument, and the chapter’s answer is not about design. It is that evolution builds from what came before.

items.stem: How does the chapter describe natural selection, and what does it say follows from that description?

options.text: Differences that are more fit are more likely to lead to survival and reproduction, so evolution is stuck building from what came before.
options.why: Correct. Selection works on differences among what already exists, so a brain’s layout is inherited, not drawn fresh.

options.text: Differences that are more fit are worked out in advance from the needs of the animal, so evolution reaches the best layout for each job.
options.why: Nothing is worked out in advance, and there is no guarantee of a best layout. Evolution builds from what came before.

options.text: Differences that are more fit arise only in response to a new demand, so every part of a brain was favored for a reason of its own.
options.why: The chapter denies that every division was favored for a reason. Some features are side effects.

options.text: Differences that are more fit are passed on only when an animal learns them, so evolution follows whatever animals learn.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter makes selection follow learning. What follows from it is that evolution builds from what came before.

items.stem: A textbook says: “The brain sits in the head because that is the best place for it”. Which reply fits the chapter’s account?

options.text: The arrangement suited a fish-shaped ancestor whose whole body acted as one, and later vertebrates inherited it.
options.why: Correct. The chapter’s answer is historical. Short wiring and one meeting place for proposals favored keeping the arrangement, but it was inherited, not picked out as the best.

options.text: The statement is right, since each organ ends up in the location where it works best, and the head is that location.
options.why: Organs do not end up wherever they would work best. Evolution builds from what came before.

options.text: The brain sits in the head only in mammals, while fish brains are spread along the body so as to be near the fins.
options.why: A fish’s nervous system is centered in the head, between the eyes. The fish is where the arrangement came from.

options.text: The brain sits in the head because the eyes are there, and every other sense later moved forward to join them.
options.why: The chapter does not say the other senses moved. The arrangement came from a fish-shaped body acting as one.

items.stem: How does a fish’s body differ from an octopus’s in the way it is controlled?

options.text: Nearly everything a fish does uses the whole body, run from the head, while each octopus arm carries many neurons and runs much of its own control.
options.why: Correct. Nothing in a fish’s body works as independently as an octopus arm, and its nervous system is organized around a body acting as one.

options.text: Each of a fish’s fins carries its own share of neurons and runs much of its own control, like an octopus arm, while the octopus runs every arm directly from its head.
options.why: That reverses them. The octopus’s arms act with much independence; a fish acts with its whole body.

options.text: A fish and an octopus are controlled the same way, since both have one brain in the head that runs every movement.
options.why: The octopus is the chapter’s contrast case, because each arm runs much of its own control.

options.text: A fish’s body is run by its spinal cord alone, while the octopus is run by one brain between its eyes.
options.why: A fish’s nervous system is centered in the head, between the eyes. The octopus distributes much of its control into its arms.

items.stem: A fish turns, darts forward, strikes prey and escapes. What do these actions have in common that matters for how its nervous system is organized?

options.text: Each is done with the whole body, so the nervous system is organized around one body acting as one, centered in the head.
options.why: Correct. A fish has no arms, claws or tentacles to act with separately.

options.text: Each is done by a different fin or part of the body, so the nervous system is organized as several separate centers.
options.why: A fish acts with its whole body, not fin by fin, and its nervous system is centered in the head.

options.text: Each is a reflex of the spinal cord, so the nervous system needs no organ in the head at all to organize any of these actions.
options.why: A fish’s nervous system is centered in the head, between the eyes.

options.text: Each is learned from experience, so the nervous system is organized around a store of learned movements.
options.why: Learning is not the point here. What matters is that each action uses the body as one unit.

items.stem: The bilaterians of Module 4 reached a point where neurons had gathered at the front into fewer and larger clusters. What does the chapter say the vertebrate step added?

options.text: Differentiation: the same concentration of neurons at the front was divided into distinct parts, each specialized for some jobs more than others.
options.why: Correct. The step goes from gathering to differentiation. Gathering got the neurons to one place; dividing gave jobs their own parts.

options.text: Gathering itself: before the vertebrates, neurons were spread fairly evenly through the whole body, with no real concentration of them at the front.
options.why: Gathering at the front had already happened among the bilaterians. The vertebrate step divided the gathered neurons.

options.text: Dispersal: the gathered neurons were spread back out along the length of the body, into a separate control center for each of its parts.
options.why: That is closer to the octopus, which a fish does not resemble. The vertebrate step divided the concentration at the front.

options.text: Duplication: the gathered cluster was copied into a second brain at the tail, so that the two ends could act on their own.
options.why: The chapter describes no second brain. The concentration at the front was divided into parts.

items.stem: Two specialists in a fish’s brain exchange signals many times every second. Why does the chapter say they are better off close together?

options.text: Short connections take less space and carry signals sooner.
options.why: Correct. This is the wiring cost turned into a reason for one organ.

options.text: Close neurons share a blood supply and so each costs less energy.
options.why: Neurons are billed one by one, wherever they sit. The benefit of closeness is space and speed.

options.text: Close neurons learn each other’s jobs and so need no chooser at all.
options.why: Closeness does not remove the need to settle competing outputs. Its benefit is shorter wiring.

options.text: Short connections let each specialist ignore the other’s signals.
options.why: Specialists that exchange signals constantly need each other’s signals. Short wires deliver them sooner.

items.stem: Suppose a fish’s specialist for turning toward light sat in its tail, and its specialist for darting away from touch sat in its head. Besides longer wiring, what problem would the chapter point to?

options.text: Their competing proposals would have no single place to meet and be compared before one of them is chosen.
options.why: Correct. When specialists propose competing actions, the proposals have to meet in one place to be compared.

options.text: Their proposals would each drive a different half of the body, and the fish would simply split its movement in two.
options.why: A fish acts with its whole body and cannot turn two ways at once. The problem is where the proposals meet.

options.text: Their energy costs would double, since a neuron in the tail costs about twice as much to run as a neuron in the head.
options.why: Each neuron costs roughly the same wherever it is. The problem is comparing the proposals.

options.text: Their signals would all be self-caused, since any specialist outside the head produces signals the fish caused itself.
options.why: Where a specialist sits does not make its signals self-caused. The issue is getting proposals to one place to be compared.

items.stem: Human beings have limbs that can be moved independently, somewhat as an octopus’s arms can. Why is a human brain still one organ in the head rather than divided among the limbs?

options.text: Independently movable limbs came much later than the one-organ brain, which later vertebrates inherited from a fish-shaped body.
options.why: Correct. The arrangement suited a fish and was inherited. The limbs came later and are still run from the same kind of brain, centered in the head.

options.text: Human limbs are not really moved independently, since every movement of an arm is part of a whole-body movement, just as in a fish.
options.why: Human limbs can be moved independently. The reason for one organ is inheritance.

options.text: A brain divided among the limbs would cost more energy per neuron, since neurons far from the head are more expensive to run than neurons inside it.
options.why: Each neuron costs roughly the same wherever it is. The chapter’s reason is historical.

options.text: The human brain was rebuilt from scratch when limbs appeared, and a rebuilt brain works best as one organ in the head.
options.why: Brains are not rebuilt from scratch. Evolution builds from what came before, and limbs came to an existing brain.

items.stem: What senses fed the brain of early fishes, according to the chapter?

options.text: Good camera eyes, the old chemical senses of smell and taste, and the lateral line.
options.why: Correct. The senses came as a package, and the lateral line has no close equivalent in human beings.

options.text: Compound eyes like an arthropod’s, hearing through the bones of the skull, and the lateral line.
options.why: Early fishes had good camera eyes, not compound eyes like an arthropod’s, and the chapter’s package names the chemical senses of smell and taste.

options.text: Good camera eyes, echolocation like a bat’s, and pits along the snout that sense heat.
options.why: The chapter names none of these besides the eyes. It lists camera eyes, smell and taste, and the lateral line.

options.text: Smell and taste alone, since the first fishes were blind and found their food by chemicals.
options.why: Early fishes had good camera eyes. The package was eyes, chemical senses and the lateral line.

items.stem: What is the lateral line?

options.text: A line of small sensory organs along each side of a fish’s body that respond to movements of the surrounding water.
options.why: Correct. It works like touch at a distance, and human beings have no close equivalent.

options.text: A line of neurons along each side of a fish’s spinal cord that generates the rhythm of its swimming wave as it moves.
options.why: A circuit that generates a rhythm is a central pattern generator. The lateral line is a set of sense organs.

options.text: A line of small eyes along each side of a fish’s body that detect light arriving from above and below the fish.
options.why: The lateral line responds to water movement, not light. Its organs work like touch at a distance.

options.text: A line of fibers along the middle of a fish’s brain that connects its left and right halves together.
options.why: Fibers connecting the two halves form commissures. The lateral line is a line of sense organs on the body.

items.stem: What is the name for a line of small sensory organs along each side of a fish’s body that respond to movements of the surrounding water, working like touch at a distance?

options.text: The lateral line.
options.why: Correct. It is a sense with no close equivalent in human beings.

options.text: The tectum.
options.why: The tectum is the roof of the midbrain, holding a map of the space around the animal. It is part of the brain, not a line of sense organs.

options.text: The notochord.
options.why: The notochord is a stiff rod running along the back. It is a support, not a sense.

options.text: The central pattern generator.
options.why: A central pattern generator is a circuit that produces a rhythmic output, such as a swimming wave, without a rhythmic input. It is circuitry, not a line of sense organs.

items.stem: In murky water where it can see almost nothing, a fish follows the path a prey fish took several minutes earlier. Which sense is it most likely using?

options.text: The lateral line, which can feel the water displacement left by a fish that passed by minutes before.
options.why: Correct. The lateral line works like touch at a distance, sensitive enough to detect an old wake.

options.text: Its camera eyes, which even in murky water can still pick out the faint trail a fish leaves behind it.
options.why: The water is too murky to see through, and a wake is movement of water, not something to see.

options.text: Touch through the skin, which feels the prey fish directly as it brushes past the side of the hunting fish.
options.why: The prey passed minutes earlier, so nothing is touching the hunter now. The lateral line senses water movement at a distance.

options.text: A compass sense, which lets the fish steer in a straight line toward where the prey was minutes ago.
options.why: The chapter names no compass sense. Its example of sensing a fish that passed minutes earlier is the lateral line.

items.stem: A fish’s lateral line nerves include fibers that turn the sensory signal down whenever the fish’s own swimming is making the disturbance. Which demand on a moving animal’s nervous system does this help meet?

options.text: Telling its own doings from the world’s, by separating self-caused signals from the signals the world causes.
options.why: Correct. Like every other sense in a moving animal, the lateral line has to separate the fish’s own disturbances from the world’s.

options.text: Choosing one action when several are called for, by silencing every one of its own proposals except the strongest.
options.why: Choosing among actions is a different demand. The fibers damp self-caused sensation, not rival proposals.

options.text: Keeping going while changing course, by holding its own swimming rhythm steady whenever the fish turns.
options.why: The fibers act on a sensory signal, not on the swimming rhythm. They separate self-caused disturbance from the world’s.

options.text: Keeping what is learned while learning more, by protecting its old memories of water movement from new ones.
options.why: That is the plasticity–stability pair. The fibers deal with self-caused signals.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain what the cost-per-neuron finding says about how a brain’s energy cost is set, and say how far the finding reaches when it is applied to a lamprey.
items.answer: In mammals from mice to monkeys to human beings, the energy a brain uses rises in step with its number of neurons. Each neuron costs roughly the same to run, large or small, whichever brain it is in, so a brain’s cost is set mainly by how many neurons it has, not by its weight. But every measurement comes from mammals. Nobody has measured the cost per neuron in a lamprey, so applying the result to one is an inference, not a finding. It is a reasonable inference, because much of a neuron’s cost is shared by every animal with neurons: after every signal, ions have to be pumped back across the membrane.
rubric: Says cost rises with the number of neurons, not with weight.
Says each neuron costs roughly the same whatever its size or brain.
States that the measurements are mammalian only.
Calls the extension to a lamprey an inference rather than a finding.
Gives ion pumping after every signal as the reason the inference is reasonable.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the specialized parts of a vertebrate brain sit together in one organ in the head, without claiming that evolution put them there because the head was the best location.
items.answer: Evolution is stuck building from what came before, and the human brain started from a progenitor much more like a lamprey or a fish. A fish has no arms or tentacles to act with separately. Nearly everything it does, it does with its whole body, so its nervous system is organized around one body acting as one, centered in the head. Two things favored keeping the specialists together in that organ. Specialists that constantly exchange signals do better close together, since short connections take less space and carry signals sooner. And competing proposals have to meet in one place to be compared before one is chosen. The arrangement suited a fish, and later vertebrates, including those with independently movable limbs, inherited it.
rubric: Says evolution builds from what came before, not from a fresh design, starting from something much like a lamprey or a fish.
Describes the fish body acting as one, with its nervous system centered in the head.
Gives short connections as saving space and time.
Gives the need for competing proposals to meet in one place to be compared.
Says later vertebrates inherited the arrangement.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain the two costs of separate structures that are about more than energy, and why more energy would not remove them.
items.answer: The two costs are wiring and coordination. Structures that exchange signals need connections, and connections take up space and add delay, the more so the longer they are. Specialists can each produce an output at the same moment, so something has to settle which output wins. Both costs have an energy side, because wires and conflict-settling circuitry are made of neurons, and each neuron is billed. But both also cost space and time, which no amount of energy buys back. That is why they shape where the specialists end up in the body, and how they are made to agree.
rubric: Names wiring and coordination.
Says connections take space and add delay, more so when they are longer.
Says coordination means settling which of several simultaneous outputs wins.
Notes that both have an energy side, since wires and conflict-settling circuitry are made of neurons.
Says both also cost space and time that energy cannot buy back.

pools.title: First Vertebrates, the Lamprey’s Brain, and Old Parts
pools.covers: reading §6.1.7, §6.1.8, §6.1.9 · lecture 6.1 slides slivers_in_the_sea, parts_of_a_vertebrate_brain, new_structures_old_parts · lab Specimens, Plan

items.stem: What is a vertebrate?

options.text: An animal with a skull and a backbone, or at least the beginnings of a backbone.
options.why: Correct. The beginnings of a backbone are enough, which is why the jawless fishes, lampreys included, count as vertebrates.

options.text: An animal with jaws and paired fins, the body plan from which every amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal descends.
options.why: Jaws and paired fins came later. The first vertebrates had neither, and lampreys and hagfishes still have no jaws.

options.text: An animal with a large brain divided into distinct parts, and therefore among the most complex animals of its time.
options.why: Being a vertebrate is a matter of a skull and a backbone, not of complexity. The first vertebrates were small prey animals.

options.text: An animal with a stiff rod running along its back, of the kind it shares with its closest invertebrate relatives.
options.why: That rod is the notochord. The closest invertebrate relatives of the vertebrates have one too, so it does not make an animal a vertebrate.

items.stem: What is the name for the group of animals with a skull and a backbone, or at least the beginnings of one, a group that includes every fish, amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal?

options.text: Vertebrates.
options.why: Correct. Every fish counts, the jawless ones included, since the beginnings of a backbone are enough.

options.text: Jawed vertebrates.
options.why: Jawed vertebrates leave out the lampreys and hagfishes, which are fishes with a skull and the beginnings of a backbone but no jaws.

options.text: Arthropods.
options.why: Arthropods, such as insects, crabs and spiders, have an external skeleton rather than a backbone.

options.text: Bilaterians.
options.why: Bilaterians are a much larger group, including worms and insects, most of which have no skull or backbone.

items.stem: Early Cambrian rocks in southern China hold Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia, the oldest fossils most researchers accept as vertebrates. What were these animals like?

options.text: A few centimeters long, slender and toothless, and most likely prey for the arthropods around them.
options.why: Correct. The first vertebrates did not rule their seas. They were small, and the arthropods were the formidable animals.

options.text: Up to a meter long and covered in plates of bony armor, and too well protected for most predators to attack.
options.why: Armored jawless fishes up to a meter long came later, from the Ordovician onward, beginning about 485 million years ago.

options.text: Large hunters with jaws and rows of teeth, and the top predators of the seas in which they swam.
options.why: The first vertebrates had no jaws and no teeth. Jaws evolved more than 420 million years ago, long after them.

options.text: Anchored in place on the deep seafloor, filtering their food from the water through frond-shaped bodies.
options.why: Anchored frond-shaped organisms belong to the oldest Ediacaran assemblage, before the Cambrian. The first vertebrates swam.

items.stem: An octopus and a honeybee are both quite complex animals. How does the chapter use them to show what the word vertebrate does and does not mean?

options.text: Neither animal is a vertebrate, so being a vertebrate is a matter of a skull and a backbone, not of complexity.
options.why: Correct. Vertebrate is not another word for complex. It names a body plan, and some quite complex animals lack it.

options.text: Both animals are counted as vertebrates in a loose sense, since complexity is what the word vertebrate has come to mean.
options.why: No animal is a vertebrate in a loose sense. The octopus and the honeybee show that complexity and being a vertebrate come apart.

options.text: Both animals are less complex than any vertebrate, which shows that a skull and a backbone always bring complexity with them.
options.why: The chapter calls both animals quite complex, and the first vertebrates were small prey. A backbone brings no guarantee of complexity.

options.text: Neither animal is complex in the way a vertebrate is, since complexity requires a brain divided into distinct parts.
options.why: The chapter calls octopuses and honeybees quite complex. It does not define complexity by a divided brain.

items.stem: A documentary announces, “With the first vertebrates, the most advanced animals in the Cambrian seas had arrived”. Which point from the chapter corrects the announcement?

options.text: The first vertebrates were small prey in a sea full of very complex and very formidable arthropods.
options.why: Correct. This is Module 2’s warning against reading the tree of life as a ladder. The first vertebrates were not at the top of anything.

options.text: The first vertebrates did not appear in the Cambrian at all, but only after jaws evolved in the Ordovician period.
options.why: The first vertebrates are early Cambrian animals. Jaws came much later, more than 420 million years ago.

options.text: The most advanced animals were the Ediacaran grazers, which had already solved every problem a nervous system would ever face.
options.why: The Ediacaran grazers faced a small control problem, of still food and no hunting. The chapter ranks no animal as most advanced.

options.text: The first vertebrates were ahead of the arthropods in their jaws and teeth, but behind them in everything else.
options.why: The first vertebrates were toothless and had no jaws. In that sea they were most likely prey for the arthropods.

items.stem: What is the notochord?

options.text: A stiff rod running along the back, which vertebrates share with their closest invertebrate relatives.
options.why: Correct. The earliest vertebrates had one, and in most later vertebrates it is largely replaced by the backbone.

options.text: A cord of neural tissue running along the back, which carries signals between the brain and the body.
options.why: That is the spinal cord, which is neural tissue. The notochord is a stiff supporting rod, not part of the nervous system.

options.text: A population of cells that forms along the edges of the developing nervous system and then migrates through the body.
options.why: That is the neural crest. The notochord is a rod along the back, not a migrating population of cells.

options.text: A braincase of cartilage enclosing the front end of the nervous system, found in vertebrates and in none of their relatives.
options.why: A braincase belongs to the vertebrate new head. The notochord is shared with invertebrate relatives, which is why it does not make an animal a vertebrate.

items.stem: What is the name for the stiff rod running along the back that vertebrates share with their closest invertebrate relatives, and that in most vertebrates is largely replaced by the backbone?

options.text: The notochord.
options.why: Correct. The earliest vertebrates had a notochord, and in most later vertebrates it is largely replaced by the backbone.

options.text: The spinal cord.
options.why: The spinal cord also runs along the back, but it is neural tissue carrying signals, and the backbone encloses it rather than replacing it.

options.text: The neural crest.
options.why: The neural crest is a population of cells that migrates through the embryo. It is not a rod along the back.

options.text: The neural tube.
options.why: The neural tube is the hollow tube from which the brain and spinal cord are built. The stiff supporting rod is a different structure.

items.stem: Worms and insects have heads, with sense organs and neurons gathered at the front. What, then, was new about the head of the first vertebrates?

options.text: A particular package of paired camera eyes, a nose, ears, and an enlarged front end of the nervous system, all inside a braincase.
options.why: Correct. Concentrating senses and neurons at the front was old, as Module 4 showed. What was new was this particular package, enclosed in a skull.

options.text: The fact of having any neurons gathered at the front at all, since no animal before the vertebrates had ever concentrated them there.
options.why: That is the easy reading the chapter refuses. Module 4 followed neurons gathering at the front of bilaterians long before the vertebrates.

options.text: A pair of jaws lined with teeth, which let the head seize prey instead of scooping or filtering food from the water.
options.why: The first vertebrates were toothless and had no jaws. Jaws evolved more than 420 million years ago, long after the new head.

options.text: A front end of the nervous system divided into three layers of neurons, where a worm’s had only a single layer.
options.why: Three layers describes a lamprey’s pallium, not what was new about the head. The new head was a package of senses in a braincase.

items.stem: A reconstructed early Cambrian fossil shows a small braincase holding paired eyes, a nose and ears, but no jaws and no teeth. Which phrase from the chapter names what the braincase and its contents make up?

options.text: The new head: the package that the anatomists Carl Gans and Glenn Northcutt picked out as distinctive of vertebrates.
options.why: Correct. Gans and Northcutt’s phrase names the package of paired camera eyes, nose, ears and enlarged front of the nervous system, in a braincase.

options.text: The neural crest: the braincase and its sense organs themselves, which only vertebrates have in full.
options.why: The neural crest is a population of cells that builds much of the new head. It is the builder, not the package.

options.text: The notochord: the stiff rod that vertebrates share with their closest invertebrate relatives.
options.why: The notochord runs along the back and is shared with invertebrate relatives, so it is not what was new about the head.

options.text: The brainstem: the stalk connecting the spinal cord to the front of the brain, enlarged to serve the senses of the head.
options.why: The brainstem is the midbrain and hindbrain together. The package of senses in a braincase is the new head.

items.stem: What is the neural crest?

options.text: A population of cells that forms along the edges of the developing nervous system, then leaves it and migrates through the body.
options.why: Correct. Only vertebrates have it in full, and much of the new head is built from it.

options.text: A ridge of neurons along the roof of the midbrain that holds a map of the space around the animal and turns its eyes toward events.
options.why: That describes the tectum, the roof of the midbrain. The neural crest is a migrating population of embryonic cells.

options.text: A stiff rod running along the back of the embryo, which is later replaced by the backbone in most vertebrates.
options.why: That is the notochord. The neural crest is a population of cells, not a supporting rod.

options.text: A crest of bone along the top of the skull, where the muscles that work the jaws attach in the jawed fishes.
options.why: The name suggests a bony crest, but the neural crest is a population of cells. It does help build the skull, as cartilage and bone.

items.stem: What is the name for the population of cells, found in full only in vertebrates, that forms along the edges of the developing nervous system and migrates through the body, building much of the face and skull?

options.text: The neural crest.
options.why: Correct. Its cells become cartilage and bone of the face and skull, pigment cells, and most of the nerve cells outside the brain.

options.text: The neural plate.
options.why: The neural plate is the strip of cells that becomes the nervous system. The migrating cells leave from its edges once it has folded into a tube.

options.text: The radial glia.
options.why: Radial glia are progenitor cells inside the growing brain, whose fibers newborn neurons climb. They do not migrate out through the body.

options.text: The reticular formation.
options.why: The reticular formation is a network of cells in the brainstem that sets how awake an animal is. It is not an embryonic cell population.

items.stem: Suppose the neural crest cells of a fish embryo could be marked with a dye and followed as the animal develops. Where would the marked cells be expected to turn up?

options.text: In cartilage and bone of the face and skull, in pigment cells, and in most of the nerve cells lying outside the brain.
options.why: Correct. Those are what neural crest cells become. They leave the developing nervous system and build much of the head.

options.text: In the layers of the pallium, in the tectum, and in most of the nerve cells lying inside the brain and the spinal cord.
options.why: Crest cells leave the developing nervous system. They become most of the nerve cells outside the brain, not those inside it.

options.text: In the notochord, and in the backbone that largely replaces the notochord in most later vertebrates.
options.why: The notochord is shared with invertebrate relatives and is not built by the crest. The chapter names the face and skull, pigment cells, and nerve cells outside the brain.

options.text: In the muscles that bend the body from side to side, and in the blood cells that carry oxygen through it.
options.why: The chapter names neither muscle nor blood. Crest cells become cartilage and bone of the head, pigment cells, and nerve cells outside the brain.

items.stem: The invertebrate relatives of the vertebrates have cells with some of the neural crest’s features. How does the chapter describe the difference between those relatives and the vertebrates?

options.text: The relatives have cells with some of the features, and only vertebrates have the full set.
options.why: Correct. That is why the chapter calls the neural crest a population that only vertebrates have in full.

options.text: The relatives have the full set too, and vertebrates differ only in having more of those cells.
options.why: If the relatives had the full set, the neural crest would not be a vertebrate novelty. The chapter says only vertebrates have it in full.

options.text: Vertebrates have lost some of the features the relatives have, and gained others the relatives lack.
options.why: The chapter describes no loss. Vertebrates have the whole set of features that the relatives have only some of.

options.text: The relatives’ features arose independently, so the vertebrate crest owes nothing to any older cells or genes.
options.why: The chapter’s point runs the other way. The crest was assembled mostly out of old instructions the relatives already had.

items.stem: A fossil from the Ordovician shows a jawless fish nearly a meter long, its head covered in plates of bony armor. How did fishes like this one most likely feed?

options.text: By scooping, sucking or filtering food, since for all their fearsome look they had no way to bite.
options.why: Correct. Some armored jawless fishes looked fearsome, but without jaws they could not bite.

options.text: By biting large prey with the sharp edges of their head armor, which served them as a kind of jaw.
options.why: The chapter says they had no way to bite. Jaws came later, built on the supports of the front gills.

options.text: By hunting small arthropods with rows of sharp teeth set around the rim of a round, jawless mouth.
options.why: The armored fishes had no way to bite, and the chapter credits them with no teeth. They probably scooped, sucked or filtered.

options.text: By grazing on microbial mats and moving on, leaving rows of faint body-shaped impressions behind them.
options.why: That is how Dickinsonia, an Ediacaran grazer, fed, long before the Ordovician.

items.stem: Jaws evolved more than 420 million years ago. According to the chapter, what structure did they build on?

options.text: The supports of the front gills.
options.why: Correct. Jaws were built from material already there, the supports of the front gills.

options.text: The plates of bony armor on the head.
options.why: The armored jawless fishes had head plates but no way to bite. The chapter names the gill supports as what jaws built on.

options.text: The notochord running along the back.
options.why: The notochord is a rod along the back, largely replaced by the backbone. It has nothing to do with jaws in the chapter.

options.text: The toothed disc of a lamprey’s mouth.
options.why: A living lamprey is not an ancestor of the jawed fishes, and its disc takes the place of a jaw. Jaws built on the front gill supports.

items.stem: How did the fishes of around 360 million years ago differ from those of the Ordovician, and what remains of the jawless fishes today?

options.text: Jawed fishes had diversified and most jawless fishes were gone; only the hagfishes and the lampreys survive.
options.why: Correct. Two jawless lineages survive, and the lamprey belongs to one of them.

options.text: Jawless fishes had diversified and most jawed fishes were gone; only the sharks and the bony fishes still survive.
options.why: That reverses the two groups. It was the jawed fishes that diversified and the jawless ones that mostly disappeared.

options.text: Jawed and jawless fishes had both diversified; dozens of jawless lineages survive in the deep sea today.
options.why: Most jawless fishes were gone by about 360 million years ago. Only two jawless lineages survive.

options.text: Armored jawless fishes had given rise to the lampreys; the hagfishes arose much later, from a jawed ancestor.
options.why: The chapter names the hagfishes and lampreys as the two surviving jawless lineages. Neither is said to descend from a jawed ancestor.

items.stem: Put these events in the order in which they happened: jaws evolve; the first vertebrates appear; armored jawless fishes up to a meter long appear; most jawless fishes are gone.

options.text: First vertebrates, then armored jawless fishes, then jaws, then most jawless fishes gone.
options.why: Correct. The first vertebrates are early Cambrian; armored jawless fishes date from about 485 million years ago, jaws from more than 420, and the loss of most jawless fishes from about 360.

options.text: First vertebrates, then jaws, then armored jawless fishes, then most jawless fishes gone.
options.why: The armored jawless fishes, from about 485 million years ago, came before jaws, which evolved more than 420 million years ago.

options.text: Armored jawless fishes, then first vertebrates, then jaws, then most jawless fishes gone.
options.why: Armored jawless fishes were themselves vertebrates, so they cannot come before the first vertebrates.

options.text: First vertebrates, then armored jawless fishes, then the loss of most jawless fishes, then jaws.
options.why: Most jawless fishes were gone after jawed fishes had diversified, so jaws must come before that loss.

items.stem: To learn what the brain of the earliest vertebrates contained, the chapter compares a lamprey’s brain with a mouse’s. Why is the lamprey more useful for this purpose than another mammal, such as a rat, would be?

options.text: The lamprey’s jawless lineage split off early, so what it shares with a mouse points to the ancestor of both jawless and jawed vertebrates.
options.why: Correct. What two brains share is best evidence about their common ancestor. A rat and a mouse share a recent mammal ancestor; a lamprey and a mouse share a far older one.

options.text: The lamprey is the ancestor of the mouse and the other jawed vertebrates, so its brain shows the mouse’s as it was before later changes.
options.why: No living animal is an ancestor of another. A lamprey is a modern animal whose lineage has been evolving as long as the mouse’s.

options.text: The lamprey’s brain is a simpler rough draft of a mammal’s, so its parts are easier to see there, before the mammals elaborated them further.
options.why: The chapter says outright that a lamprey’s brain is not a rough draft of a mammal’s. Its usefulness comes from the comparative inference.

options.text: The lamprey’s brain has every one of the parts a mouse’s has, so the comparison needs no inference about any part that is missing.
options.why: The lamprey lacks a cerebellum in the form jawed vertebrates have. Its usefulness comes from what it shares, read as an inference.

items.stem: What is the spinal cord?

options.text: The cord of neural tissue along the back, which carries signals between brain and body and runs some movements on its own.
options.why: Correct. It is the long tail end of the vertebrate nervous system, and at its front it widens into the brain.

options.text: The stiff rod running along the back, which is shared with the closest invertebrate relatives and later replaced by the backbone.
options.why: That is the notochord, a supporting rod. The spinal cord is neural tissue.

options.text: The stalk formed by the midbrain and the hindbrain together, which connects the front of the brain to the rest of the body.
options.why: That is the brainstem. The spinal cord lies behind it and runs along the back.

options.text: The rearmost division of the brain, which controls breathing, the heartbeat and other jobs that keep an animal alive.
options.why: That is the hindbrain, which is continuous with the spinal cord but is a division of the brain itself.

items.stem: What is the name for the cord of neural tissue running along a vertebrate’s back, which carries signals between the brain and the body and runs some movements on its own?

options.text: The spinal cord.
options.why: Correct. The spinal cord is the tail end of the nervous system, and it widens at its front into the brain.

options.text: The notochord.
options.why: The notochord also runs along the back, but it is a stiff supporting rod rather than neural tissue.

options.text: The brainstem.
options.why: The brainstem is the midbrain and hindbrain, the stalk joining the spinal cord to the front of the brain. It lies inside the head.

options.text: The central pattern generator.
options.why: A central pattern generator is a circuit that produces a rhythm, such as the ones in a lamprey’s spinal cord. It is a circuit within the cord, not the cord itself.

items.stem: What is the hindbrain?

options.text: The rearmost of the three main divisions, continuous with the spinal cord, which controls breathing, the heartbeat and other jobs that keep an animal alive.
options.why: Correct. The spinal cord widens at its front into three divisions, and the hindbrain is the rearmost of them.

options.text: The front of the brain’s three main divisions, whose roof receives signals from the senses and sends commands down to the brainstem and spinal cord.
options.why: That describes the forebrain and its roof, the pallium. The hindbrain is at the other end, joined to the spinal cord.

options.text: The middle of the brain’s three main divisions, whose roof holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and the eyes toward events.
options.why: That describes the midbrain and its roof, the tectum. The hindbrain lies behind the midbrain.

options.text: A large structure attached to the back of the brain, which in jawed vertebrates adjusts movements by learning from the errors they make.
options.why: That is the cerebellum, which is attached to the back of the hindbrain. It is not one of the three main divisions.

items.stem: What is the name for the rearmost of the three main divisions of the vertebrate brain, continuous with the spinal cord, which controls breathing and the heartbeat?

options.text: The hindbrain.
options.why: Correct. It runs the jobs that keep an animal alive.

options.text: The midbrain.
options.why: The midbrain lies in front of the hindbrain, and its roof is the tectum. It is not the rearmost division.

options.text: The cerebellum.
options.why: The cerebellum is attached to the back of the hindbrain in jawed vertebrates. It adjusts movements rather than running breathing and heartbeat.

options.text: The brainstem.
options.why: The brainstem is the hindbrain and midbrain together, so it names more than the rearmost division alone.

items.stem: What is the midbrain?

options.text: The middle of the brain’s three main divisions, lying in front of the hindbrain, with the tectum as its roof.
options.why: Correct. The midbrain sits between the hindbrain and the forebrain, and together with the hindbrain it forms the brainstem.

options.text: The front of the brain’s three main divisions, holding the hypothalamus, the thalamus, the basal ganglia and the pallium.
options.why: That is the forebrain. The midbrain lies behind it.

options.text: The stalk formed by the hindbrain and the forebrain together, which connects the spinal cord to the pallium.
options.why: The stalk is the brainstem, and it is made of the midbrain and hindbrain, not the hindbrain and forebrain.

options.text: The deep middle of the forebrain, where connected clusters of neurons determine which proposed action is released.
options.why: That describes the basal ganglia, deep in the forebrain. The midbrain is a division of its own.

items.stem: What is the name for the division of the vertebrate brain that lies in front of the hindbrain and behind the forebrain, and whose roof is the tectum?

options.text: The midbrain.
options.why: Correct. It is the middle of the three main divisions.

options.text: The brainstem.
options.why: The brainstem includes the midbrain, but it also includes the hindbrain, so it is more than the one division.

options.text: The thalamus.
options.why: The thalamus is in the forebrain, above the hypothalamus. It relays sense signals rather than being a division of its own.

options.text: The hypothalamus.
options.why: The hypothalamus sits at the base of the forebrain. The division with the tectum as its roof lies behind the forebrain.

items.stem: What is the tectum?

options.text: The roof of the midbrain, which holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and eyes toward what appears there.
options.why: Correct. The map is built from what the eyes and the other senses report.

options.text: The roof of the forebrain, a sheet of neurons that receives relayed signals from the senses and sends commands down to the brainstem and spinal cord.
options.why: That is the pallium. The tectum is the roof of the midbrain, one division further back.

options.text: A structure in the forebrain that relays signals from the senses into the pallium and carries signals back out again.
options.why: That is the thalamus. The tectum holds a map of surrounding space and turns the head and eyes.

options.text: A large structure on the back of the hindbrain that adjusts movements by learning from their errors.
options.why: That is the cerebellum, found in every jawed vertebrate. The tectum is the roof of the midbrain.

items.stem: What is the name for the roof of the midbrain, which holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and eyes toward what appears there?

options.text: The tectum.
options.why: Correct. The tectum is the roof of the midbrain in every vertebrate, lamprey included.

options.text: The pallium.
options.why: The pallium is a roof too, but of the forebrain, and it sends commands down to the brainstem and spinal cord.

options.text: The thalamus.
options.why: The thalamus relays signals from the senses into the pallium. It is not the roof of the midbrain.

options.text: The cerebellum.
options.why: The cerebellum sits on the back of the hindbrain in jawed vertebrates and adjusts movements. It holds no map of the space around the animal.

items.stem: A small object moves into view off to one side of a frog, and the frog’s head and eyes turn toward the object. Which structure, the one that received most of the frog’s visual input in Module 2, carries out this turn?

options.text: The tectum, the roof of the midbrain, which holds a map of the space around the animal.
options.why: Correct. The tectum’s map is built from what the eyes and other senses report, and it turns the head and eyes toward what appears there.

options.text: The pallium, the roof of the forebrain, which receives relayed sense signals and sends commands down.
options.why: The pallium does receive sense signals, but most of the frog’s visual input went to the tectum, which does the orienting.

options.text: The thalamus, above the hypothalamus, which relays signals from the senses into the roof of the forebrain.
options.why: The thalamus relays signals into the pallium. The turn toward something in view is the tectum’s job.

options.text: The cerebellum, on the back of the hindbrain, which adjusts movements by learning from their errors.
options.why: The cerebellum tunes movements from their errors. Turning toward an object that has just appeared is the tectum’s job.

items.stem: What is the brainstem?

options.text: The midbrain and hindbrain together, forming the stalk that connects the spinal cord to the front of the brain.
options.why: Correct. The brainstem is two of the three main divisions, taken together.

options.text: The hindbrain and spinal cord together, forming the cord that carries signals between the brain and the rest of the body.
options.why: The spinal cord is not part of the brainstem. The brainstem is the midbrain and hindbrain.

options.text: The forebrain and midbrain together, forming the swollen front end of the nervous system that sits inside the skull.
options.why: The forebrain is the front of the brain that the brainstem connects to. The brainstem is the midbrain and hindbrain.

options.text: The thalamus and hypothalamus together, forming the base of the forebrain beneath its roof, the pallium.
options.why: Those two are forebrain structures. The brainstem lies behind the forebrain.

items.stem: What is the name for the midbrain and hindbrain taken together, the stalk that connects the spinal cord to the front of the brain?

options.text: The brainstem.
options.why: Correct. It joins the spinal cord to the forebrain.

options.text: The forebrain.
options.why: The forebrain is the front of the brain that the stalk connects to, not the stalk itself.

options.text: The spinal cord.
options.why: The spinal cord runs along the back and widens at its front into the brain. The stalk it connects to is the brainstem.

options.text: The neural tube.
options.why: The neural tube is the embryonic tube from which the whole brain and spinal cord are built.

items.stem: What is the forebrain?

options.text: The front of the three main divisions, holding several structures with distinct jobs, among them the hypothalamus, thalamus, basal ganglia and pallium.
options.why: Correct. The forebrain is found in every vertebrate, lamprey included, and holds several structures.

options.text: The front of the brain’s three main divisions, which is found only in mammals and is made up entirely of the six-layered neocortex.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a forebrain. The neocortex is the mammalian form of just one of its structures, the pallium.

options.text: The middle of the brain’s three main divisions, whose roof holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and eyes toward what appears there.
options.why: That is the midbrain, whose roof is the tectum. The forebrain lies in front of it.

options.text: The swollen front end of the spinal cord, which runs the jobs that keep an animal alive, such as breathing and the heartbeat.
options.why: That describes the hindbrain, the rearmost division. The forebrain is at the other end of the brain.
