options.text: The part’s outputs run directly to the circuits that drive the muscles, and to nothing else in the brain.
options.why: Wiring confined to the motor circuits would count in favor. Doubt comes when a part’s activity simply mirrors whatever it is wired to.

items.stem: In the lab, recordings were taken from a generic mammal’s brain while it learned to freeze to a tone paired with a shock, and while it learned to approach a light that predicted food. What did the recordings show for the amygdala across those two tasks?

options.text: It recorded high in both of them, in the task about a threat and in the task about food alike.
options.why: Correct. A structure recorded high during a threat task and during a food task is not selective for threat, which is the first crack in a recording-only table.

options.text: It recorded high during the tone and shock and low during the light and food, as a structure for threat would.
options.why: That is the pattern a structure dedicated to threat would show, and it is not what the recording showed. The amygdala was high during the food task too.

options.text: It recorded high during the light and food and low during the tone and shock, as a structure for reward would.
options.why: This reverses the threat-only reading but keeps the idea of one job. The recording was high during both tasks.

options.text: It showed no result for either task, since the chapter reports nothing about the amygdala in a learning task.
options.why: Gray cells did appear on the bench wherever the chapter supports no result, but not for the amygdala in these two tasks. It recorded high during both.

items.stem: In the lab’s record-only step, the basal ganglia were recorded at their input stage, the striatum, during each of six tasks. What pattern did the striatum show?

options.text: Activity in several quite different tasks, from orienting toward a flash to approaching a cue that predicted food.
options.why: Correct. Like the recordings the chapter describes, the striatum was active across tasks, so a job assigned from its row alone was a reverse inference.

options.text: Activity during the lever task alone, since that is the one task in which the animal worked for a reward.
options.why: The striatum was not confined to the lever. It was active while the animal oriented to a flash and while it approached a food cue.

options.text: Activity only in the tasks that were trained, and none at all while the animal oriented toward a flash.
options.why: Orienting is not a trained task, and the striatum still recorded activity during it. Its activity was not restricted to learning.

options.text: No activity in any task until the dopamine clusters were stimulated, since the striatum waits on dopamine before it can act at all.
options.why: The striatum recorded activity in the record-only step, before any stimulation. The row was broad, not empty.

items.stem: Reverse inference has now appeared three times in the book: for a region in brain imaging, for a mechanism, and for the structures of a vertebrate brain. In a short paragraph, define reverse inference and say what the three cases have in common.
items.answer: Reverse inference is going from “this region was active during the task” to “therefore, the task involved the process that region does”. In brain imaging, a region active during fear is also active during a great many other things, so its activation is weak evidence that fear was what mattered. For a mechanism, the coincidence detection and gating that change a synapse during learning also wire a nervous system during development, so finding them at work does not show which job is being done. The cerebellum and the basal ganglia are active during movement, perception, planning and thought. In all three cases one thing turns up in many jobs, and something active during many different things licenses very little on its own.
rubric: Defines reverse inference as the move from a region’s activity during a task to the conclusion that the task used that region’s process.
Describes the imaging case: a region active during fear is also active during many other things.
Describes the mechanism case as a mechanism, not a region, serving both learning and development.
Describes the vertebrate case: the cerebellum and basal ganglia active during movement and much else.
States the common thread: something active during many different things licenses little on its own.

items.stem: In the lab, a table of what each structure is for was filled in using recordings alone. In a short paragraph, explain why every entry in that column was a reverse inference, and use one structure’s recorded pattern from the lab as the example.
items.answer: Each entry went from “this structure was active during these tasks” to “so it is for the process those tasks involve”, which is the definition of reverse inference. The inference is only as good as the structure’s selectivity, and most structures were not selective. The amygdala, for example, recorded high during the tone paired with a shock and also during the light that predicted food, so writing that it is for fear or threat ignored half of its own row. The striatum was active in tasks as different as orienting to a flash and approaching a food cue. A recording shows that a structure is active, not what it is for, and a structure active during many different things licenses very little on its own.
rubric: Identifies each entry as a move from activity during a task to the process the structure performs.
Gives a structure’s recorded pattern from the lab accurately, such as the amygdala high in both the threat task and the food task.
Explains why that pattern undercuts a single-job entry, since the structure was not selective.
States that a structure active during many different things licenses very little on its own.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the chapter’s two levels of a single change in learning, and use them to say what the question “where does reinforcement learning happen?” is really asking.
items.answer: Two different things get called learning. A family of learning is usually named for what the whole animal ends up able to do, such as finding food or avoiding what hurt it last time. But the change itself happens at individual connections, and a single synapse cannot be told what the animal should have done, since it has no way to understand the meaning of anything that complex. Whatever reaches a synapse has to be about its own inputs and its own output. So each family is a pairing: an animal-level problem, and the particular information that has to reach a synapse for the synapse to help solve it. Anatomy answers the second half. Asking where reinforcement learning happens is asking where the machinery is that delivers a verdict to the synapses that produced the action, not where the animal’s goals are.
rubric: Names the animal-level half: what the whole animal ends up able to do.
Names the synapse-level half: the change at an individual connection, which can use only information about its own inputs and output.
States that each family of learning is a pairing of the two.
Says the anatomical question concerns the second half, what has to reach the synapse.
Applies it to reinforcement learning as where a verdict is delivered to the synapses that produced the action.

pools.title: Learning Without a Teacher, from an Error, and from a Verdict
pools.covers: reading §6.2.3, §6.2.4, §6.2.5 · lecture 6.2 slides learning_without_a_teacher, error_output_by_output, learning_from_a_verdict · lab Bench

items.stem: What does unsupervised learning, the family Module 5 called Hebbian, need before a connection will change?

options.text: Nothing but the activity of the two cells that the connection joins.
options.why: Correct. Both quantities the rule needs are already at the connection, so nothing has to be delivered from anywhere else.

options.text: An error computed for each output, which the world delivers a moment later.
options.why: That is what prediction learning needs. Unsupervised learning needs no error at all, only the two cells’ own activity.

options.text: A statement of what the output should have been, from something that knows it.
options.why: That is what supervised learning needs, and it almost never exists inside an animal. Unsupervised learning needs no target.

options.text: A broadcast report of how things went, addressed to no output in particular.
options.why: That is what reinforcement learning needs. Unsupervised learning needs nothing from outside the connection.

items.stem: A rat hears a tone, and food arrives a moment later. Why does the connection from the cells carrying the tone to the cells driving the response to food get stronger?

options.text: Food already makes the response cells fire, and the tone cells are firing at that same moment, so both ends of the connection are active together.
options.why: Correct. Both ends active together is the entire condition Hebb’s rule requires, and nothing else has to reach the connection.

options.text: The food releases a reward signal that reaches the tone connection and reports that the tone was the right thing for the rat to have heard at that moment.
options.why: A reward signal is what reinforcement learning uses. The tone connection strengthens simply because both of its ends are active together.

options.text: The rat notices that the tone predicts food and strengthens the connection because doing so will bring it food more quickly.
options.why: Nothing in the rat has to know that the tone predicts food. That is what makes the learning unsupervised.

options.text: An error signal reports that the response cells fired too late after the tone, and the tone connection is adjusted until the timing is right.
options.why: An error about timing is what the rabbit’s blink needs, delivered by a climbing fiber. The rat’s tone connection needs only co-occurrence.

items.stem: After enough pairings of a tone with food, what happens when the rat hears the tone alone, and what is the result called?

options.text: The tone alone drives the response, and that is classical conditioning.
options.why: Correct. The strengthened tone connection can now drive the response cells without the food.

options.text: The food alone no longer drives the response, and that is called blocking.
options.why: The food still drives the response, since it did so before any training. Blocking is a different result, about cues that were already predicted.

options.text: The tone drives the response only when food follows, and that is supervised learning.
options.why: After conditioning the tone drives the response by itself. Supervised learning needs a teacher holding the correct output, which the rat never had.

options.text: The rat presses a lever more often when the tone sounds, and that is reinforcement learning.
options.why: Pressing a lever more often is the animal-level problem of the lever task. The tone-and-food case ends in a conditioned response.

items.stem: The chapter calls the rat’s tone-and-food conditioning unsupervised. What makes it so?

options.text: Nothing in the rat had to know that the tone predicted food, or that any learning was going on.
options.why: Correct. The change is driven by co-occurrence alone, with no signal saying what should have happened.

options.text: No experimenter stood by to reward the rat each time that it responded to the tone correctly.
options.why: Whether an experimenter rewards the rat is not the point. The learning needs nothing delivered to the connection at all.

options.text: No older rat was present in the chamber to show the young rat how to respond to the tone.
options.why: No demonstrator was present, but that is not the chapter’s reason. The learning is unsupervised because nothing in the rat had to know the tone predicted food, or that it was learning.

options.text: The tone and the food arrived at random times, so nothing linked one to the other in the rat’s world.
options.why: The tone reliably came just before the food, which is why the connection strengthened. Unsupervised means no knowledge was needed, not that nothing was regular.

items.stem: A tone is paired again and again with a second stimulus that produces no response of any kind in an untrained animal. On the chapter’s account of what happens at the synapse, what becomes of the connection from the cells carrying the tone to the response cells?

options.text: It does not change, since nothing makes the response cells fire and so there is no co-occurrence to detect.
options.why: Correct. That is what an unconditioned stimulus is for at the synapse: something has to make the postsynaptic cell fire, or nothing changes.

options.text: It strengthens, since the tone and the second stimulus arrive together in time on every single pairing.
options.why: Two stimuli arriving together is not enough. The rule needs both ends of the tone connection active, and the response cells never fire.

options.text: It weakens, since the second stimulus fails to produce a response and so counts as an error for the tone.
options.why: No error is computed in unsupervised learning. With no firing at the response cells, there is simply nothing for the rule to detect.

options.text: It strengthens slowly, since a weak second stimulus still adds a little activity at the response cells each time.
options.why: The second stimulus produces no response at all, so it adds no activity at the response cells. There is nothing for the connection to pair with.

items.stem: Run the co-occurrence rule across everything an animal senses. What do its connections come to mirror, and how does that relate to learning the statistics of its input?

options.text: Which things in its world turn up together; learning that and learning the statistics of the input are one event described at two levels.
options.why: Correct. What goes with what, at the level of the animal, is the statistics of the input, at the level of the connections.

options.text: Which things in its world were followed by a reward; learning that and learning the statistics of the input are two separate processes at work.
options.why: Reward plays no part in the co-occurrence rule. What the connections mirror is simply what turns up together.

options.text: Which of its movements succeeded; learning that and learning the statistics of the input happen in two different structures.
options.why: Success of a movement needs an error or a verdict. The co-occurrence rule mirrors only which things turn up together.

options.text: Which things the animal attended to; learning that and learning the statistics of the input compete for the same connections.
options.why: The rule needs no attention; it strengthens whatever is active together. The two descriptions are of one event, not two in competition.

items.stem: While a rat was being conditioned to a tone paired with food, a ventilation fan happened to be running. What does the co-occurrence rule do with the connection carrying the fan’s sound?

options.text: It strengthens that connection too, since the fan’s sound was present while the response cells fired.
options.why: Correct. The rule cannot tell a meaningful sound from one that happened to be there. That is one of the limits Module 5 put on it.

options.text: It leaves that connection alone, since the rule can tell a meaningful sound apart from background noise.
options.why: The rule has no way to judge meaning. Anything active when the response cells fire is strengthened.

options.text: It weakens that connection, since the fan was running before the food arrived as well as while it was eaten.
options.why: The rule described in the chapter strengthens what is active together. It does not punish a sound for being present at other times.

options.text: It strengthens that connection only if the fan’s sound predicted the food better than the tone did.
options.why: Sensitivity to what was already predicted is what blocking showed in actual conditioning. The bare co-occurrence rule has no such sensitivity.

items.stem: What did the blocking result show about actual conditioning, and what does that mean for the co-occurrence rule as an account of conditioning?

options.text: Conditioning tracks only what was not already predicted, so the rule is the beginning of an account rather than the whole.
options.why: Correct. A bare co-occurrence rule would strengthen every cue that co-occurs. Real conditioning does not, so something more is at work.

options.text: Conditioning tracks every co-occurrence equally, so the co-occurrence rule is a complete account of conditioning.
options.why: That is exactly what blocking ruled out. Conditioning skips cues whose outcome was already predicted.

options.text: Conditioning is blocked whenever no teacher is present, so the co-occurrence rule needs a teacher to supply the part that is missing.
options.why: Blocking has nothing to do with teachers. It shows that conditioning tracks what was not already predicted.

options.text: Conditioning blocks background sounds such as a ventilation fan automatically, so the fan problem never arises in practice.
options.why: Blocking concerns cues that add no new prediction. It does not rescue the rule from strengthening the fan’s connection.

items.stem: Why does unsupervised learning need no special circuitry to deliver its signal, and where in a vertebrate brain are its synapses found?

options.text: Only local information is needed, so nothing has to be delivered, and co-occurrence-sensitive synapses are found throughout the brain.
options.why: Correct. A rule that needs only the two cells a connection joins needs no delivery route, so it is not confined to one structure.

options.text: Its signal is carried by the thalamus, so its synapses are found wherever the thalamus sends its fibers up into the roof of the forebrain, the pallium.
options.why: The thalamus relays signals from the senses; it is not a teaching route. Unsupervised learning needs no delivered signal at all.

options.text: Its signal is carried by the climbing fibers, so its synapses are found in the cerebellum and in no other structure.
options.why: Climbing fibers deliver an error for one output cell, which prediction and supervised learning need. Unsupervised learning needs no error.

options.text: Its signal is made inside the pallium, so its synapses are found in the pallium and nowhere else in the brain.
options.why: The pallium is Doya’s candidate for where this learning matters most, but co-occurrence-sensitive synapses are found throughout the brain.

items.stem: Co-occurrence-sensitive synapses are found throughout a vertebrate brain. Why, then, does Doya single out the pallium as the place where unsupervised learning is particularly important?

options.text: Because nothing else arrives there, not because coincidence detection happens only in the pallium.
options.why: Correct. The case is an argument from absence: with no teaching pathway, the statistics of the pallium’s own input are all it has.

options.text: Because coincidence detection happens in the pallium and nowhere else, so the pallium is where this learning must occur.
options.why: That gets the argument backwards. Coincidence detection happens everywhere; the pallium is singled out because nothing else arrives there.

options.text: Because the pallium is the newest structure in the vertebrate brain, and newer structures are the more flexible learners.
options.why: The pallium is present in every vertebrate, including the lamprey. Its claim rests on what does not arrive there, not on its age.

options.text: Because a teaching pathway into the pallium has been traced, and it carries a signal reporting what went together.
options.why: No dedicated teaching pathway into the pallium has been found. That absence is the whole basis of its claim.

items.stem: Which features of the pallium does the chapter give for why the statistics of its own input are what it learns from?

options.text: It is layered, heavily recurrent, receives information from everywhere, and has no dedicated teaching pathway anyone has found.
options.why: Correct. With input from everywhere and no teaching signal arriving, the pallium has only the statistics of what it receives to learn from.

options.text: Each of its output cells gets roughly two hundred thousand ordinary inputs and a single climbing fiber from one source.
options.why: That describes a cerebellar output cell, which receives an error delivered cell by cell. The pallium receives no teaching fiber.

options.text: Dopamine fibers from the midbrain arrive at its synapses and report to it how things went after every single action the animal takes.
options.why: Dopamine fibers arrive where the pallium meets the striatum, which is the reinforcement case. The pallium’s claim is that nothing arrives.

options.text: It is small, old, and positioned to reach almost every other part of the brain with a signal that sets the brain’s global conditions.
options.why: That describes the small clusters in the brainstem and midbrain that send broad projections. The pallium receives rather than broadcasts.

items.stem: What does prediction learning need before a connection will change?

options.text: The next input, which the world delivers on its own.
options.why: Correct. The world supplies the answer a moment later, so no teacher is needed.

options.text: The activity of the two cells a connection joins, and nothing else.
options.why: That is all unsupervised learning needs. Prediction learning needs an error, supplied by the next input.

options.text: A statement of the correct output from something that already knows it.
options.why: That is supervised learning’s requirement. In prediction learning the target comes from the world.

options.text: A report of how things went, broadcast to many connections at once.
options.why: That is reinforcement learning’s requirement. Prediction learning’s error is specific to one output.

items.stem: A rabbit hears a tone, and a quarter of a second later a puff of air is delivered to its eye. After training, what does the rabbit do?

options.text: It closes its eye at just the right time, so the eye is already closed when the puff arrives.
options.why: Correct. The rabbit predicts the puff from the tone and times its blink to meet it.

options.text: It closes its eye as soon as the tone begins, and keeps the eye shut until the tone has stopped.
options.why: Closing at the tone’s onset would not be timed to the puff. What the rabbit learns is exactly when to blink.

options.text: It blinks only after the puff lands on its eye, but a little faster than it did before training.
options.why: A faster reflex after the puff would still leave the puff landing on an open eye. The trained blink comes before the puff.

options.text: It stops blinking to the puff altogether, having learned that the puff does it no lasting harm.
options.why: The rabbit learns to meet the puff, not to ignore it. Its eye is closed when the puff arrives.

items.stem: In the rabbit’s eyeblink conditioning, what exactly did the rabbit have to learn, and was there a teacher to tell it?

options.text: Not whether to blink but exactly when, and no teacher told it when.
options.why: Correct. A blink to a puff already happens without training. What is learned is its timing, and there is no teacher to supply the right time.

options.text: Whether to blink at all, and the puff of air acted as a teacher telling it that blinking was right.
options.why: The rabbit already blinks to a puff, and the puff is not a teacher. What had to be learned was the timing, not whether to blink.

options.text: Exactly when to blink, and the experimenter told it the right time on each trial.
options.why: The timing is what is learned, but no one tells the rabbit the right time. That would make it supervised learning.

options.text: Whether to fear the tone, and a reward after each closed eye told it so.
options.why: Nothing in the case involves fear or reward. The rabbit learns the timing of one output.

items.stem: The rat’s tone and food, and the rabbit’s tone and puff, are both classical conditioning at the animal level. What does the chapter say differs between them?

options.text: What had to change: an association between two events for the rat, and the timing of one output for the rabbit.
options.why: Correct. A co-occurrence rule can deliver the association but not the timing, so one animal-level name covers two synapse-level requirements.

options.text: The animal-level name: the rat’s case is classical conditioning, but the rabbit’s is really reinforcement learning.
options.why: The chapter says both are classical conditioning at the animal level. The difference is in what had to change at the synapse.

options.text: The sense involved: the rat hears its signal while the rabbit feels one, and different senses learn by different rules.
options.why: Both animals hear a tone first. The difference lies in what had to change, not in which sense carried the second event.

options.text: The species: rodents learn by co-occurrence and rabbits by error, so the same task is learned differently between the two.
options.why: The difference is in the task, not the species. A task needing an association and a task needing timing make different demands.

items.stem: Blink too soon or too late, and the puff lands on an open eye. Why is that information specific enough to teach the rabbit its blink?

options.text: It reaches the cells whose output determines the blink, and tells those cells that their own timing was wrong.
options.why: Correct. The puff supplies the target, and the error is addressed to the very cells that issued the mistimed command.

options.text: It reaches every cell in the brain at once, so every connection active at the time can adjust itself together.
options.why: A signal reaching every cell is a broadcast, which is what reinforcement learning uses. The rabbit’s error goes to particular cells.

options.text: It tells the rabbit exactly what the right moment to blink would have been, as a teacher holding the answer would.
options.why: The information goes to particular cells, not to the rabbit as a whole, and it reports that their own timing was wrong. The world supplied the target, not a teacher holding the answer.

options.text: It strengthens every connection that was active when the puff landed, whether or not those cells drove the blink.
options.why: Strengthening whatever was active is the co-occurrence rule, which cannot deliver timing. The puff’s information is addressed to the blink cells.

items.stem: What does each output cell of the cerebellum receive?

options.text: Roughly two hundred thousand ordinary inputs, and a single climbing fiber that reports the error for that cell.
options.why: Correct. One fiber, one cell, one instruction: the error arrives addressed to the cell whose output was wrong.

options.text: Roughly two hundred thousand climbing fibers, each reporting a separate error from a different part of the body.
options.why: There is one climbing fiber per output cell, not thousands. The large number is of ordinary inputs.

options.text: A single dopamine fiber shared with many other cells, which reports how things went for the animal as a whole.
options.why: A shared dopamine signal is the reinforcement case, delivered to the striatum. The cerebellum’s error is addressed cell by cell.

options.text: No input from outside the cerebellum at all, so that each cell learns from the statistics of its neighbors.
options.why: Learning from the statistics of its own input with nothing delivered is the pallium’s case. The cerebellum receives a teaching fiber.

items.stem: An animal watches a leaf drift past and predicts where the leaf will be next. Why is there nothing here for an error delivered to a commanding cell to be about?

options.text: No output is involved in the prediction, so there is no command that could be wrong.
options.why: Correct. An error delivered cell by cell needs a cell that issued a command. Predicting a leaf’s path issues none.

options.text: The leaf moves too slowly for any error to be computed before the animal has looked away.
options.why: Speed is not the issue. Even a fast leaf would involve no command by the animal, so no commanding cell could be wrong.

options.text: The prediction is always right, since a drifting leaf follows the air, so there is never an error.
options.why: Predictions about a leaf can be wrong. What is missing is not an error but an output for the error to be addressed to.

options.text: The leaf is not food, so its movement carries no reward and nothing about it can be learned.
options.why: Reward is what reinforcement learning needs. The animal can still learn to predict the leaf; it just needs no error delivered to a commanding cell.

items.stem: Predicting the next sensation and predicting the outcome of a movement are both prediction learning. Where does the first happen, and why does only the second need something carried between structures?

options.text: In the pallium, where prediction and test share tissue; for a movement, the commanding cells are not the cells that find out how it went.
options.why: Correct. When the prediction and the input that tests it are in the same tissue, nothing has to travel. When command and outcome are in different places, the error must be carried.

options.text: In the cerebellum, where all prediction learning is done; for a movement, the error must also be carried back to the muscles that moved.
options.why: Predicting the next sensation happens in the pallium, not the cerebellum. The cerebellum’s share is the part about the animal’s own output.

options.text: In the striatum, where the reward for a correct prediction arrives; for a movement, a second reward must be carried to the cerebellum.
options.why: Neither kind of prediction needs a reward. The difference is whether the commanding cells and the cells that find out are the same.

options.text: In the thalamus, which relays each sensation as it arrives; for a movement, the relay also carries a copy of the command sent to the muscles.
options.why: The thalamus relays signals; it is not where the next sensation is predicted. That prediction runs in the pallium’s recurrent circuitry.

items.stem: Two prediction problems both produce a guess about what comes next. The chapter still assigns them to different structures. What principle does it use to sort them?

options.text: The sorting goes by what has to be delivered to the synapse, rather than by what is being computed.
options.why: Correct. Two problems can compute the same kind of guess and still differ in whether an error has to be carried from elsewhere.

options.text: The sorting goes by which sense the prediction concerns, since each sense has its own structure for predicting.
options.why: The chapter does not sort by sense. It sorts by what has to be delivered, which is why prediction splits between two structures.

options.text: The sorting goes by what the animal is trying to achieve, since problems with different goals need different structures.
options.why: Goals belong to the animal-level half of the pairing. The sorting into structures uses the synapse-level half, what has to arrive.

options.text: The sorting goes by whether the prediction was learned or inborn, since learned predictions need a structure of their own.
options.why: Both problems are learned. What separates them is whether anything has to be carried between structures.

items.stem: Which part of prediction learning is the cerebellum’s share?

options.text: The part where the animal’s own output is what the prediction is about.
options.why: Correct. Predicting the next sensation is prediction learning too, and it stays in the pallium. The cerebellum takes the output-bound part.

options.text: All of it, since the cerebellum is the structure where prediction learning happens.
options.why: Predicting the next sensation involves no output and happens in the pallium. The cerebellum’s share is limited to predictions about output.

options.text: The part that concerns sensations from the eyes, such as a drifting leaf.
options.why: A drifting leaf is the chapter’s example of prediction with no output, and it stays in the pallium.

options.text: The part that is learned from rewards, such as food after a lever press.
options.why: Reward-driven learning is reinforcement, delivered to the striatum. The cerebellum learns from errors about output.

items.stem: What does supervised learning need before a connection will change?

options.text: A statement of what the output should have been, held by something that already knows the answer.
options.why: Correct. It needs the same kind of error as prediction learning, but the target comes from a teacher rather than from the world.

options.text: The next input, delivered by the world a moment after the output, with no one holding the answer in advance.
options.why: That is prediction learning, whose target comes from the world. Supervised learning needs a teacher that already knows the answer.

options.text: The activity of the two cells a connection joins, with nothing delivered to the connection from elsewhere.
options.why: That is unsupervised learning. Supervised learning needs a target delivered from something that knows it.

options.text: A single report that things went better than expected, sent to every connection that was recently active.
options.why: That is reinforcement learning’s verdict. Supervised learning needs a statement of the correct output, not a verdict.

items.stem: For a true teacher to exist inside an animal, what would it take, and how often does the chapter say that happens?

options.text: Some part of the animal would have to hold the correct output already, positioned to reach the connections that got it wrong; almost never.
options.why: Correct. The correct output would have to exist somewhere the connections that got it wrong can reach, and at the level of the animal that almost never happens.

options.text: An older animal would have to demonstrate the behavior where the young one could watch it closely; this is common among birds and mammals alike.
options.why: A demonstration is outside the animal. A teacher in the chapter’s sense must hold the correct output inside, positioned to reach the wrong connections.

options.text: A reward would have to follow each correct response closely enough in time; this is common wherever food follows a successful action.
options.why: A reward reports how things went; it is reinforcement learning’s signal. It does not state what the correct output was.

options.text: A memory of past errors would have to be kept and consulted before each new attempt; this is always available to any animal with a brain.
options.why: A memory of errors is not a statement of the correct output. And the chapter says a teacher almost never exists, not that one is always available.

items.stem: A young songbird that has heard an adult sing practices against its memory of the song. Why does the chapter not count this as a true teacher?

options.text: No part of the bird holds the right motor command; it compares each attempt with the remembered song and works from the mismatch.
options.why: Correct. The target is one the bird manufactured from memory, not a correct output handed to the connections that got it wrong.

options.text: The adult is no longer present during practice, and a teacher counts as one only when it is present during each of the learner’s attempts.
options.why: Presence is not the chapter’s criterion. Even with the adult present, no part of the young bird would hold the right motor command.

options.text: A songbird has no cerebellum, so there is no route by which an error about its singing could be delivered at all.
options.why: Songbirds are jawed vertebrates and have a cerebellum. The problem is that nothing holds the correct command, not that no route exists.

options.text: The remembered song fades from one day to the next, so the target keeps changing and never settles into one answer.
options.why: The chapter says nothing about the memory fading. The bird has a target; what it lacks is anything holding the right command.

items.stem: Why can a synapse on a cerebellar output cell not tell prediction learning apart from supervised learning?

options.text: What arrives on the climbing fiber is an error for that one cell, and the fiber does not report who supplied the target.
options.why: Correct. The two families do differ, in where the target comes from. The synapse cannot see that difference, so the two share a structure.

options.text: The two families differ in nothing at all, so there is no difference for the synapse, or for anything else in the brain, to detect.
options.why: They differ in where the target comes from, the world or a teacher. The point is that the synapse cannot tell which.

options.text: Both families arrive by dopamine, and the dopamine signal is the same whichever family produced it.
options.why: Neither family arrives by dopamine; both arrive on climbing fibers. Dopamine carries the reinforcement verdict.

options.text: The synapse can tell them apart, but the cerebellum as a whole ignores the difference when it adjusts the output.
options.why: The chapter’s claim is about the synapse itself. The fiber carries only an error, with no mark of who set the target.

items.stem: Prediction learning and supervised learning share the cerebellum. Where do most of the targets the cerebellum learns from come from?

options.text: From the world: a slipping image, a reach that missed, a swallow that went wrong.
options.why: Correct. A teacher is the exotic case, so most of the cerebellum’s errors come from targets the world supplies.

options.text: From a teacher: an instructor’s correction, or a parent guiding the young animal along.
options.why: Teachers almost never exist inside an animal. Most of the cerebellum’s targets are the world’s.

options.text: From the body: a full stomach, an injury, or a sudden change in temperature.
options.why: A full stomach or an injury is the kind of verdict reinforcement learning uses. The cerebellum learns from errors about output.

options.text: From the pallium: the statistics of whatever the senses happened to bring in.
options.why: Input statistics are what the pallium learns from, with nothing delivered. The cerebellum’s errors come from the world’s targets.

items.stem: What does reinforcement learning need before a connection will change?

options.text: A report of how things went, with no statement of what would have worked instead.
options.why: Correct. The report is a verdict, not an instruction, and it is addressed to no output in particular.

options.text: An error for each output, reporting how far that one output missed its own target.
options.why: That is what the climbing fibers deliver for prediction and supervised learning. Reinforcement learning needs only a verdict.

options.text: A statement of what the correct output was, held by something that already knew.
options.why: That is supervised learning’s requirement. Reinforcement learning never learns what the correct output was.

options.text: The activity of the two cells a connection joins, and nothing from anywhere else.
options.why: That is all unsupervised learning needs. Reinforcement learning needs a report arriving from elsewhere.

items.stem: A rat is in a chamber with a lever on one wall and a food opening on another, and pressing the lever makes a pellet arrive. At the animal level, what is the whole of the rat’s problem?

options.text: It has to end up pressing that lever more often in that chamber.
options.why: Correct. The chapter says that is the whole of the problem at the animal level, which is why a thin signal can be enough.

options.text: It has to learn which muscle movements make up a correct press of the lever in that chamber.
options.why: Which movements make up a press is an output-by-output problem. The animal-level problem is simply pressing more often.

options.text: It has to learn to predict exactly when, after pressing, the pellet will arrive.
options.why: Predicting timing is the rabbit’s kind of problem. The rat has only to press more often in that chamber.

options.text: It has to learn that the sound of the lever and the pellet occur together.
options.why: Learning what goes with what is unsupervised learning. The rat’s problem is about what it does, pressing more often.

items.stem: When the rat eats the pellet, what arrives at a synapse?

options.text: A broadcast signal reporting only that things went better than expected, addressed to no particular output.
options.why: Correct. It says nothing about what would have worked instead. The animal-level problem is rich; the synapse-level signal is thin.

options.text: A signal telling the cells that produced the lever press that pressing was the right action to take.
options.why: A signal like that would be addressed to particular outputs, and the reward signal is not. It reports only how things went.

options.text: An error for each cell that drove the press, reporting how far each movement was from the ideal press.
options.why: An error per output is what climbing fibers deliver in the cerebellum. The reward signal is not addressed cell by cell.

options.text: Nothing at all, since the pellet is eaten too long after the press for any signal to reach the right synapses.
options.why: A signal does arrive; the gap in time is what Module 5’s traces bridge. The signal itself is a broadcast verdict.

items.stem: On its way to the lever, the rat groomed and sniffed. The reward signal is addressed to no particular output. What sorts the grooming and sniffing from the lever press?

options.text: The traces and estimates of future outcomes described in Module 5, since the signal itself cannot say which action earned it.
options.why: Correct. The verdict does not pick out the press. Module 5’s traces and estimates do the sorting.

options.text: The reward signal itself, since it is delivered only to the synapses that produced the press and not to the others.
options.why: The reward signal is not addressed to particular outputs, so it cannot pick out the press. Something else must do the sorting.

options.text: The climbing fibers, since they report an error to the cells that drove the grooming and to the cells that drove the sniffing.
options.why: Climbing fibers carry errors in the cerebellum for prediction and supervised learning. They do not sort actions by reward.

options.text: Nothing does, so grooming and sniffing are strengthened exactly as much as the press, and the rat grooms more from then on.
options.why: The chapter names what does the sorting, the traces and estimates of future outcomes. The problem is real but it is handled.

items.stem: How hard is it for a body to generate the kind of signal reinforcement learning needs, and from what?

options.text: Easily, from something like a full stomach or an injury.
options.why: Correct. A verdict of how things went is easy for a body to produce, since it says nothing about which output should change.

options.text: With difficulty, from a teacher that holds the answer.
options.why: A teacher is what supervised learning needs, and it almost never exists. A verdict is easy to produce.

options.text: Slowly, after many pairings of a tone with food.
options.why: Pairings of tone and food are the rat’s classical conditioning. A verdict comes directly from how things went.

options.text: Only from a dedicated fiber to each output cell.
options.why: A fiber per output cell is the cerebellum’s arrangement for errors. A verdict needs no address.

items.stem: What is the striatum?

options.text: The input stage of the basal ganglia, where signals from the pallium arrive and the dopamine fibers meet them.
options.why: Correct. It is where the reward signal meets the pallium’s report of the situation, which is what makes a thin signal useful there.

options.text: The roof of the midbrain, which holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and eyes toward what appears.
options.why: That is the tectum. The striatum is in the forebrain, at the input stage of the basal ganglia.

options.text: A large structure attached to the back of the hindbrain, which learns from errors delivered to it one output cell at a time.
options.why: That is the cerebellum, which receives climbing fibers. The striatum receives dopamine fibers.

options.text: A structure above the hypothalamus that relays signals from the senses into the pallium and carries signals back out.
options.why: That is the thalamus. The striatum is where the pallium’s signals enter the basal ganglia.

items.stem: What is the name for the input stage of the basal ganglia, where signals from the pallium arrive and where the dopamine fibers that carry the reward signal meet them?

options.text: Striatum.
options.why: Correct. The striatum is where reinforcement learning’s verdict arrives, at synapses joining the pallium’s report to units that propose actions.

options.text: Thalamus.
options.why: The thalamus relays signals from the senses into the pallium and carries signals back out. It is not where dopamine meets the pallium’s signals.

options.text: Cerebellum.
options.why: The cerebellum learns from errors delivered by climbing fibers, one to each output cell, not from a dopamine signal.

options.text: Hypothalamus.
options.why: The hypothalamus keeps the body’s internal conditions near their set points. It is not the input stage of the basal ganglia.

items.stem: Which cells carry the information reinforcement learning requires, and where do their fibers arrive?

options.text: Dopamine neurons of the midbrain, whose fibers arrive where the pallium meets the striatum.
options.why: Correct. That is the address of the verdict: synapses at the input stage of the basal ganglia.

options.text: Climbing fibers from one source below the cerebellum, one to each of its many output cells.
options.why: Climbing fibers deliver errors for prediction and supervised learning. The verdict travels on dopamine fibers.

options.text: Cells of the hypothalamus, whose fibers arrive at every synapse in the pallium at once.
options.why: The hypothalamus keeps internal conditions near their set points. The reward signal comes from the midbrain.

options.text: Cells of the thalamus, whose fibers carry each sensation from the senses into the pallium.
options.why: The thalamus relays sensation. The reward signal is carried by midbrain dopamine neurons to the striatum.

items.stem: At the algorithmic level the reward signal is usually written as a single number. The dopamine cells, though, are a population, and what they report differs from one target to another. What survives either description?

options.text: The signal is not addressed to particular outputs, so it cannot say what any one of them should have done.
options.why: Correct. The chapter qualifies the single number and then keeps what matters for the argument: the signal is unaddressed.

options.text: The signal is identical everywhere it lands, since a population of cells can still report one shared number.
options.why: The chapter says what the dopamine cells report is not identical everywhere. The single number is an idealization.

options.text: The signal tells each striatal cell which action was right, since a population can address each target separately.
options.why: Differences across targets do not make the signal an instruction. It still cannot say what any output should have done.

options.text: The signal carries a separate error to each output cell, much as a climbing fiber does in the cerebellum.
options.why: An error addressed to each output cell is the climbing-fiber arrangement. The dopamine signal is not addressed to outputs.

items.stem: Module 5 described a third factor: a signal broadcast from elsewhere that settles whether eligible synapses change at all. What does the chapter now say about that third factor?

options.text: It has an address: the dopamine fibers arriving where the pallium meets the striatum.
options.why: Correct. The algorithmic third factor from Module 5 is given a place in a vertebrate brain.

options.text: It is the climbing fiber, which settles whether each cerebellar output cell changes.
options.why: A climbing fiber carries an error addressed to one cell. The third factor is a broadcast, carried by dopamine.

options.text: It turns out not to exist in vertebrates, whose synapses change by co-occurrence alone.
options.why: The chapter locates the third factor rather than dropping it. Co-occurrence alone is only the unsupervised case.

options.text: It is the firing of the postsynaptic cell, which settles whether co-occurrence is detected.
options.why: Postsynaptic firing is one of the two local factors. The third factor arrives from elsewhere.

items.stem: The reward signal is thin: it says only that things went better than expected. Why is so thin a signal useful at the synapses where the pallium meets the striatum?

options.text: Those synapses join the pallium’s report of the situation to units that propose actions, so strengthening one makes an action likelier to win there.
options.why: Correct. Strengthening there corrects no output, and it does not need to, because the rat’s problem was only to press more often in that chamber.

options.text: Those synapses drive the muscles directly, so strengthening one corrects the movement the pallium has just commanded.
options.why: The striatum does not drive muscles directly, and the signal corrects no output. It shifts which action wins.

options.text: Those synapses also receive climbing fibers from below the cerebellum, which add the detail about what should have been done that the reward signal lacks.
options.why: Climbing fibers arrive in the cerebellum, not the striatum. The reward signal is useful without any added detail.

options.text: Those synapses are so few that a single number is enough to address each of them separately in turn.
options.why: The signal is not addressed to particular synapses at all. Its usefulness comes from what the synapses connect.

items.stem: In the lab, the climbing fibers to the cerebellum were silenced during training only, and the animal was then trained and tested on the tone followed by a puff to the eye. What did the two blink readouts show?

options.text: The learned, timed blink never developed, while the reflex blink to the puff itself was unaffected.
options.why: Correct. Showing the two separately is the point: the cerebellum was needed to learn the timing, not to blink at all.

options.text: Both blinks were lost, the timed blink never developing and the reflex blink to the puff failing as well.
options.why: The reflex blink to the puff survived. Losing it would suggest a problem with blinking itself rather than with learning.

options.text: The timed blink was learned normally, while the reflex blink to the puff itself was slowed down.
options.why: This reverses the result. The timed blink failed to develop and the reflex blink was unaffected.

options.text: Both blinks were normal, since the climbing fibers were restored before the test was run.
options.why: The fibers were restored before the test, but the learning had been missed during training. The timed blink never developed.

items.stem: In the lab, with the climbing fibers to the cerebellum silenced during training, the animal was trained to press a lever for food and then tested. What happened?

options.text: The lever was learned normally, and at test the animal pressed about as often as it did with no silencing.
options.why: Correct. Lever pressing is learned from a verdict delivered by dopamine, so cutting the error route to the cerebellum leaves it intact.

options.text: The animal moved normally at test, but pressed the lever no more than an untrained animal would.
options.why: That is what happened when the dopamine fibers to the striatum were silenced. With the climbing fibers silenced, the lever was learned normally.

options.text: The animal moved slowly and with difficulty at test, and pressed the lever only a few times a minute.
options.why: Slow movement and few presses came from removing the dopamine clusters. Silencing the climbing fibers did not touch the lever.

options.text: No result was shown for the lever, since the chapter reports nothing about the cerebellum and lever pressing.
options.why: A gray cell did appear with the climbing fibers silenced, but for the tone and shock task. The lever result was shown: it was learned normally.

items.stem: In the lab, the dopamine fibers to the striatum were silenced during training only and restored before the test. How did the lever task and the timed blink come out?

options.text: At test the animal moved normally but pressed no more than an untrained animal, and the timed blink was learned normally.
options.why: Correct. Cutting the verdict’s route stopped the learning that depends on a verdict and spared the learning that depends on an error.

options.text: At test the animal moved slowly and pressed very little, and the timed blink could not be scored at all in that animal either.
options.why: Slowed movement across tasks came from removing the dopamine clusters. With only the fibers silenced during training, movement at test was normal.

options.text: The lever was learned normally, and the timed blink never developed, while the reflex blink was unaffected.
options.why: That pattern belongs to silencing the climbing fibers. Silencing the dopamine fibers stopped the lever and spared the blink.

options.text: Neither was learned, since both the lever task and the timed blink depend on a dopamine signal reaching the striatum.
options.why: The timed blink depends on an error delivered by climbing fibers, not on dopamine. It was learned normally.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how a rule that needs nothing but the two cells a connection joins produces classical conditioning in a rat that hears a tone before food, and say why the chapter calls that rule only the beginning of an account of conditioning.
items.answer: Food already makes the response cells fire without training. The cells carrying the tone contact those same response cells and are firing at the same moment, so both ends of the tone connection are active together, which is all Hebb’s rule requires. The tone connection strengthens, and after enough pairings the tone alone drives the response. This is unsupervised, because nothing in the rat had to know the tone predicted food. But the same rule strengthens the connection carrying the sound of a ventilation fan that happened to be running, and blocking showed that actual conditioning tracks only what was not already predicted. So a co-occurrence rule is the beginning of an account, not the whole of one.
rubric: Says food already makes the response cells fire, and the tone cells fire at the same moment.
Says both ends of the tone connection being active together strengthens it, until the tone alone drives the response.
Says the learning is unsupervised because nothing in the rat had to know the tone predicted food.
Gives at least one limit: the fan’s sound is strengthened too, or blocking shows conditioning tracks only what was not already predicted.
Concludes that the rule is the beginning of an account of conditioning rather than the whole.

items.stem: Prediction learning and supervised learning are different families, yet the chapter assigns both to the cerebellum. In a short paragraph, say how the two families differ, and explain why they nonetheless share a structure.
items.answer: The two differ in where the target comes from. In prediction learning the world supplies it a moment later, as when the puff tells the rabbit its blink was mistimed. In supervised learning a teacher that already knows the answer supplies it, and at the level of the animal such a teacher almost never exists. But both need the same thing at a synapse: an error computed for one output. In the cerebellum each output cell gets a single climbing fiber that reports the error for that cell. The fiber does not report whether the world or a teacher set the target, so a synapse cannot tell the two families apart, and they share the structure. Most of what the cerebellum learns from is the world’s targets, such as a slipping image or a reach that missed.
rubric: States that the families differ in where the target comes from: the world, or a teacher that holds the answer.
States that both need an error for one output delivered to the synapse.
Names the climbing fiber as delivering one error to one cerebellar output cell.
Explains that the fiber does not report who supplied the target, so a synapse cannot tell the families apart.

items.stem: In the lab, an animal with its dopamine clusters removed pressed a trained lever very little. In a short paragraph, say why that result alone is ambiguous, and explain how the lab’s two silencing experiments separate a learning deficit from a movement deficit.
items.answer: Removing the dopamine clusters made every movement slow and hard to start, in every task. So an animal pressing a lever very little could have failed to learn, or could have learned and simply been unable to move well enough to show it. Silencing the dopamine fibers to the striatum during training only, and restoring them for the test, separates the two: at test the animal moved normally but pressed no more than an untrained animal, so the problem was learning, not movement. The contrast with the climbing fibers makes it sharper. Silencing the dopamine fibers left the timed blink learned normally, while silencing the climbing fibers stopped the timed blink and left the lever learned normally. Each route was needed for its own kind of learning.
rubric: Says removing the dopamine clusters slowed every movement, so a low lever score could reflect movement or learning.
Says silencing the dopamine fibers during training only left movement normal at test.
Says the silenced animal pressed no more than an untrained one, so the deficit was in learning.
Uses the contrast with the climbing fibers: the blink was spared by the dopamine silencing, or the lever was spared by the climbing-fiber silencing.

items.stem: A rat learns to press a lever that delivers food. In a short paragraph, state this case as the chapter’s pairing of an animal-level problem with what reaches a synapse, and explain why a signal that corrects no output is still enough.
items.answer: At the animal level the whole of the problem is that the rat has to end up pressing that lever more often in that chamber. At a synapse, what arrives when the pellet is eaten is a broadcast signal reporting only that things went better than expected. It is addressed to no particular output and says nothing about what would have worked instead. Dopamine neurons of the midbrain carry it to the synapses where the pallium meets the striatum. Those synapses join the pallium’s report of the situation the animal is in to the units that propose actions. So strengthening one of them corrects no output, but it makes one action more likely to win in one kind of situation, which is exactly what the rat had to end up doing.
rubric: States the animal-level problem as pressing that lever more often in that chamber.
States the synapse-level signal as a broadcast report that things went better than expected, addressed to no particular output.
Places its delivery at the synapses where the pallium meets the striatum, carried by midbrain dopamine neurons.
Says those synapses connect a report of the situation to units that propose actions.
Concludes that strengthening there makes one action more likely to win in that situation, which is all the problem requires.

items.stem: Supervised learning, with a teacher supplying the correct output, was ranked as the exotic case of learning. Yet the cerebellum learns from errors all the time. How do the two fit together?

options.text: A teacher almost never exists at the level of the animal, and most of the cerebellum’s errors are supplied by the world instead: a slipping image, a missed reach.
options.why: Correct. The cerebellum’s machinery would serve a teacher, but what actually reaches it is mostly error the world supplies, which is prediction learning.

options.text: A teacher exists inside every vertebrate, and the cerebellum is that teacher, holding the correct motor command for every movement in advance.
options.why: No part of the animal holds the correct output in advance. That is why a teacher is the exotic case, and why even the songbird manufactures its own target.

options.text: The cerebellum learns only in the rare cases where another animal demonstrates a movement, so its errors are rare in practice as well.
options.why: The cerebellum learns constantly, from a slipping image, a reach that missed, a swallow that went wrong. Those errors come from the world, not from a demonstrator.

options.text: The cerebellum learns without any error at all, from co-occurrence alone, so neither teachers nor errors bear on what it learns.
options.why: Learning from co-occurrence alone is unsupervised learning. The cerebellum is where errors delivered output by output arrive, along the climbing fibers.

pools.title: Three Structures, and Working Together
pools.covers: reading §6.2.6, §6.2.7 · lecture 6.2 slides four_families_three_structures, maps_and_loops · lab Bench

items.stem: Module 5 described four families of learning, but the chapter assigns them to only three structures in a vertebrate brain. Why are three enough?

options.text: Prediction learning and supervised learning differ in where the target comes from, but both need the same thing at a synapse: an error for each output.
options.why: Correct. Two of the four families make the same demand of a synapse, so one delivery route, the climbing fibers of the cerebellum, serves both.

options.text: Unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning both need a single number reporting how things went, so one structure can deliver it for both.
options.why: Only reinforcement learning needs a verdict. Unsupervised learning needs nothing delivered at all, since both quantities it uses are already at the connection.

options.text: Supervised learning almost never happens in vertebrates, so the chapter drops that family and gives one structure to each of the remaining three.
options.why: A teacher is the exotic case, but supervised learning is not dropped. It shares the climbing fibers with prediction learning.

options.text: Prediction learning happens everywhere in the brain rather than in one place, so it needs no structure of its own, and each of the other three families gets one.
options.why: Predicting the next sensation does happen in the pallium’s own circuitry, but prediction learning about the animal’s own output is the cerebellum’s. The pairing is with supervised learning.

items.stem: A classmate argues that supervised learning should need a structure of its own, since a teacher is a different source of information from the world. What is the chapter’s answer?

options.text: The source changes, but what arrives does not: a climbing fiber carries an error for one output cell and never reports who supplied the target.
options.why: Correct. The wiring does not distinguish the supplier, so the two families share the cerebellum.

options.text: The source is the same, because in a vertebrate the world is always the teacher, and no animal ever receives a target from anywhere else at all.
options.why: The chapter keeps the two sources distinct: a teacher already holds the correct answer, while the world delivers it a moment later. What they share is the signal at the synapse.

options.text: The teacher’s signal is broadcast to every output at once, so supervised learning belongs with reinforcement learning, where the pallium meets the striatum.
options.why: A broadcast verdict is what reinforcement learning uses. A teacher’s signal is an error computed for each output, which is the climbing fibers’ kind of signal.

options.text: The teacher’s signal needs no delivery, since the correct answer is already present at the connection, so supervised learning belongs in the pallium.
options.why: Needing nothing delivered describes unsupervised learning. Supervised learning needs an error for each output, delivered from outside the connection.

items.stem: A lamprey has two of the three learning structures in Doya’s proposal. Which one is missing, and when did it arrive?

options.text: The structure specialized for errors delivered output by output, which arrived later, with the jawed fishes.
options.why: Correct. The cerebellum, in the form jawed vertebrates have it, arrived with the jawed fishes. The lamprey already has the other two.

options.text: The structure specialized for a broadcast verdict, which arrived later, with the first mammals.
options.why: A lamprey already has dopamine delivered to its striatum; a lamprey whose dopamine is depleted has trouble starting movements. The missing structure is the one for errors delivered output by output.

options.text: The structure specialized for learning with nothing delivered, which arrived later, with the first land animals.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, the lamprey included. The missing structure is the one for errors delivered output by output.

options.text: The structure specialized for errors delivered output by output, which arose before any vertebrate and was then lost in the lamprey’s lineage.
options.why: The structure is right, but the history is not. The chapter says it arrived later, with the jawed fishes, not that the lamprey’s lineage lost it.

items.stem: A lamprey has two of the three learning structures. If Doya’s mapping holds, which families of learning have their structure in a lamprey, and which lack the structure specialized for them?

options.text: Unsupervised and reinforcement learning have theirs; prediction and supervised learning lack the one specialized for errors delivered to each output.
options.why: Correct. A lamprey has a pallium and a striatum reached by dopamine fibers. The cerebellum in its jawed form, which serves both error-driven families, is the one it lacks.

options.text: Prediction and supervised learning have theirs; unsupervised and reinforcement learning lack the ones specialized for them, which arrived with the mammals.
options.why: That reverses it. A lamprey has a pallium and a striatum reached by dopamine; the structure for errors delivered output by output is the later one.

options.text: Unsupervised, prediction and reinforcement learning all have theirs; only supervised learning lacks one, because a vertebrate almost never has a teacher.
options.why: Prediction and supervised learning share one structure, so they cannot come apart this way. The rarity of a teacher is a fact about the animal, not about which structures a lamprey has.

options.text: Reinforcement learning alone has its structure; the other three families lack theirs, because a lamprey has neither a pallium nor a cerebellum.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, the lamprey included. The only one of the three a lamprey lacks is the structure for errors delivered output by output.

items.stem: Doya is careful about how much of the three-structure proposal is settled. What makes the cerebellar case the best supported of the three?

options.text: Its anatomy, what its climbing fibers fire for, and the loss of learning when those fibers are silenced all point the same way.
options.why: Correct. Three lines of evidence agree: the wiring of one fiber to one cell, the fibers’ firing for errors, and the learned blink never developing when they are silenced.

options.text: Reward-related activity has been recorded in it and nowhere else, so no other structure could be doing that kind of learning.
options.why: That confuses the cerebellum with the place where the pallium meets the striatum, and even there the chapter says reward-related activity also turns up in parts of the cortex.

options.text: It has no dedicated teaching pathway that anyone has found, so it can only be learning from the statistics of its own input.
options.why: That is the case for the pallium, which is the weakest of the three, not the strongest.

options.text: It is the oldest of the three structures, present in the lamprey as well as in every jawed vertebrate, so it has been studied longest.
options.why: The cerebellum in its jawed form is the newest of the three, arriving with the jawed fishes. Its support comes from the evidence, not from its age.

items.stem: The case for the pallium as the structure specialized for unsupervised learning rests on the weakest evidence of the three. Why does the chapter say that weakness is partly the point?

options.text: The case is made from an absence: this kind of learning needs nothing delivered, so there is no dedicated teaching pathway to find.
options.why: Correct. The other two cases can point to a delivery route and test it. The pallium’s case is that nothing arrives there but its own input, which leaves nothing to trace or silence.

options.text: The pallium has been studied in only a few kinds of fish, so the experiments that would support the case have simply not been done yet.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, and the chapter does not blame the weakness on missing experiments. The weakness is built into what unsupervised learning needs.

options.text: The pallium learns by every method at once, so no single family of learning could ever be shown to belong to it more than the others.
options.why: The chapter does say the mapping is not exclusive, but that is not why the pallium’s case is weak. The weakness is that there is no teaching pathway to find.

options.text: The pallium’s teaching pathway is too small to record from, so its signal can be inferred from behavior but never measured directly.
options.why: There is no teaching pathway to record from at all. That absence is the point, not a pathway too small to measure.

items.stem: A research team reports reward-related activity in part of the cortex, well away from where the pallium meets the striatum. Does that finding contradict the chapter’s mapping of four families of learning onto three structures?

options.text: No. The mapping says where each family’s signal is delivered, and reward-related activity is known to turn up in parts of the cortex as well.
options.why: Correct. The mapping is not exclusive. As the lecture puts it, the mapping assigns each family to where its signal is delivered, and does not say that nothing else can learn that way.

options.text: Yes. The mapping assigns each family to exactly one structure, so reward-related activity found anywhere outside the striatum would show the table to be wrong.
options.why: The chapter explicitly denies that the mapping is exclusive. Reward-related activity in the cortex is something it reports, not something it rules out.

options.text: No. Reward-related activity in the cortex is really the climbing fibers’ error signal, which is easily mistaken for a reward report in recordings.
options.why: Climbing fibers belong to the cerebellum and carry an error for one output cell. Nothing in the chapter reinterprets reward-related activity in the cortex this way.

options.text: Yes. The cortex is where unsupervised learning happens, which needs nothing delivered, so no reward signal of any kind could reach it.
options.why: The pallium is Doya’s candidate for unsupervised learning, but that does not rule out other learning there. The chapter reports reward-related activity in parts of the cortex.

items.stem: The chapter grades the evidence for each pairing of a family of learning with a structure, rather than asserting all three. How does it rank them?

options.text: The cerebellum’s pairing is the best supported, and the pallium’s rests on the weakest evidence of the three.
options.why: Correct. The three cases are not equally strong. The cerebellar case has anatomy, firing and silencing behind it; the pallium’s case is made from the absence of a teaching pathway.

options.text: The pallium’s pairing is the best supported, and the cerebellum’s rests on the weakest evidence of the three.
options.why: That reverses the ranking. The cerebellum is the best supported, and the pallium is the weakest because there is no teaching pathway to find.

options.text: The striatum’s pairing is the best supported, and the cerebellum’s rests on the weakest evidence of the three.
options.why: Reward-related activity at the striatum is well established, but the chapter names the cerebellar case as the best supported of the three.

options.text: All three pairings are equally well supported, since each has been confirmed by silencing its own delivery route.
options.why: The chapter says outright that the three cases are not equally strong, and the pallium has no delivery route to silence.

items.stem: On the lab bench, one delivery route at a time was silenced during training only and restored before the test, and the timed blink and the lever were each trained and then tested. What pattern did the two silencings produce?

options.text: Climbing fibers silenced: no timed blink, lever learned. Dopamine fibers silenced: blink learned, and the animal moved normally at test but pressed no more than an untrained one.
options.why: Correct. Each route was needed for one task and not the other, and the dopamine result is not a movement problem, since the animal moved normally at test. That is why prediction learning, and supervised learning with it, go in the climbing-fiber row, and reinforcement learning in the dopamine row.

options.text: Climbing fibers silenced: no timed blink, lever learned. Dopamine fibers silenced: blink learned, but every movement at test was slow and hard to start, so the lever could not be scored.
options.why: Slow movements that are hard to start are what removing the dopamine clusters produced. With the fibers silenced only during training, the animal moved normally at test and simply had not learned the lever.

options.text: Climbing fibers silenced: no timed blink and no lever. Dopamine fibers silenced: no lever and no timed blink, since both are learned movements that need every learning structure.
options.why: No behavior uses one structure alone, but that is not what the silencings showed. Each route was needed for one task and not the other.

options.text: Climbing fibers silenced: no lever, blink learned. Dopamine fibers silenced: no timed blink, and the animal moved normally at test but pressed as much as a trained one.
options.why: That reverses the result. The timed blink depends on an error delivered to each output cell, and the lever press on a broadcast verdict.

items.stem: The lab bench labels each result either as an experiment the reading reports, naming the animal it was found in, or as a result that only follows from what the reading says a structure does. How were the two silencing results labeled, and how does that fit the chapter’s grading of the evidence?

options.text: The climbing-fiber result was reported, in the rabbit, and the dopamine-fiber result only followed. That fits the cerebellar case being the best supported.
options.why: Correct. The loss of the timed blink with the climbing fibers silenced is an experiment the reading describes. The dopamine silencing is an inference from the mapping, and the bench says so.

options.text: The dopamine-fiber result was reported, in the rat, and the climbing-fiber result only followed. That fits the reinforcement learning case being the best supported.
options.why: That reverses the labels. The bench reports the climbing-fiber experiment, in the rabbit, and marks the dopamine silencing as following from the reading.

options.text: Both results were reported, each in its own animal. That fits the chapter’s view that the three cases are all about equally well supported.
options.why: The chapter says the three cases are not equally strong, and the bench agrees: only the climbing-fiber silencing is an experiment the reading reports.

options.text: Neither result was reported, since both only followed from what the reading says. That fits the chapter’s view that none of the three pairings has been tested.
options.why: The chapter counts silencing the climbing fibers as part of the evidence for the cerebellar case, and the bench reports that experiment, in the rabbit.

items.stem: Filling in Doya’s table from the lab bench, each family of learning gets the pathway whose silencing stopped it. What goes in the unsupervised learning row, and why?

options.text: None, because there is no route to cut: it needs nothing delivered, so no dedicated teaching route exists for it.
options.why: Correct. The bench can silence only the climbing fibers and the dopamine fibers. Unsupervised learning uses the activity of the two cells a connection joins, which is already there.

options.text: The dopamine fibers, because unsupervised learning is how the animal learned to approach the food cue, and dopamine fibers carry news about food.
options.why: Dopamine fibers carry a verdict, which is the signal reinforcement learning needs. Unsupervised learning needs nothing delivered.

options.text: The climbing fibers, because unsupervised learning is how the animal learned the timing of the blink, and climbing fibers carry that timing.
options.why: The timing of the blink is prediction learning, which needs an error for one output. Unsupervised learning needs nothing delivered.

options.text: Both pathways, because unsupervised learning happens at synapses everywhere, and so it is stopped by silencing any route into the brain.
options.why: Co-occurrence-sensitive synapses are everywhere, which is exactly why no single delivery route serves them and there is nothing to silence.

items.stem: Suppose we traced every connection leaving the cerebellum, looking for a direct link to the basal ganglia. What would we find, and how do the two structures work together anyway?

options.text: No direct connections at all; each exchanges signals with the pallium by way of the thalamus, and the pallium is where their work meets.
options.why: Correct. The two cooperate without touching each other, and every route between them runs through the pallium and the thalamus.

options.text: A dense direct bundle between them, which lets the cerebellum pass its errors straight to the basal ganglia for use in choosing which program runs.
options.why: That is the intuitive guess, and the chapter says the opposite: there are no direct connections between the two at all.

options.text: No direct connections at all; the two never work together, since each learns by its own method and serves only its own behaviors.
options.why: There are no direct connections, but the chapter says no behavior uses one of the three structures alone. They cooperate by way of the pallium.

options.text: A single direct link, carried by the dopamine fibers, which reach both structures from the midbrain and so connect them.
options.why: Dopamine fibers arrive where the pallium meets the striatum. They are not a link between the cerebellum and the basal ganglia.

items.stem: The cerebellum and the basal ganglia both exchange signals with the pallium. What does the pallium supply to both of them?
