items.answer: As the stimulated point moved along the tectum, the animal’s head turned in order, from far to the left, through straight ahead, to far to the right. Neighboring points on the tectum turned the head toward neighboring directions. That makes the tectum a topographic map: neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells, so the tissue is an ordered copy of the space around the animal, which is what lets the eyes and head be aimed from it. A map keeps wires short, because cells that compare nearby points sit near each other. And it makes comparison easy, because the circuitry that sharpens a difference between neighbors can be the same everywhere on the sheet.
rubric: Reports that the head turned in order, from one side through straight ahead to the other, as the point moved.
Names the arrangement as a topographic map, with neighboring points in the world handled by neighboring cells.
Gives short wires as one payoff, because cells comparing nearby points sit together.
Gives easy comparison as the other, because the same sharpening circuitry works everywhere on the sheet.

pools.title: Hindbrain, Midbrain, and the Forebrain’s Old Core
pools.covers: reading §6.3.1, §6.3.2, §6.3.3 · lecture 6.3 slides running_the_body, the_midbrain, forebrains_old_core · lab Plan, Tree, Bench

items.stem: What is a central pattern generator?

options.text: A circuit that produces a rhythmic output without needing a rhythmic input to drive it.
options.why: Correct. The wave that travels down a swimming lamprey is made this way, by circuits in the spinal cord, segment by segment.

options.text: A circuit that copies a rhythm arriving from the senses and passes it on, beat for beat, to the muscles.
options.why: A relay of that kind needs a rhythmic input to drive it. What defines a pattern generator is that it makes the rhythm without one.

options.text: A small cluster of hindbrain cells whose fibers reach nearly the whole brain and set the pace of its activity.
options.why: That describes the norepinephrine cluster, which turns the arousal dial. A pattern generator is a circuit that makes a rhythm.

options.text: A loose network of cells along the brainstem that sets how awake an animal is and takes it into sleep.
options.why: That is the reticular formation. It sets arousal; it does not generate the rhythm of a movement.

items.stem: What is the name for a circuit that makes a rhythmic output with no rhythmic input driving it, such as the circuits in a lamprey’s spinal cord that produce its swimming wave?

options.text: Central pattern generator.
options.why: Correct. The lamprey’s swimming wave is made by pattern generators segment by segment along the cord.

options.text: Reticular formation.
options.why: The reticular formation runs the length of the brainstem and sets how awake an animal is. It makes no swimming rhythm.

options.text: Tectum.
options.why: The tectum is the roof of the midbrain. It holds maps of the space around the animal and turns the animal toward a position.

options.text: Basal ganglia.
options.why: The basal ganglia settle which proposed action is released. They select among actions rather than generating a rhythm.

items.stem: In an experiment, the connection between a lamprey’s spinal cord and its brain is cut. What happens to the swimming rhythm, and what does the result show?

options.text: The rhythm can still be produced, showing that circuits in the cord generate it without rhythmic drive from the brain.
options.why: Correct. This is the classic isolated-cord result. It is what makes the pattern generator more than a definition: the rhythm is made segment by segment in the cord itself.

options.text: The rhythm stops at once, which shows that the brain sends the swimming rhythm down the cord one beat at a time.
options.why: That is the expectation the experiment overturns. With the brain disconnected, the rhythm can still be produced.

options.text: The rhythm survives in the segments nearest the head, which shows that each wave is passed backward from the brain.
options.why: The wave is generated segment by segment along the cord, so no segment waits for a wave arriving from the head.

options.text: The rhythm turns into random twitching, which shows that the reticular formation must keep the cord awake for it to run.
options.why: The reticular formation sets how awake an animal is, but a cord cut off from the brain can still produce an orderly swimming rhythm.

items.stem: The spinal cord and the hindbrain are continuous with each other. How does the chapter divide the work between them?

options.text: The cord carries signals between brain and body and runs much behavior itself; the hindbrain runs breathing, heart rate, blood pressure and swallowing.
options.why: Correct. The cord is more than a cable, since it runs a good deal of behavior on its own. The hindbrain controls the jobs that keep an animal alive.

options.text: The cord carries signals between brain and body and nothing more; the hindbrain generates all the rhythmic movements, the lamprey’s swimming wave included.
options.why: The cord runs a good deal of behavior by itself. The swimming wave in particular is made by pattern generators in the cord, segment by segment.

options.text: The cord controls breathing and heart rate; the hindbrain carries signals between the brain and the body and runs nothing by itself.
options.why: That swaps the two. The jobs that keep an animal alive, like breathing and heart rate, belong to the hindbrain.

options.text: The cord holds a map of the body and turns it toward a touch; the hindbrain holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the eyes.
options.why: Maps that turn the animal toward a position belong to the tectum, in the roof of the midbrain. Neither the cord nor the hindbrain is described that way.

items.stem: A patient’s injury is confined to the hindbrain. Which of these functions does the chapter give us most reason to worry about?

options.text: Breathing, heart rate, blood pressure and swallowing, the jobs that keep the body alive and cannot stop.
options.why: Correct. The parts of the brain that look oldest do the jobs that cannot stop, and the hindbrain controls exactly these.

options.text: Turning the eyes and head toward a sudden flash, which depends on maps of the space around the animal.
options.why: Orienting toward a position is the tectum’s job, in the roof of the midbrain, in front of the hindbrain.

options.text: Keeping body temperature, water balance and blood sugar near the values they are supposed to have.
options.why: Holding internal conditions near their set points is the hypothalamus’s job, at the base of the forebrain.

options.text: Quickly evaluating whether something that has just appeared is good or bad for the animal, before it acts on it.
options.why: Quick evaluation of what matters is the amygdala’s job, at the front and base of the forebrain.

items.stem: On the lab bench, a student tries to remove the generic mammal’s hindbrain, and the bench refuses. What reason does the refusal give?

options.text: The animal would not survive, because the hindbrain runs breathing and heart rate.
options.why: Correct. The bench removes nothing and cites the hindbrain’s role in the jobs that keep an animal alive. It is the one removal the scene will not perform.

options.text: The reading reports no experiment in which a hindbrain was removed, so there is no result to show.
options.why: A missing experiment is what the bench’s gray “no result reported” marks, and it is shown as a gap rather than a refusal. The refusal gives survival as its reason.

options.text: The animal would stay asleep, because the reticular formation that sets arousal runs through the hindbrain.
options.why: The reticular formation does run the length of the brainstem, but the refusal does not cite arousal. It cites breathing and heart rate.

options.text: The spinal cord’s pattern generators would keep the animal moving, so the tasks would look just as before.
options.why: The cord does run locomotion by itself, but that is not the bench’s reason. The refusal says the animal would not survive without breathing and heart rate.

items.stem: What is the reticular formation?

options.text: A loose network of cells running the length of the brainstem that sets how awake an animal is and takes it in and out of sleep.
options.why: Correct. The reticular formation is where arousal, a capacity met earlier without a location, gets part of its address.

options.text: A cluster of nuclei at the front and base of the forebrain that quickly evaluates whether what has happened is good or bad.
options.why: That is the amygdala. It evaluates what matters; it does not set how awake the animal is.

options.text: A set of circuits in the spinal cord, one in each segment, that produce the rhythm of swimming with no rhythmic input.
options.why: Those are central pattern generators. They make rhythms like the swimming wave; they do not set arousal.

options.text: A dense bundle of fibers running between the two hemispheres of the forebrain, letting the two sides share what each of them has seen.
options.why: That describes a connection between the hemispheres, such as the corpus callosum of placental mammals. The reticular formation sets arousal.

items.stem: What is the name for the loose network of cells, running the length of the brainstem, that sets how awake an animal is and takes it in and out of sleep?

options.text: Reticular formation.
options.why: Correct. It runs the length of the brainstem, the midbrain and hindbrain together.

options.text: Central pattern generator.
options.why: A central pattern generator makes a rhythmic output, such as the swimming wave, without a rhythmic input. It does not set arousal.

options.text: Hypothalamus.
options.why: The hypothalamus keeps internal conditions such as temperature and water balance near their set points. It sits at the base of the forebrain, not along the brainstem.

options.text: Tectum.
options.why: The tectum is the roof of the midbrain. It holds maps of space and turns the animal toward a position.

items.stem: Module 4 treated norepinephrine as the vertebrate’s arousal dial but gave arousal no location in the brain. Where does the chapter say the dial is turned from?

options.text: A small cluster of hindbrain cells that makes most of the brain’s norepinephrine, with fibers reaching nearly the whole brain.
options.why: Correct. Arousal, left without an address in Module 4, has one here. The cluster’s reach is what lets one small place act on the whole brain.

options.text: Two clusters of cells in the midbrain, whose fibers run forward into the striatum and the pallium above them.
options.why: Those are the dopamine clusters. They are not where most of the brain’s norepinephrine comes from.

options.text: A series of clusters along the midline of the brainstem, sending norepinephrine back into the hindbrain and across the brain.
options.why: That is where the serotonin neurons sit. Most norepinephrine comes from one small cluster in the hindbrain.

options.text: The hypothalamus at the base of the forebrain, which regulates the internal states that set how a circuit treats the very same input.
options.why: The hypothalamus does regulate internal states, but the norepinephrine that turns the arousal dial comes mostly from one hindbrain cluster.

items.stem: On the lab bench, a student records from the generic mammal’s brain while it turns toward a flash, and again while it learns that a tone predicts a shock. How does the norepinephrine cluster’s recorded activity compare between the two tasks?

options.text: It is low while the animal turns toward the flash and high in the task where a tone predicts a shock.
options.why: Correct. The arousal dial is turned up when a shock is coming and barely moves for a simple orienting turn, which fits a source that sets how aroused the whole animal is.

options.text: It is high in both tasks, since the cluster’s fibers reach nearly the whole brain and any task needs the animal awake.
options.why: Reach is not the same as activity. The cluster records low during the orienting turn and high when a tone predicts a shock.

options.text: It is high while the animal turns toward the flash and low in the task where a tone predicts a shock, since orienting is arousal.
options.why: That reverses the result. The orienting turn is the tectum’s job, and the tectum is the structure that records high there.

options.text: It is grayed out in both tasks, since the reading describes norepinephrine as a dial and reports no recordings of it.
options.why: The cluster does have results on the bench, low for the orienting turn and high for tone and shock. The rows grayed out in both are other structures.

items.stem: In the lab’s tour of the lamprey model, the norepinephrine cluster is drawn as a small dot. Hovering over it shows how far its fibers reach. What does the model show?

options.text: A pale tint spreading over nearly the whole brain, from a source hardly bigger than a dot.
options.why: Correct. The fibers reach nearly the whole brain. A small source positioned to reach almost everything is what a broadcast needs.

options.text: A pale tint confined to the hindbrain around the dot, since the cluster acts locally on breathing and heart rate.
options.why: The hindbrain does run breathing and heart rate, but the norepinephrine cluster’s fibers reach nearly the whole brain.

options.text: A pale tint over the forebrain roof, since the cluster’s fibers run forward into the pallium and stop there.
options.why: Fibers running forward into the striatum and the pallium describe the dopamine clusters. The norepinephrine tint covers nearly the whole brain.

options.text: A pale tint over one side of the brain, since each of the paired clusters reaches its own hemisphere and not the other.
options.why: The model shows no such split. The tint covers nearly the whole brain, on both sides.

items.stem: A student has learned that there is no walking organ or eating organ, because behaviors that compete for one body share machinery with something to select among them. The student concludes that no part of the vertebrate nervous system is dedicated to a single behavior. What does the chapter say?

options.text: Near the bottom of the nervous system the conclusion fails: breathing, chewing, swallowing and locomotion each have their own pattern generator.
options.why: Correct. The chapter concedes that the shared-machinery answer holds near the top of the nervous system and fails near the bottom.

options.text: The conclusion holds all the way down: even breathing and swallowing are proposed by shared machinery and then released by the basal ganglia.
options.why: That carries the shared-machinery picture too far down. Breathing and swallowing have dedicated pattern generators of their own.

options.text: The conclusion fails in the forebrain, where the hypothalamus is dedicated to drinking and the amygdala to escaping from threats.
options.why: The chapter does not give forebrain structures single behaviors; one structure takes part in many capacities. Its dedicated circuits sit low in the nervous system.

options.text: The conclusion holds for the vertebrate nervous system, whose dedicated circuits were all replaced by shared machinery, and fails for invertebrates.
options.why: Vertebrates keep dedicated circuits of their own, in the hindbrain and spinal cord. Nothing in the chapter says those circuits were replaced.

items.stem: Breathing and swallowing each get a circuit of their own, while the choice between feeding and fleeing is settled by shared machinery. What reason does the chapter give for the difference?

options.text: Breathing and swallowing are stereotyped and must keep running while everything else changes; feeding and fleeing are chosen rather than generated.
options.why: Correct. Behaviors that are stereotyped and cannot stop are the keep-going half of the conflict with changing course, built into anatomy. Behaviors that are chosen share machinery with a selector.

options.text: Breathing and swallowing arose after the machinery for choosing between feeding and fleeing did, so they were added as separate circuits beside it.
options.why: The chapter gives no such timing. Its reason is what the behaviors are like: stereotyped, and unable to stop.

options.text: Breathing and swallowing are learned from reward, and reward learning needs a separate structure for each of the behaviors that it learns to perform.
options.why: Learning from reward belongs to the basal ganglia, and it is not what makes these behaviors dedicated. They are stereotyped and must keep going.

options.text: Breathing and swallowing use muscles that feeding and fleeing leave alone, so there is nothing to compete over while the animal moves.
options.why: Swallowing is part of feeding, so the muscles are not left alone, and the chapter does not argue from muscles. Its reason is that these behaviors are stereotyped and must keep running.

items.stem: The nerves that carry signals to and from the face, mouth, ears and eyes are the cranial nerves. From which parts of the brain does the chapter say they leave?

options.text: From the hindbrain, and from the midbrain in front of it.
options.why: Correct. The cranial nerves leave from those two divisions, which together make up the brainstem.

options.text: From the thalamus, which relays them up into the pallium.
options.why: The thalamus relays signals into the pallium, but the cranial nerves leave from the hindbrain and the midbrain.

options.text: From the pallium, which sends its commands straight out to the face.
options.why: The pallium’s output cells reach down to the brainstem and the cord. The cranial nerves themselves leave from the hindbrain and the midbrain.

options.text: From the hypothalamus, by way of the pituitary gland hanging below.
options.why: The pituitary releases hormones into the blood. It does not send nerve signals to the face.

items.stem: An animal whose tectum builds maps from hearing as well as from vision sees a flicker off to its left and, at the same moment, hears a splash from the same spot. How does the chapter say the roof of its midbrain handles the two signals?

options.text: Its maps of vision and hearing are in register, so the flicker and the splash mark the same position in each.
options.why: Correct. The tectum’s maps are built from the eyes and, in many animals, from hearing and touch as well, and a position in one is the same position in the others.

options.text: Its visual map turns the eyes toward the flicker, and the periaqueductal gray, also in the midbrain, turns the head toward the splash.
options.why: The periaqueductal gray organizes defensive responses, not orienting. The tectum’s maps are in register, so one position serves both signals.

options.text: Its maps of vision and hearing are laid out as mirror images, so a sound on the left marks a point on the right.
options.why: The maps are in register rather than mirrored: a position in one is the same position in the others.

options.text: Its maps keep vision and hearing apart, and the pallium has to work out afterward that the two positions match.
options.why: The point of maps in register is that no further step is needed to line them up. The tectum holds them already matched.

items.stem: Module 4’s worm and a vertebrate both steer toward things they sense. The lecture says the contrast between them is worth stating exactly. What is the difference?

options.text: The worm compares a signal now with a signal a moment ago; the vertebrate finds a place on a map. The difference is the map, not the accuracy.
options.why: Correct. The tectum solves Module 4’s problem of aiming again at a larger scale. What it adds is a map of positions, not a better score.

options.text: The vertebrate aims far more accurately, because it has millions of neurons to the worm’s few hundred. The difference is the accuracy.
options.why: The lecture says the opposite in so many words: the difference is the map, not the accuracy.

options.text: The worm aims by a map held in its head, and the vertebrate compares signals over time. The difference is which animal holds the map.
options.why: That reverses them. The worm’s aiming has no map anywhere in it; the vertebrate’s is built on one.

options.text: The worm drifts at random until it bumps into its food, while the vertebrate aims at a position. The difference is whether aiming happens at all.
options.why: The worm does aim, by comparing a signal against itself a moment earlier. Aiming is the shared problem, and the map is the difference.

items.stem: A frog’s tectum and a mammal’s superior colliculus go by different names. How does the chapter relate them?

options.text: They are the same structure, the roof of the midbrain; the frog’s retina sends most of its output there, and in mammals it still turns the eyes.
options.why: Correct. The superior colliculus is the mammalian name for the tectum, and the old job has survived the renaming.

options.text: They are different structures: the tectum was lost in mammals, and the superior colliculus is a new part of the pallium that took over its old job.
options.why: The superior colliculus is the tectum itself under another name. Nothing was lost and replaced.

options.text: They are the same structure, but in mammals it has given up turning the eyes, having handed that job over to the pallium.
options.why: In mammals the same structure still turns the eyes.

options.text: They are different structures: the frog’s retina sends its output to the pallium, and the frog’s tectum handles hearing.
options.why: In the frog, the retina sends most of its output to the tectum. That is the frog met in Module 2.

items.stem: A researcher traces a set of fibers in the striatum back to their source and finds two clusters of cell bodies in the midbrain. Which modulator are these cells most likely to release?

options.text: Dopamine, whose neurons sit in two midbrain clusters with fibers running forward into the striatum and pallium.
options.why: Correct. The dopamine neurons sit in two clusters in the midbrain, and their fibers run forward into the striatum and the pallium.

options.text: Serotonin, whose neurons sit in a series of clusters along the brainstem’s midline, from the midbrain back into the hindbrain.
options.why: Serotonin’s sources are a series of clusters along the midline, not a pair. The pair of midbrain clusters is dopamine’s.

options.text: Norepinephrine, whose neurons sit mostly in one small hindbrain cluster, reaching the striatum and nearly all the rest.
options.why: Norepinephrine comes mostly from one cluster, and that cluster is in the hindbrain, not the midbrain.

options.text: A pituitary hormone, released below the hypothalamus into the blood rather than along fibers, reaching the rest of the body.
options.why: Pituitary hormones travel in the blood. The fibers traced here are nerve fibers from clusters in the midbrain.

items.stem: The dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine sources sit in different places. What does the chapter say the three have in common?

options.text: Each is small and old, and positioned to reach almost everything, so the brain’s broad projections start in a few little places.
options.why: Correct. The broad projections, modulator signals that reach almost the whole brain, start in a few small, old clusters.

options.text: Each is a large structure in the forebrain’s old core, so the broad projections start in the places where homeostasis and valence are handled.
options.why: The three sources sit in the midbrain and hindbrain, not in the forebrain’s old core, and each is small.

options.text: Each releases its molecule into the blood through the pituitary, so the broad projections reach the brain by way of the body.
options.why: Release into the blood is how the pituitary’s hormones travel. The modulator sources reach the brain through their own fibers.

options.text: Each sends its fibers to a single target, the striatum, so the broad projections are really one narrow projection repeated.
options.why: Only the dopamine fibers are singled out as running into the striatum, and even they reach the pallium too. The three sources reach almost everything.

items.stem: Module 4 placed four molecules on a plane of valence and arousal. How many of their sources does the chapter locate in the brainstem?

options.text: Three: dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine, each from a small cluster or a series of clusters.
options.why: Correct. That accounts for three of the four molecules on the valence–arousal plane. The chapter does not locate the fourth here.

options.text: All four, each from a cluster of its own in the midbrain, which is where the broadcasts of the brain start.
options.why: The chapter accounts for three of the four. It does not locate the fourth here, and not all three sources it does locate sit in the midbrain.

options.text: One, norepinephrine, since the other molecules are released all over the brain and lack a fixed source of their own.
options.why: Dopamine and serotonin have sources of their own, in the midbrain and along the brainstem midline.

options.text: Two, dopamine and serotonin, since the norepinephrine that sets arousal is made outside the brain in the body.
options.why: Most of the brain’s norepinephrine comes from one small cluster of cells in the hindbrain.

items.stem: The chapter says the periaqueductal gray does for defense what the tectum does for orienting. What do the two structures have in common?

options.text: Each organizes a whole response from one place: turning the whole animal toward a position, or the whole defensive pattern.
options.why: Correct. Stimulating the periaqueductal gray produces the entire defensive pattern rather than a fragment, the same organizing logic as the tectum’s.

options.text: Each holds a map of the space around the animal, one of places worth approaching and one of places worth fleeing from.
options.why: The tectum holds maps, but the periaqueductal gray is not described as holding one. What the two share is organizing a whole response.

options.text: Each is the source of a broad projection, sending one modulator from a small cluster of cells to almost the whole of the brain.
options.why: The broad projections start in the dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine clusters. Neither the tectum nor the periaqueductal gray is one of them.

options.text: Each learns its response from errors, adjusting it each time the response falls short of what the situation needed.
options.why: Learning from errors, output by output, is the cerebellum’s family. Neither structure is described as learning here.

items.stem: What kind of response does the periaqueductal gray organize?

options.text: Whole defensive responses: freezing, fleeing, and the dulled pain, or analgesia, that comes with either.
options.why: Correct. It organizes the whole defensive response, including the reduced sensitivity to pain that goes with freezing or fleeing.

options.text: Rhythmic behaviors that must keep going while everything else changes: breathing, chewing, swallowing and locomotion.
options.why: Those behaviors have pattern generators of their own, in the hindbrain and spinal cord.

options.text: Orienting responses: turning the eyes, the head, and in a fish the whole body toward a spot.
options.why: Orienting is the tectum’s job. The periaqueductal gray does the same kind of thing for defense.

options.text: Corrections to internal conditions: seeking out water, and releasing hormones into the blood.
options.why: Correcting drift in internal conditions is the hypothalamus’s job, behaviorally and through the pituitary.

items.stem: On the lab bench, a student stimulates the periaqueductal gray. What result does the bench give, and how is it labeled?

options.text: The whole defensive pattern, freezing or fleeing with a reduced response to pain, labeled as reported and found in the rat.
options.why: Correct. The reading describes this experiment, so the result is labeled reported and names the rat. It is the entire pattern rather than a fragment.

options.text: Freezing by itself, with the response to pain unchanged, labeled as following from the reading rather than as reported.
options.why: Freezing by itself would be a fragment. The bench shows the whole pattern, with a reduced response to pain, and marks it as reported from the rat.

options.text: Fleeing by itself, with a stronger response to pain, labeled as reported and found in a cat with its basal ganglia left intact.
options.why: The cat with its basal ganglia intact belongs to the removal of the neocortex. Stimulating the periaqueductal gray gives the whole defensive pattern, found in the rat.

options.text: A gray “no result reported”, since the reading describes recordings of the periaqueductal gray but not stimulation of it.
options.why: The reading does describe stimulating the periaqueductal gray in a rat, so the bench reports a result.

items.stem: Three structures at the base and center of the forebrain give addresses to capacities met in earlier modules. Which pairing of structure and capacity matches the chapter?

options.text: The hypothalamus with internal states, the basal ganglia with choosing an action, and the amygdala with valence.
options.why: Correct. The hypothalamus regulates the internal states that set how a circuit treats an input, the basal ganglia select among actions, and the amygdala is part of the address of valence.

options.text: The hypothalamus with valence, the basal ganglia with internal states, and the amygdala with choosing an action.
options.why: Each structure has been given another’s capacity. Valence is the amygdala’s, and choosing an action is the basal ganglia’s.

options.text: The hypothalamus with choosing an action, the basal ganglia with valence, and the amygdala with internal states.
options.why: Each structure has been given another’s capacity. Internal states are regulated from the hypothalamus.

options.text: The hypothalamus with arousal, the basal ganglia with orienting, and the amygdala with learning from each of its errors.
options.why: Arousal is set from the brainstem, orienting is the tectum’s, and learning from errors is the cerebellum’s. None of those belongs to the forebrain’s old core.

items.stem: What is homeostasis?

options.text: Keeping the body’s internal conditions, such as temperature, water balance and blood sugar, within limits.
options.why: Correct. The hypothalamus does much of this work, with cells that detect drift and circuits that correct it.

options.text: Keeping the learned connections of a circuit stable, so that new learning does not overwrite what is already known.
options.why: Keeping what was learned while learning more is a real problem, but it is not homeostasis, which is about the body’s internal conditions.

options.text: Keeping the two halves of the brain in balance, so that neither side takes over a job that both of them should share.
options.why: A difference between what the two sides do is lateralization. Homeostasis is about internal conditions like temperature and water.

options.text: Keeping an animal awake enough to respond, raising and lowering its arousal over the course of a day.
options.why: Setting how awake an animal is belongs to the reticular formation. Homeostasis is about internal conditions like temperature and blood sugar.

items.stem: What is the general name for keeping the body’s internal conditions, such as temperature, water balance and blood sugar, within limits?

options.text: Homeostasis.
options.why: Correct. The hypothalamus holds these conditions near their set points, partly through behavior and partly through the pituitary.

options.text: Lateralization.
options.why: Lateralization is a difference between what the left and right sides of a brain do.

options.text: Action selection.
options.why: Action selection is choosing which available action is performed now, which the basal ganglia do.

options.text: Reverse inference.
options.why: Reverse inference is the move from “this region was active during the task” to “the task involved what this region does”.

items.stem: A lizard that has been in the sun too long moves into the shade, and a deer short of water walks to a stream. What does the chapter say produces behavior like this?

options.text: Hypothalamus cells detect how far a condition has drifted from its set point, and circuits act to correct it, here by driving behavior.
options.why: Correct. Some of the hypothalamus’s correction is behavioral, which is why an animal short of water looks for water.

options.text: The amygdala evaluates the heat or the thirst as bad, and the animal learns to avoid that bad outcome by moving away from what caused it.
options.why: The amygdala evaluates what matters, but correcting drift from a set point is the hypothalamus’s job, and no learning is needed for it.

options.text: The basal ganglia release a habit learned from reward, since the behavior of moving to shade or to water has paid off many times before.
options.why: The basal ganglia select actions, but the drive here comes from a condition drifting from its set point, which the hypothalamus detects.

options.text: The reticular formation raises arousal until the animal is awake enough to notice the heat or the thirst and move.
options.why: Arousal matters for any behavior, but detecting and correcting drift in temperature or water is the hypothalamus’s job.

items.stem: The hypothalamus corrects drift in the body’s internal conditions in two ways. How do the two differ?

options.text: One is behavioral, driving the animal to act, as in seeking water; the other is physiological, through pituitary hormones released into the blood.
options.why: Correct. The pituitary gland hangs below the hypothalamus and releases hormones that reach the rest of the body.

options.text: One is behavioral, through pituitary hormones released into the blood; the other is physiological, driving the animal to seek out water.
options.why: That swaps the two. Seeking water is the behavioral correction; the pituitary’s hormones are the physiological one.

options.text: One is fast, through nerves from the hypothalamus that trigger reflexes; the other is slow, through norepinephrine that raises the animal’s arousal.
options.why: Norepinephrine comes mostly from a hindbrain cluster and sets arousal. The hypothalamus’s two routes are behavior and the pituitary’s hormones.

options.text: One is learned, through reward signals from the dopamine clusters; the other is innate, through pattern generators in the hindbrain.
options.why: Neither route is described that way. One correction works through behavior, and the other through hormones in the blood.

items.stem: Where do the basal ganglia sit, and what reaches their input stage, the striatum?

options.text: Deep in the forebrain, wrapped around its sides; the striatum receives signals from almost the whole pallium and the thalamus, with dopamine fibers among them.
options.why: Correct. The dopamine fibers from the midbrain’s two clusters arrive in the striatum alongside the signals from the pallium and the thalamus.

options.text: In the roof of the midbrain, behind the forebrain; the striatum receives maps of the space around the animal, built from the eyes and ears and held in register.
options.why: Maps held in register belong to the tectum, in the roof of the midbrain. The basal ganglia are in the forebrain.

options.text: At the base of the forebrain, below the thalamus; the striatum receives hormones from the pituitary and signals about how far each internal condition has drifted.
options.why: That describes the hypothalamus and its link to the pituitary. The striatum’s input comes from the pallium and the thalamus, with dopamine fibers.

options.text: Along the midline of the brainstem, in a series of clusters; the striatum receives rhythms from the pattern generators of the spinal cord.
options.why: A series of clusters along the brainstem midline is where the serotonin neurons sit. The basal ganglia are deep in the forebrain.

items.stem: Module 5 separated habits, which run off automatically, from goal-directed actions, which depend on what the animal currently wants. How does the chapter map the two onto the striatum?

options.text: They map onto different parts of it, with habits leaning toward one end and goal-directed action toward the other.
options.why: Correct. The distinction drawn in Module 5 has an address: two ends of the same input stage.

options.text: They share one part of it, and differ in how much dopamine arrives in that part while each of them is being performed.
options.why: The chapter maps habits and goal-directed action onto different parts of the striatum, not onto one part with different dopamine levels.

options.text: Habits map onto the striatum, while goal-directed action is handled entirely in the pallium, outside the basal ganglia.
options.why: Both map onto the striatum, at different ends of it.

options.text: Goal-directed action maps onto the striatum, while habits move out to the cerebellum once they become automatic.
options.why: Habits are not moved to the cerebellum. Both kinds of action map onto the striatum, at its two ends.

items.stem: What is the amygdala?

options.text: A cluster of nuclei at the front and base of the forebrain that evaluates what matters, quickly, before much else has happened.
options.why: Correct. Part of the address of valence is here: some of its neurons respond to good outcomes and others to bad ones.

options.text: A cluster of cells at the base of the forebrain that keeps temperature, water balance and blood sugar near each of their set points.
options.why: That describes the hypothalamus. The amygdala evaluates what matters rather than holding internal conditions near set points.

options.text: The input stage of the basal ganglia, where signals from the pallium arrive and the dopamine fibers meet them.
options.why: That is the striatum. The amygdala is a separate cluster of nuclei at the front and base of the forebrain.

options.text: A structure deep in the forebrain that stores frightening memories and produces the feeling of being afraid.
options.why: This is a common belief, but the chapter describes quick evaluation of what matters, good or bad. The circuits that produce a defensive response are not the ones that produce the feeling of fear.

items.stem: What is the name for the cluster of nuclei at the front and base of the forebrain that quickly evaluates what matters, with some of its neurons tuned to good outcomes and others to bad ones?

options.text: Amygdala.
options.why: Correct. Its good-tuned and bad-tuned neurons are intermingled in the same tissue.

options.text: Hypothalamus.
options.why: The hypothalamus sits at the base of the forebrain too, but it keeps internal conditions near their set points.

options.text: Striatum.
options.why: The striatum is the input stage of the basal ganglia, where signals from the pallium and the dopamine fibers arrive.

options.text: Thalamus.
options.why: The thalamus sits above the hypothalamus, and almost everything that reaches the pallium passes through it.

items.stem: Researchers record from many neurons in one small patch of a rat’s amygdala, first while the rat receives a sweet reward and then while it receives a mild shock. What does the chapter lead us to expect?

options.text: Some neurons respond selectively to the reward and others to the shock, intermingled in the same patch of tissue.
options.why: Correct. That is the literal form of the valence claim: populations tuned to good outcomes and to bad ones, mixed together in the same tissue.

options.text: The reward neurons and the shock neurons sit in separate subregions of the patch, one for good outcomes and one for bad ones.
options.why: This is the picture the chapter’s wording rules out. The two populations are intermingled in the same tissue, not divided into a good region and a bad one.

options.text: Nearly all the neurons respond to the shock, since the amygdala is the part of the brain concerned with threats rather than rewards.
options.why: The amygdala is part of the address of valence, good as well as bad. Some of its populations respond selectively to good outcomes.

options.text: Nearly all the neurons respond to both outcomes equally, since the amygdala tracks how strong an event is and not whether it is good.
options.why: Responding to whatever is salient is one job the amygdala has been credited with, but the chapter’s valence claim is that separate populations respond selectively to good and to bad outcomes.

items.stem: What can the chapter say about a lamprey’s amygdala, and how does that compare with what it can say about the lamprey’s selection circuitry?

options.text: Whether it has an amygdala-like region is not settled, so the amygdala claim covers jawed vertebrates; its selection circuit matches a mammal’s part for part.
options.why: Correct. The two claims carry different weight. Reptiles, birds and jawed fishes have an amygdala-like region; for the lamprey the question is open, while its selection circuit is not in doubt.

options.text: It clearly lacks both, since an amygdala and a selection circuit each arose with the jawed fishes, after the lamprey’s lineage had split from theirs.
options.why: The lamprey has basal ganglia matching a mammal’s part for part, and whether it lacks an amygdala-like region is not settled.

options.text: It has both, each matching a mammal’s part for part, since reptiles, birds and jawed fishes all have an amygdala-like region with similar circuitry of their own.
options.why: What reptiles, birds and jawed fishes have does not settle the lamprey. The chapter restricts its amygdala claim to jawed vertebrates.

options.text: It has an amygdala-like region matching a mammal’s, but whether it has selection circuitry of the mammalian kind is not settled.
options.why: That swaps the hedge. The selection circuit is the part that matches a mammal’s, and the amygdala is the part that is not settled.

items.stem: In the lab’s tree activity, a student places the card for an amygdala-like region at the root of all the vertebrates, the lamprey included. How does the reveal treat that placement?

options.text: As neither right nor wrong: the key’s ring is solid on the jawed-vertebrate branch and dashed at the root, as the question is open.
options.why: Correct. The dashed ring marks a question that is not settled, which is why the root placement is shown in amber rather than struck out.

options.text: As wrong: the key places the card with the mammals, since an amygdala-like region is a late mammalian addition to the forebrain.
options.why: Reptiles, birds and jawed fishes have an amygdala-like region too, so the card does not belong with the mammals.

options.text: As right: the key places the card at the root, since the lamprey has an amygdala-like region matching a mammal’s part for part.
options.why: Matching a mammal’s part for part is true of the lamprey’s selection circuit. Whether it has an amygdala-like region is not settled.

options.text: As wrong: the key places the card on the jawed-vertebrate branch alone, since the lamprey is known to lack an amygdala-like region altogether.
options.why: The key’s solid ring is on the jawed-vertebrate branch, but the lamprey is not known to lack one. The question is open, so the root placement is not marked wrong.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the vertebrate nervous system has circuits dedicated to single behaviors near its bottom but shares machinery among behaviors higher up. Name at least two of the dedicated behaviors.
items.answer: In the hindbrain and spinal cord, dedicated circuitry for a particular behavior really does exist. Breathing has its own pattern generator, and so do chewing, swallowing and locomotion. Each of these behaviors is stereotyped, and each has to keep running while everything else changes, so it pays to give each a circuit of its own. That is the keep-going half of the conflict between keeping going and changing course, built into anatomy. Higher up, actions are chosen rather than generated. Behaviors like walking and eating compete for the same body, so there the arrangement is shared machinery, with something to select which action is released.
rubric: Names at least two of breathing, chewing, swallowing and locomotion as having pattern generators of their own.
Says these behaviors are stereotyped.
Says they must keep running while everything else changes, as the keep-going half of the conflict with changing course.
Says that higher up actions are chosen rather than generated, by shared machinery with something to select among the options.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, say where the dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine that reach so much of the brain come from, and what the three sources have in common.
items.answer: The dopamine neurons sit in two clusters in the midbrain, and their fibers run forward into the striatum and the pallium. The serotonin neurons sit in a series of clusters along the midline of the brainstem, reaching back into the hindbrain. Most of the norepinephrine comes from one small cluster of cells in the hindbrain, whose fibers reach nearly the whole brain. All three sources are small and old, and positioned to reach almost everything. So the brain’s broad projections start in a few little places.
rubric: Places the dopamine neurons in two clusters in the midbrain, with fibers to the striatum and the pallium.
Places the serotonin neurons in clusters along the midline of the brainstem.
Places most of the norepinephrine in one small hindbrain cluster whose fibers reach nearly the whole brain.
Says the three sources are small and old and reach almost everything, so the broad projections start in a few small places.

items.stem: On a hot day, a dog pants less once it has had a long drink and lain down in the shade. In a short paragraph, use the chapter’s account of the hypothalamus to say what is being regulated and the two ways it is corrected, and name the general term for this.
items.answer: The dog’s body temperature and water balance are internal conditions that the hypothalamus keeps near their set points. The hypothalamus has cells that detect how far each condition has drifted and circuits that act to correct it. Some of the correction is behavioral: the drift drives the dog to look for water and to move into the shade. Some is physiological, working through the pituitary gland below the hypothalamus, which releases hormones into the blood that reach the rest of the body. Keeping internal conditions within limits like this is homeostasis.
rubric: Identifies temperature or water balance as an internal condition held near a set point by the hypothalamus.
Says the hypothalamus detects drift and acts to correct it.
Gives the behavioral correction, such as seeking water or shade.
Gives the physiological correction, through pituitary hormones released into the blood.
Names the general term, homeostasis.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, say what the amygdala does, what makes the chapter’s valence claim about it “more literal than one might expect”, and why the chapter’s claim about the amygdala is narrower than its claim about the lamprey’s selection circuitry.
items.answer: The amygdala is a cluster of nuclei at the front and base of the forebrain that evaluates what matters, quickly, before much else has happened. Its valence claim is literal because populations of amygdala neurons respond selectively to good outcomes and other populations to bad ones, intermingled in the same tissue. Reptiles, birds and jawed fishes have an amygdala-like region with similar circuitry, but whether a lamprey has one is not settled, so the claim is about jawed vertebrates. The lamprey’s selection circuitry, by contrast, matches a mammal’s part for part, so that claim needs no such restriction.
rubric: Says the amygdala evaluates what matters quickly.
Says separate populations respond to good and to bad outcomes.
Says those populations are intermingled in the same tissue, not in separate regions.
Says whether a lamprey has an amygdala-like region is not settled, so the claim covers jawed vertebrates.
Contrasts the lamprey’s selection circuitry, which matches a mammal’s part for part.

items.stem: A fish’s tectum registers a flicker at a particular position off to its left. What does the tectum do with that position?

options.text: It turns the fish toward it: the eyes, the head and the whole body.
options.why: Correct. The tectum’s job with a position on its map is to orient the animal toward that place.

options.text: It stores the position as a memory, so that the fish can return to the same place on a later day.
options.why: Remembering places is a different capacity, and the chapter does not give it to the tectum. What the tectum does with a position is turn the animal toward it.

options.text: It turns the fish away from it, since anything unexpected off to one side is treated as a threat.
options.why: Responding to a threat is closer to the defensive patterns the periaqueductal gray organizes. The tectum orients the animal toward what appears on its map.

options.text: It passes the position up to the pallium, which then decides whether the fish should look toward it or not.
options.why: The tectum does not wait on the pallium to orient. It turns the eyes, head and body toward the position itself.

pools.title: The Pallium, What Came Later, and Two Halves
pools.covers: reading §6.3.4, §6.3.5, §6.3.6 · lecture 6.3 slides pallium_and_thalamus, what_came_later, two_halves · lab Specimens, Tree

items.stem: Every vertebrate has a pallium, the roof of the forebrain. How does a lamprey’s pallium compare with a mammal’s?

options.text: The lamprey’s is thin, with three layers; the mammal’s grew enormously and acquired six layers, which is the neocortex.
options.why: Correct. The structure is the same one, and what it is made of differs. Its six-layered mammalian form is what the word neocortex names.

options.text: The lamprey has none; a pallium first appears in mammals, where it grew enormously and acquired its six layers, the neocortex.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, the lamprey included. What arrived with the mammals is the six-layered form.

options.text: The lamprey’s has six layers like the mammal’s, but it is far smaller, and so the name neocortex is kept for the mammal’s.
options.why: A lamprey’s pallium has three layers. The six layers are the mammalian form.

options.text: The two are built alike, three thin layers in each, and differ in size, the mammal’s having grown enormously larger.
options.why: The mammalian pallium did grow enormously, but it also acquired six layers. The difference is in what it is made of, not only in size.

items.stem: Recent experiments suggest that a lamprey’s pallium has output cells reaching the basal ganglia, the tectum, the brainstem and the spinal cord, much as a mammal’s does. How firmly does the chapter hold that resemblance?

options.text: As a promising result rather than a settled one, since the evidence is recent and comes largely from one laboratory.
options.why: Correct. The chapter hedges its most attention-getting lamprey claim at once. The resemblance may well hold, but it has not yet been confirmed widely enough to be treated as settled.

options.text: As settled beyond reasonable doubt, since the same result has been found in lampreys, hagfishes and every jawed fish that has been tested.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite about the evidence: it is recent and comes largely from one laboratory.

options.text: As disproved, since a lamprey’s pallium is too thin to contain output cells and receives smell alone, with no other input.
options.why: A lamprey’s pallium is thin, with three layers, but the chapter does not treat the result as disproved. It holds it as promising.

options.text: As settled for the lamprey’s inputs but doubtful for its outputs, since recent work confirms its visual signals and not its output cells.
options.why: The chapter’s hedge covers the arrangement as a whole, inputs and outputs alike. It does not split them.

items.stem: According to the recent evidence the chapter reports, what does a lamprey’s pallium already send out, and what does it already take in?

options.text: It sends output cells to the basal ganglia, tectum, brainstem and cord, and takes in vision relayed through the thalamus and smell arriving directly.
options.why: Correct. Even in a lamprey, the pallium already has the outputs and inputs of a sheet that receives signals from the senses and sends commands down.

options.text: It sends output only to the basal ganglia, and takes in smell relayed through the thalamus and vision arriving directly from the retina.
options.why: That swaps the two inputs. Vision arrives by way of the thalamus, and smell arrives directly. The outputs also reach far past the basal ganglia.

options.text: It sends no output of its own, and takes in every sense by way of the thalamus, which does the work of commanding the body instead.
options.why: The lamprey’s pallium already has output cells reaching the brainstem and the spinal cord, and smell reaches it without passing through the thalamus.

options.text: It sends output to the cerebellum alone, and takes in touch and hearing through the tectum, which relays its maps of the space around the animal up to the forebrain roof.
options.why: A lamprey lacks a cerebellum of the jawed kind, and the outputs the chapter reports go to the basal ganglia, tectum, brainstem and cord.

items.stem: Three words are in play for the roof of the forebrain. How does the chapter use pallium, neocortex and cortex?

options.text: Pallium is the structure in any vertebrate, neocortex is its six-layered mammalian form, and cortex alone is loose usage for the neocortex.
options.why: Correct. The convention keeps one word for the structure every vertebrate has and another for its mammalian form.

options.text: Cortex is the structure in any vertebrate, pallium is its six-layered mammalian form, and neocortex is loose usage for the pallium of birds.
options.why: That scrambles the three words. Pallium is the general word, and neocortex is the mammalian six-layered form.

options.text: Neocortex is the structure in any vertebrate, pallium is the three-layered form in fishes, and cortex is the six-layered form in mammals.
options.why: Neocortex is the mammalian form, not the general one. Pallium is the word for the structure in any vertebrate.

options.text: Pallium, neocortex and cortex are three names for one structure, and the chapter uses them interchangeably for every vertebrate.
options.why: The chapter separates the words deliberately, and it does not apply cortex to a fish.

items.stem: A student’s lab report describes stimulating “the cortex of a trout”. How would the chapter’s convention phrase the same thing?

options.text: Stimulating the trout’s pallium, since the chapter keeps the word cortex for the neocortex and does not apply it to a fish.
options.why: Correct. A trout has a pallium, as every vertebrate does. Cortex on its own is loose usage for the mammalian neocortex.

options.text: Stimulating the trout’s neocortex, since every vertebrate’s pallium becomes a neocortex once it has more than three layers.
options.why: The neocortex is the six-layered mammalian form. A fish’s pallium is not a neocortex.

options.text: Stimulating the trout’s tectum, since a fish has no forebrain roof and handles everything in the roof of its midbrain instead.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium. The tectum is a different structure, the roof of the midbrain.

options.text: Stimulating the trout’s cortex, since the chapter treats cortex as loose usage for the forebrain roof of any vertebrate, fishes included.
options.why: The chapter’s convention says cortex is loose usage for the neocortex, and this chapter does not apply it to a fish.

items.stem: In the lab’s tree activity, one card reads “a pallium” and another reads “a six-layered pallium (neocortex)”. Where does the key place the card that reads “a pallium”?

options.text: On the branch at the root of the vertebrates, the lamprey included, since every vertebrate has a pallium.
options.why: Correct. The lamprey has a pallium, thin and three-layered, so the card belongs where the lamprey joins the rest. The six-layered card is the one that belongs with the mammals.

options.text: On the branch leading to the mammals, since the pallium is the part of the forebrain that grew enormously in them.
options.why: This is the trap the activity is built around. The mammals’ card is the six-layered pallium, the neocortex; a pallium itself is in every vertebrate.

options.text: On the branch leading to the jawed vertebrates, since the pallium arrived with the jawed fishes, together with the cerebellum.
options.why: The cerebellum arrived with or shortly before the jawed fishes. The pallium is older, and the lamprey already has one.

options.text: On the branches leading to the birds and the mammals separately, since the forebrain roof grows largest in those two lineages.
options.why: The forebrain roof does grow largest in birds and mammals, but growing large is not arising. The lamprey already has a pallium.

items.stem: Where is the thalamus, and what passes through it?

options.text: It sits above the hypothalamus, in the middle of the forebrain, and almost everything that reaches the pallium passes through it.
options.why: Correct. The thalamus is the gate on the way into the pallium, for nearly all of what arrives there.

options.text: It sits below the hypothalamus, at the very base of the forebrain, and the hormones of the pituitary pass through it into the blood.
options.why: The pituitary hangs below the hypothalamus. The thalamus sits above the hypothalamus, and signals bound for the pallium pass through it.

options.text: It sits in the roof of the midbrain, and the maps of the space around the animal pass through it on their way to the eyes.
options.why: The roof of the midbrain is the tectum. The thalamus is in the forebrain, above the hypothalamus.

options.text: It sits deep in the forebrain, wrapped around its sides, and every proposed action passes through it to be released or held back.
options.why: Releasing one action and holding back the others is the basal ganglia’s job. The thalamus is where their output returns on its way back up.

items.stem: The basal ganglia and the cerebellum each work on signals that start in the pallium, and each sends its result back up. Through which structure do those loops return?

options.text: Through the thalamus, which relays the output of the basal ganglia and the cerebellum back up toward the pallium.
options.why: Correct. The thalamus is where the loops return. It relays both structures’ output back up.

options.text: Through the hypothalamus, which relays the output of the basal ganglia and the cerebellum into the blood by way of the pituitary.
options.why: The hypothalamus works through the pituitary’s hormones. The loops of the basal ganglia and the cerebellum return through the thalamus.

options.text: Through the tectum, which turns the output of the basal ganglia and the cerebellum into a turn of the eyes and head.
options.why: The tectum turns the animal toward a position. It is not where these loops return.

options.text: Through the striatum, which receives the output of the basal ganglia and the cerebellum and sends it up to the pallium.
options.why: The striatum is the input stage of the basal ganglia, where signals from the pallium arrive. The loops return through the thalamus.

items.stem: Because almost everything that reaches the pallium passes through the thalamus, a student calls the thalamus a passive relay station, a switchboard that forwards signals unchanged. What does the chapter say?

options.text: The thalamus is not a passive relay station, although what it does to the signals it passes is left to later modules.
options.why: Correct. The chapter denies the passive picture and defers the positive account, so it says what the thalamus is not before saying what it is.

options.text: The student is right: the thalamus is a relay station that forwards signals unchanged, which is why the chapter says nothing more about what it does to them.
options.why: The chapter says outright that a thalamus is not a passive relay station. It defers what the thalamus does, not whether it does anything.

options.text: The thalamus is not a relay at all, since almost every signal bound for the pallium reaches it directly and never passes through the thalamus.
options.why: Almost everything that reaches the pallium does pass through the thalamus. The correction is to “passive”, not to “relay”.

options.text: The thalamus is a passive relay for vision and an active one for smell, since smell is the one sense the thalamus reshapes on its way to the pallium.
options.why: Smell reaches a lamprey’s pallium directly, without passing through the thalamus. The chapter makes no sense-by-sense split.

items.stem: Where does the chapter place the hippocampus?

options.text: As an old region of the pallium, curled along its medial edge, with what it does left to later modules.
options.why: Correct. The chapter names the hippocampus and leaves it alone. Its role is the subject of Modules 9 and 10.

options.text: As a part of the basal ganglia, wrapped around the sides of the forebrain, where it helps settle which action is released.
options.why: The basal ganglia are wrapped around the sides of the forebrain. The hippocampus is a region of the pallium.

options.text: As a structure in the roof of the midbrain, next to the tectum, where it helps turn the animal toward remembered places.
options.why: The roof of the midbrain is the tectum. The hippocampus is in the forebrain, part of the pallium.

options.text: As a recent region added to the mammalian neocortex, curled along its outer surface, and missing from every other vertebrate.
options.why: The chapter calls the hippocampus an old region of the pallium, not a recent mammalian addition.

items.stem: Set a lamprey’s brain beside a mouse’s. What does the chapter say has changed between the two?

options.text: The same parts are there in the same order, with one exception, and what changed is mostly proportion and number.
options.why: Correct. One plan runs through both brains. The differences are mostly in how big each part is and how many copies of it there are.

options.text: The mouse’s brain has a different set of parts in a different order, since half a billion years of change rebuilt it from scratch.
options.why: The parts and their order are the same, with a single exception. What changed is mostly proportion and number.

options.text: Nothing has changed: the two brains have the same parts in the same proportions, and differ only in their overall size.
options.why: The proportions differ markedly, and one part is missing from the lamprey in the form jawed vertebrates have it.

options.text: The same parts are there, but their order along the brain is reversed, with the forebrain at the back in the lamprey.
options.why: The order is the same in both, from the hindbrain at the back to the forebrain at the front.

items.stem: A cerebellum of the jawed kind is found in sharks, bony fishes, birds and mammals, but not in lampreys. What does the chapter conclude about its history?

options.text: It arrived with or shortly before the jawed fishes, and then enlarged independently in sharks, in bony fishes, in birds and in mammals.
options.why: Correct. The cerebellum arrived after the lamprey’s lineage had separated, and then grew larger separately in four groups.

options.text: It was present in the common ancestor of all vertebrates and was lost in the lamprey’s lineage, which split away before the jawed fishes and had little need for it.
options.why: Loss is not what the chapter concludes. The cerebellum arose with or shortly before the jawed fishes, after the lamprey’s lineage had separated.

options.text: It arose in mammals and was added later to birds, fishes and sharks, each of which acquired it from the lineage before it.
options.why: Sharks and fishes had a cerebellum long before mammals existed, and no lineage acquires a part from another.

options.text: It arose once in the common ancestor of birds and mammals, and enlarged in that single lineage toward its largest size in mammals.
options.why: Sharks and bony fishes have a cerebellum too, and it enlarged independently in all four groups rather than in one line.

items.stem: A mammal’s indirect pathway through the basal ganglia runs through more stops than a lamprey’s. What does the chapter say accounts for the difference?

options.text: In mammals the output nucleus of the basal ganglia divided into two, where a lamprey’s remains a single nucleus.
options.why: Correct. The indirect route passes through the output stage, so an output stage split in two adds a stop.

options.text: In mammals the cerebellum was inserted into the indirect pathway, adding the stops that a lamprey’s pathway lacks.
options.why: The cerebellum’s loops return through the thalamus. The extra stops come from the output nucleus dividing in two.

options.text: In mammals the indirect pathway was added for the first time, since a lamprey’s basal ganglia have a direct pathway alone.
options.why: The lamprey’s basal ganglia already have both a direct and an indirect pathway. What differs is how many stops the indirect one passes through.

options.text: In mammals the striatum began to receive dopamine, which a lamprey’s striatum does not, and each dopamine input adds a stop.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter says a lamprey’s striatum lacks dopamine. The extra stops come from the output nucleus dividing in two.

items.stem: After the lamprey’s lineage separated from the one leading to mammals, which changes of number happened in the forebrain?

options.text: More basal ganglia units were added, and the front of the forebrain went from about six distinct cell groups in a lamprey to about sixty-six in a rat.
options.why: Correct. Both are changes of number: more copies of the same kind of selection unit, and many more distinct cell groups at the front of the forebrain.

options.text: The basal ganglia were reduced to a single unit, and the front of the forebrain went from about sixty-six distinct cell groups in a lamprey to about six in a rat.
options.why: That reverses both changes. Basal ganglia units were added, and the rat is the one with sixty-six cell groups.

options.text: The number of basal ganglia units stayed the same, and the front of the forebrain kept the same dozen or so cell groups, each of them simply growing larger.
options.why: Number is one of the things that changed. Units were added, and six cell groups became sixty-six.

options.text: The basal ganglia appeared for the first time, since a lamprey has none, and the front of the forebrain gained its first distinct cell groups in the rat.
options.why: A lamprey already has basal ganglia matching a mammal’s part for part, and six distinct cell groups at the front of its forebrain.

items.stem: When the mammalian pallium acquired its six layers, what else came with them that a lamprey’s pallium does not have?

options.text: Kinds of inhibitory neuron that are absent from the lamprey’s pallium.
options.why: Correct. The six layers came along with new kinds of inhibitory neuron, which a lamprey does not have.

options.text: Output cells projecting down to the brainstem and the spinal cord, absent from the lamprey’s pallium.
options.why: The lecture points out that the output cell sending commands down to the brainstem and cord is present in the lamprey, the reptile and the mammal alike.

options.text: Visual signals relayed through the thalamus, which the lamprey’s pallium receives from the tectum instead.
options.why: A lamprey’s pallium already receives visual signals relayed through the thalamus.

options.text: A direct input of smell, which reaches a lamprey’s forebrain through the thalamus.
options.why: Smell already reaches a lamprey’s pallium directly. The new arrivals in mammals were six layers and new kinds of inhibitory neuron.

items.stem: Many students expect every part of the brain to reach its most elaborate form in mammals. How does the tectum, the roof of the midbrain, compare across vertebrates?

options.text: It is already layered in a lamprey, and has more layers in fishes and birds than it does in mammals.
options.why: Correct. The lecture calls this the surprise that runs the other way: in the tectum the mammals are the less layered case.

options.text: It has no layers in a lamprey, gains a few in fishes and birds, and reaches its most layered form in mammals.
options.why: That is the mammalian peak the tectum contradicts. It is layered already in a lamprey, and more layered in fishes and birds than in mammals.

options.text: It is missing from a lamprey, which orients by comparing signals over time, and first appears in the jawed fishes.
options.why: The lamprey has a tectum that maps space and orients the animal. It is part of the plan from the start.

options.text: It is the same in every vertebrate, since the roof of the midbrain is one of the parts that has changed least since the lamprey.
options.why: The hindbrain and the hypothalamus changed little. The tectum’s layering differs across groups, with more layers in fishes and birds than in mammals.

items.stem: Across living vertebrates, brain size for a given body size varies about thirtyfold. Where does the chapter say the increases in relative brain size happened?

options.text: Independently, in some members of every major group: in sharks, in bony fishes, in birds and in mammals.
options.why: Correct. The thirtyfold range and the independent increases are one fact in two parts. Brains got bigger more than once.

options.text: Once, in the lineage leading to mammals, so that every mammal has a larger brain for its size than any other vertebrate.
options.why: Relative brain size increased independently in several groups, not once, and not only in mammals.

options.text: Once, in the common ancestor of birds and mammals, whose descendants all inherited the enlarged brain from it.
options.why: Sharks and bony fishes include large-brained members too. The increases happened separately in each group.

options.text: Gradually along a single line, from lampreys to fishes to amphibians to reptiles, and then to birds and mammals at the top.
options.why: That is the ladder the chapter rejects. The plan was elaborated many times over, in parallel.

items.stem: In the lab’s tree activity, one card reads “a large brain for its body size”. How many separate origins does the key give it?

options.text: Three separate origins, since relative brain size increased independently in several lineages rather than once.
options.why: Correct. The card cannot be placed once. The key marks three origins on this tree, and the reveal also names large-brained members of other groups, including sharks and bony fishes.

options.text: One origin, on the branch leading to the mammals, since large brains for their body size are a mammalian feature.
options.why: A single origin with the mammals is the ladder picture. The key uses three separate origins.

options.text: One origin, at the root of the vertebrates, since every vertebrate descends from an ancestor with a large brain for its size.
options.why: The key places no single ancestral origin. Brains got bigger more than once, in separate lineages.

options.text: Two separate origins, one with the birds and one with the mammals, since only warm-blooded animals have large brains for their size.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim about warm blood, and the reveal points past birds and mammals to sharks and bony fishes as well.

items.stem: A lineage evolves a larger brain for its body size. What does the chapter say such a brain generally has more of?

options.text: More distinct parts, rather than simply more of the same tissue.
options.why: Correct. Larger brains generally have more distinct parts, as in the front of the forebrain, where six cell groups became sixty-six.

options.text: More of the same tissue, with the same number of parts, each one scaled up to the new size.
options.why: That is the picture the chapter corrects. Larger brains generally have more distinct parts, not just more of the same.

options.text: Larger neurons, with the number of neurons and parts left unchanged.
options.why: The chapter’s point is about parts, not about the size of individual neurons.

options.text: More folding of its surface, with the number of parts left unchanged.
options.why: Folding is a matter of how a sheet is packed, not how many parts there are. Larger brains generally have more distinct parts.

items.stem: A museum case lines up brains from a lamprey, a shark, a frog, a lizard, a bird and a mouse, labeled as steps from “primitive” to “advanced”. What does the chapter say is wrong with that arrangement?

options.text: The vertebrate plan was elaborated many times over, in parallel, rather than climbed once toward mammals.
options.why: Correct. Size increased independently in sharks, bony fishes, birds and mammals, and birds built a large pallium in their own way. There is no single climb for the case to show.

options.text: Nothing, since each group in the case descends from the one before it, adding one new part at each step on the way to mammals.
options.why: Living groups do not descend from one another; they share common ancestors. And the additions came in parallel, not one step at a time.

options.text: The order is wrong, since birds have larger brains than mammals and belong at the top of the case instead of the mouse.
options.why: Reordering the case keeps the ladder. The chapter’s objection is to the ladder itself.

options.text: The case should show one brain only, since every vertebrate brain is identical in its parts and in their proportions.
options.why: The parts are the same, but the proportions differ markedly. What the chapter rejects is reading those differences as steps on one ladder.

items.stem: The lab’s true-scale view carries one line: size and folding evolved more than once. What does that mean for a strategy of identifying a brain by how large and how folded it is?

options.text: Size and folding are poor guides to relatedness, since distantly related lineages with big brains can arrive at similar size and folding on their own.
options.why: Correct. A feature that evolved more than once tells us about size or lifestyle rather than about descent, so it can make unrelated brains look alike.

options.text: Size and folding are the best guides to relatedness, since a feature shared by two brains was most likely inherited from their common ancestor.
options.why: The common-ancestor inference applies to parts shared by descent. A feature that evolved more than once can be shared without being inherited.

options.text: Size and folding show how old a lineage is, since lineages that split from ours earlier have had less time to grow and fold their brains.
options.why: Every living lineage has been evolving for exactly as long as ours. Size and folding do not measure age.

options.text: Size and folding pick out the primates, since a large, folded brain arose once in the primate lineage and nowhere else.
options.why: Large, folded brains arose in several lineages, including the dolphin’s, far from the primates. The line under the view says as much.

items.stem: Crows and parrots solve problems with a flexibility that rivals some mammals’. How is the bird pallium that supports this organized?

options.text: It is large, and organized in clusters rather than in layers.
options.why: Correct. The bird pallium is the clearest case of independent elaboration: large, supporting flexible behavior, and built in clusters.

options.text: It is large, and organized in six layers like the mammalian neocortex.
options.why: The six layers are the mammalian form. The bird pallium is organized in clusters rather than in layers.

options.text: It is thin, with the three layers of a lamprey’s pallium, and simply spread over a larger area.
options.why: The bird pallium is large and clustered, not a stretched three-layered sheet.

options.text: It is small, and the flexible behavior is handled instead by an enlarged cerebellum at the back of the brain.
options.why: The forebrain roof grows largest in birds and mammals. The bird pallium itself is large.

items.stem: Researchers have argued for decades over whether particular parts of the bird pallium correspond to particular parts of the mammalian neocortex. Why is the question so hard to settle?

options.text: Homology is hard to establish when two lineages have been separate for three hundred million years, and here they are also organized differently.
options.why: Correct. The bird pallium is a good illustration of how hard homology can be to establish across such a long separation, with clusters on one side and layers on the other.

options.text: It is not hard to settle; the matter was decided long ago, and the bird pallium is known to be a six-layered neocortex in another shape.
options.why: The chapter says the question has been argued for decades, and the bird pallium is organized in clusters, not six layers.

options.text: Birds have no pallium at all, so the comparison is between a mammalian structure and a bird structure that is not part of the forebrain roof.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, birds included. The dispute is about which parts of it correspond to which parts of the neocortex.

options.text: Birds and mammals are so closely related that their pallia are hard to tell apart, which makes any difference between them difficult to measure.
options.why: The difficulty runs the other way. Birds and mammals have been separate for three hundred million years, and their pallia look very different.

items.stem: What is lateralization?

options.text: A difference between what the left and right sides of a brain do.
options.why: Correct. The departures from symmetry that it names are real, widespread across vertebrate groups, and old.

options.text: A difference between what the front and back of a brain do.
options.why: The front-to-back plan is the one the chapter lays out part by part. Lateralization is about left and right.

options.text: The bundle of fibers that connects the two sides of a brain.
options.why: That describes a connection between the hemispheres, such as the corpus callosum. Lateralization is a difference in what the two sides do.

options.text: The mirror-image match between the two sides of most brain structures.
options.why: Most paired structures are near mirror images, but lateralization is the name for the departures from that symmetry.

items.stem: What is the general name for a difference between what the left and right sides of a brain do?

options.text: Lateralization.
options.why: Correct. The domestic chick is the case of it worked out in most detail.

options.text: Corpus callosum.
options.why: The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres in placental mammals. It is a bridge between the sides, not a difference between them.

options.text: Modularity.
