options.text: Separate structures, or a single network settling among constraints; which one an animal took is answered by looking at that animal.
options.why: Correct. Both solutions are real, and neither is the default. Which one an animal took is an empirical question about that animal.

options.text: Separate structures, or a single network settling among constraints; separate structures always win once an animal has enough neurons.
options.why: Having enough neurons makes division possible, not obligatory. The chapter leaves the choice to evidence about each animal.

options.text: Separate structures, or one general learning rule; the general rule wins in small animals and separate structures win in large ones.
options.why: The rival to separate structures is a network settling among constraints, and no size rule settles between them.

options.text: A single network settling among constraints, or no solution at all; animals that cannot resolve the conflict simply die out.
options.why: Separate structures are one of the two solutions the chapter keeps live, alongside the settling network.

items.stem: The chapter compares its caution about reading a demand off a brain’s arrangement with Module 2’s caution about adaptation. How does it describe the relation between the two cautions?

options.text: They are the same caution, arriving now from the inside of a brain rather than from the outside of an organism.
options.why: Correct. In both cases the form of a thing does not by itself tell us what it answers. Only the vantage point has changed.

options.text: They are opposite cautions, since adaptation explains a trait by its use while a brain is explained by its parts.
options.why: The chapter presents them as one caution, not two opposed ones.

options.text: The brain version is a weaker caution, since each brain structure can be traced to a single demand in a way whole-body traits cannot.
options.why: The chapter denies that a structure can be traced to a single demand. That denial is the caution.

options.text: The brain version replaces the one about adaptation, which no longer applies once brains are understood part by part.
options.why: The earlier caution still stands. The chapter meets it again from a new direction.

items.stem: What is the thesis the chapter was built around?

options.text: The structures are new, but the parts they are built from are not.
options.why: Correct. Vertebrates added structures given over largely to one job, built from material already in place before there were vertebrates.

options.text: The parts are new, but the structures they make up are ancient.
options.why: That reverses the thesis. The structures are the new thing, and the parts are old.

options.text: Both the structures and the parts are new, arising together with the first vertebrates.
options.why: The parts, from genes that mark position to learning rules, were in place before there were vertebrates.

options.text: Both the structures and the parts are ancient, and vertebrates only enlarged the brain that held them.
options.why: Vertebrates did add structures, such as a cerebellum with the jawed fishes. What is old is what they were built from.

items.stem: Which of these does the chapter say was already in place before there were vertebrates?

options.text: The rules by which a growth cone finds its way, and by which too many neurons are made and then reduced.
options.why: Correct. These developmental rules, along with the genes that mark position and the kinds of cells neurons are, are among the old parts.

options.text: A cerebellum that adjusts movements by learning from their errors, with climbing fibers carrying the error signal.
options.why: The cerebellum is one of the new structures. It arose with, or shortly before, the jawed fishes.

options.text: An output nucleus of the basal ganglia divided in two, which gives the indirect pathway its extra stops.
options.why: The output nucleus divided in two in mammals. That is a late change to the machinery, not an old part.

options.text: A six-layered pallium, laid down from the inside out, with its areas staked out by gradients.
options.why: Six layers are the mammalian form of the pallium, a late change to the machinery. The old parts are things like the genes that mark position and the rules a growth cone follows.

items.stem: The cerebellum and the basal ganglia are vertebrate structures, yet the chapter says the learning rules they use are old. What, then, do those two structures add?

options.text: A way of getting a particular signal delivered to a synapse, not a new kind of synapse.
options.why: Correct. The rules at the synapse were already there. What is new is the route that brings an error or a reward signal to it.

options.text: A new kind of synapse that can change its strength, which no earlier nervous system had.
options.why: Synapses that change with experience are much older than vertebrates; the worm of earlier modules learns.

options.text: A separate new learning rule for each structure, which is why the two structures learn differently.
options.why: The structures differ in what signal reaches their synapses, not in having new rules. The rules are old.

options.text: Nothing to do with learning at all, since both structures only relay signals between the pallium and the brainstem.
options.why: Both structures are sites of learning. What they add is delivery of a particular signal to the synapses there.

items.stem: Of all the parts of the vertebrate brain, which grew the most, and what did it become in mammals?

options.text: The pallium, which became a large, nearly uniform sheet running one kind of circuit, with the same six layers throughout.
options.why: Correct. The mammalian pallium runs one kind of circuit over and over across its whole extent.

options.text: The cerebellum, which became a large, folded structure running a different circuit for each kind of movement.
options.why: The cerebellum did enlarge in several lineages, but the part that grew most is the pallium.

options.text: The basal ganglia, which became a stack of many copies, one copy for each action a mammal can perform.
options.why: More basal ganglia units were added, but they are not one per action, and they are not what grew most.

options.text: The pallium, which became a patchwork of different circuits, each one built separately for the particular kind of signal that reaches it.
options.why: The right structure, but the wrong result. The striking thing about the mammalian sheet is that it is nearly uniform.

items.stem: A piece of mammalian cortex that receives signals from the eyes is compared with a piece that receives signals from the skin. What does the chapter lead us to expect about how the two pieces are built?

options.text: Both have the same six layers and run the same kind of circuit, although the signals arriving differ.
options.why: Correct. The sheet is nearly uniform, with the same six layers whether its signals come from the eyes, the skin or the ears.

options.text: Each has a layered structure suited to its own sense, with more layers where the arriving signals are more complex.
options.why: That is what one might expect, and it is not what the chapter reports. The layers are the same whatever the signals.

options.text: The piece for vision has six layers and the piece for touch has three, like the pallium of a lamprey.
options.why: Three layers describes the pallium of a lamprey or a reptile. Across the mammalian sheet the count is six.

options.text: Neither has layers, since the mammalian pallium is organized in clusters in the way a bird’s pallium is.
options.why: Clusters describe the bird pallium. The mammalian pallium is the six-layered form.

items.stem: Much is known about the mammalian cortical sheet. Which question about the sheet does the chapter treat as still open?

options.text: What the one kind of circuit repeated across the sheet actually computes.
options.why: Correct. Where the sheet is, what it is made of, how it is laid down and how its areas are staked out are all given. What its circuit computes is not.

options.text: Where the sheet sits in the brain and what kinds of cells the sheet is made of.
options.why: Both of these are given. What is missing is what the circuit computes.

options.text: How the sheet is laid down in its layers, from the inside out.
options.why: The inside-out building of the layers is described, with a neuron’s birthday setting its layer.

options.text: How the sheet’s areas are staked out by opposing gradients.
options.why: The gradients that stake out areas are described. What is left open is what the circuit computes.

items.stem: The mammalian cortical sheet does the same thing everywhere, to whatever signals reach it. What dilemma does that uniformity pose?

options.text: It is either doing something very general or doing nothing in particular, and what such a structure extracts from its signals is still open.
options.why: Correct. Both horns are live, and the chapter does not choose between them. The question it leaves is what a uniform sheet can extract from its input.

options.text: It is either a single structure or many separate structures, and imaging has now shown that it is really many structures working side by side.
options.why: The sheet is one structure with areas staked out by gradients. The dilemma is about what its one circuit does, not about how many structures it is.

options.text: It either learned its job or was built for its job, and its six uniform layers show that it was built for one job only.
options.why: Uniform layers are what make the sheet’s job puzzling. They do not settle it in either direction.

options.text: It either handles signals from the eyes or signals from the skin, and each area chooses between the two before birth by its layers.
options.why: Areas are staked out by gradients, and every area has the same six layers. The dilemma is about generality, not about which sense.

items.stem: On the lab’s bench, the amygdala was removed, and the animal was then trained and tested on the tone-and-shock task, the cue-and-food task and the lever task. What did the bench report?

options.text: Freezing to the tone and approach to the food cue both failed to be learned, and no result was reported for lever pressing.
options.why: Correct. Both cue tasks failed, one about a threat and one about food, in results found in the rat. The lever cell was gray, because the chapter reports no result for it.

options.text: Freezing to the tone failed to be learned, but approach to the food cue and lever pressing were both learned normally.
options.why: That is what calling the amygdala a fear center would predict. The food-cue approach failed too, because the amygdala is needed for learning about rewards.

options.text: Freezing to the tone and lever pressing both failed to be learned, while approach to the food cue was learned normally all the same.
options.why: The food task that failed was approach to the cue. The lever task produced no result at all, not a failure.

options.text: All three were learned, but the animal moved slowly and was hard to start in every task it was given.
options.why: Slow movement that is hard to start is what the bench showed after the dopamine clusters were removed, not the amygdala.

items.stem: After the amygdala was removed on the bench, the lever task showed a gray cell. A lab partner writes that the amygdala is therefore not involved in lever pressing. What is wrong with that conclusion?

options.text: The gray cell means the chapter reports no experiment for that case, which is a gap in the evidence, not a finding that the amygdala plays no part.
options.why: Correct. A gray cell is an honest gap. Since one capacity can draw on many structures, silence about a structure is not evidence that it is uninvolved.

options.text: The gray cell means the lever was pressed only at the untrained rate, which shows that the amygdala is needed for lever pressing after all, rather than uninvolved.
options.why: A gray cell carries no number and no result. Reading it as a failure is the same mistake as reading it as uninvolvement.

options.text: The gray cell means the animal could not survive the removal, so no task at all could be tested after the amygdala was gone.
options.why: The refusal on grounds of survival was for the hindbrain, and it was shown in red. The animal without an amygdala was tested on the two cue tasks.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since a structure the bench reports nothing for was recorded as inactive during that task.
options.why: A gray cell is not an inactive structure, whether in a recording or after a removal. It marks a case the chapter does not report.

items.stem: On the lab’s bench, the periaqueductal gray was stimulated. What did the result show, and what could it not show?

options.text: The whole defensive pattern appeared, freezing or fleeing with a reduced response to pain, but nothing in it could show that the animal felt afraid.
options.why: Correct. The bench reads out behavior, activity and pain response, and nothing on it measures what the animal feels. The circuits for a defensive response are not those for the feeling.

options.text: Freezing appeared alone, as a fragment of the defensive pattern, which showed that the structure handles only one part of defense.
options.why: The stimulation produced the whole pattern, not a fragment of it. That is what makes the result striking.

options.text: The whole defensive pattern appeared, and the reduced response to pain, coming along with the freezing or the fleeing, showed that the animal also felt afraid.
options.why: A reduced pain response is a readout of behavior, not of feeling. Nothing on the bench, and no method from Module 2, measures what the animal feels.

options.text: The head and eyes turned toward one point in space, which showed that the structure holds a map of the space around the animal.
options.why: Turning toward a point is what stimulating the tectum produced, with the direction set by where the tectum was stimulated.

items.stem: On the lab’s bench, the pallium was recorded during the open-field task, and then the neocortex was removed and the open field was run again. What did the two results show, taken together?

options.text: The pallium was active in the open field, yet the animal walked, groomed and explored without it: its activity was a correlation, not a sign of need.
options.why: Correct. Recording is correlational and removal tests necessity, so the two results answer different questions and do not conflict. The removal result was found in the cat, with the basal ganglia intact.

options.text: The pallium was silent in the open field, and removing it stopped the walking and grooming: the two methods agreed that it is needed for movement in general.
options.why: The pallium was recorded active in every task, and the animal kept moving without it. Neither half of this matches the bench.

options.text: The pallium was active in the open field, and removing it stopped all exploring: the recording and the removal agreed that it is what runs exploration in that task.
options.why: The recording was right, but the removal left exploring intact. That mismatch is the lesson about reading a job off a recording.

options.text: The pallium was silent in the open field, and removing it left behavior unchanged: the two methods agreed that it takes no part in any of the bench’s tasks.
options.why: The pallium was active in every task. Activity without necessity is not the same as taking no part.

items.stem: The lab’s bench offered four methods: recording from a structure, removing it, stimulating it, and silencing one delivery route during training only. In a short paragraph, say what kind of claim each method supports, and illustrate at least two of them with a result the bench gave.
items.answer: Recording is correlational: it shows that a structure is active during a task, not that the task needs it. The pallium was recorded active in every task, yet removing the neocortex left walking, grooming and exploring in the open field intact. Removing a structure tests necessity: without an amygdala, the animal learned neither to freeze to a tone paired with shock nor to approach a light paired with food. Stimulating tests sufficiency: stimulating the periaqueductal gray produced the whole defensive pattern, freezing or fleeing with a reduced response to pain. Silencing a route only during training separates learning from the ability to perform. With the dopamine fibers to the striatum silenced during training and restored for the test, the animal moved normally but pressed the lever no more than an untrained animal. Removing the dopamine clusters outright could not show that, because it made every movement slow and hard to start.
rubric: Says recording is correlational, showing activity but not need.
Says removal tests necessity and stimulation tests sufficiency.
Says silencing a route during training only separates what was learned from the ability to move or perform at test.
Gives at least two correct bench results, each matched to its method.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe how the computational and implementational levels behaved differently across vertebrate history, give two examples of the implementational change, and say what the pattern implies about inferring a demand from a brain’s arrangement.
items.answer: The computational level has barely moved. The demands on a Cambrian animal are the demands on a lamprey and on a mouse, and they would be the demands on anything that moves through a world with other animals in it. The implementational level, meanwhile, has been rebuilt over and over. A cerebellum arrived with the jawed fishes, and the output nucleus of the basal ganglia divided in two. The pallium acquired six layers in one lineage and clusters in another, and the whole plan was scaled up independently in sharks, bony fishes, birds and mammals. So a problem can stand still for half a billion years while the machinery that answers it is remade several times. It follows that one demand can be met by many arrangements. Finding an arrangement therefore does not tell us which demand it answers.
rubric: States that the computational level, the demands, has barely changed from the Cambrian to the mouse.
States that the implementational level has been rebuilt repeatedly.
Gives two correct examples of that rebuilding, such as the cerebellum arriving, the output nucleus dividing, six layers against clusters, or independent enlargement.
Concludes that finding an arrangement does not reveal which demand it answers, keeping the direction from arrangement to demand.

items.stem: A friend calls the amygdala “the brain’s fear center”. In a short paragraph, explain what is right in the idea behind that phrase and what is wrong with the phrase itself, using the two findings the chapter gives.
items.answer: What is right is that the amygdala drives the cascade of a frightening moment: the heart rate, the freezing, the turn of attention. That still holds. What is wrong is two steps taken beyond it, from driving the threat response to being where fear lives, and from one region to one function. First, the amygdala is also needed for learning about rewards. Its reward-tuned and threat-tuned neurons are mixed together in the same tissue, so this is one structure with more than one job, not two neighboring structures. Second, the circuits that produce a defensive response are not the circuits that produce the feeling of being afraid. For that reason the researcher who did most to establish the amygdala’s role in threat rejects the phrase.
rubric: Keeps the claim that the amygdala drives the threat cascade, without calling it withdrawn.
Names the amygdala’s role in learning about rewards.
Says the reward and threat neurons are intermingled in the same tissue, so this is not two neighboring structures.
Says the circuits for a defensive response are not those for the feeling of being afraid.
Identifies at least one failing step: response to feeling, or one region to one function.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain the chapter’s claim that the vertebrate brain’s structures are new but its parts are old. Give at least two examples of old parts, and say what the cerebellum and the basal ganglia add.
items.answer: Vertebrates added structures given over largely to one job, but they built those structures from material that was already there. The genes that mark position along a body, the kinds of cells that neurons are, the rules by which a growth cone finds its way, and the rules by which too many neurons are made and then reduced were all in place before there were vertebrates. Even the learning rules are old. What the cerebellum and the basal ganglia add is not a new kind of synapse but a way of getting a particular signal delivered to one.
rubric: States that the structures are new and the parts are old.
Gives at least two correct old parts: position genes, neuron cell types, growth-cone rules, overproduce-and-compete rules, or learning rules.
Says these parts were in place before there were vertebrates.
Says the cerebellum and basal ganglia add delivery of a particular signal to a synapse, not a new kind of synapse.
